div.head: Examiner Saturday, December 5, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner Saturday, December 5, 1903.
ALWAYS IicDOUGALL'S Pateo SELF-RAISING FLOUR TH IT IS E BEST -FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
C I

There are many little details in connection with our garments which are apt to be over- looked by careless women, which, if accorded sufficient attention, would be found of great use and real importance. The girl who knows how to put away her dresses, etc., is not only always neat and smart in appearance, but is at the same time economical, for her be,longings wear much longer than they would if carelessly treated. Coats, to keep their shape, should always be hung up on a coat- hanger in the wardrobe if not required again that day ; or if shortly to be used again are neat disposed over the back of a chair. In no case ought a coat to be carelessly flung on a bed or chair, especially if it be at all

espeCially at this season of the year. The new lace scarves too, which are intended for draping about the decolletage, crossing and looping at the bacl,,the ends falling to the edge of the skirt, are likely to be much appreciated. These scarves are also being shewn in silk muslin, chiffon, and crêpe de chine. They are needless• to say, . much less expensive than the lace varieties, and quite as effective. MADGE.

A NEAT BLOUSE. damp, as in. this way it loses its smartness of cut and tit. Skirts also deserve due :attention • if expected to keep their look and avoid that objectionable draggled appearance that many develop after a time. • A tailor-made skirt should always be hung up on a skirt-hanger which is somewhat similar to that used fora coat, but with."he ends more depressed, as the skirt keeps in excellent shape and hangs in even folds. If a skirt-hailger is not used, it is best to hook the band Of the skirt and then hang it Up by the two loops inside the band. Blouses also should be hung up by two loops at the armholes ; or, if of a dressy description, be carefully stuffed with tissue paper and laid smoothly in a drawer. The .neat blouse sketched is of a simple vet smart and up-to-date mode, with strap.. pings fastened with small gilt buttons. A broad box-pleat finishes the front, under which the blouse is fastened. One of the pretty fancy flannels with an ornamental border would make up into a smart 'blouse of this description, the border being used for the strappings and box-pleat down the front. A cream flannel spotted with black and trimmed with black or cream lace treated
in the same fashion as the strappings wotild look very chic, while a bright red flannel finished with strappings of silk piped with _

black and worn ith -a white sioCk, collar and a smart black and red silk cravat would look cosy and prove exceedingly serviceable for morning wear. Yak lace is one of the most fashionable varieties used for trimming flannel or cloth blouse. Cloth blouse to be correctly worn should be of the same colour or tone of colour as the skirt worn with it, so that the two together give the effect of a complete costume without any patchiness or contrast. A most useful skirt for wear with all sorts and conditions of blouses is one of accordion-pleated voile- or cashmere, the latter being the most durable material. In my second sketch a pretty evening bodice is shown, worn in 'conjunction with a pleated and gauged skirt. The bodice is also of pleated material, simply arranged, and finished only by some sequined embroidery. A very useful frock in this style for dinner or home wear is fashioned of black glace silk 'accordion- pleated, trimmed with spark- ling sequined embroidery, finished by a narrow edging or piping of geranium red velvet, the front of the corsage having a large bow of the same brightly - tinted velvet,
((Jopyright.)

"I did not come as the walk was se lonely. Besides, I did not want to shock the propriety of your tame sheep a third time." The curate stirred his tea furiously. • The term "tame sheep" for his congregation seemed to him a sacrilege. "That wL.s very considerate of you, Miss Lee," he said.

"Yes, wasn't it ? " she agreed, cheerfully. "Oh, Mr. Haynes, why do you so object to cycling? You wouldn't if once you learnt to ride." "I strongly disapprove of it. It is expensive and unnecessary." "You think it very wicked of me to ride ? " "Not wicked "—hastily---"but I would rather you didn't." "Why should you mind ? " The Reverend Alick Haynes rose, frowning. - "It has nothing to do with me," he said, in his most clerical tones; "at least, only so far as example goes. I hope I shall never ride a bicycle." He bowed and moved away, wishing he had spent the afternoon anywhere than at the Vicarage.

The congregation of St. Peter's grew almost accustomed to Miss Lee's late arrival at church; but the effect those tardy footsteps had upon the curate was only to make him turn his head rigidly. away. On the third Sunday evening after the introduction atthe Vicarage, however, it came on very wet during the service, and as the congrega- tion )eft the church, summer gowns were bundled up under dingy mackintoshes. But one figure remained in the porch with neither umbrella nor waterproof wherewith to brave the elements, and another figure under an umbrella, hurrying from the vestry door towards the church- yard gate, paused on seeing a bicycle near the porch, its owner carefully studying the church notices, apparently unconscious that anyone was near.
"Miss Lee, haven't. you an umbrella ? " It is startling to be spoken to when you fancy your.3elf alone, and Dorothy turned with a very flushed face.

"No, Mr. Haynes. I must wait till the rain stops." "If you will come with me, I can shelter you as far as the Vicarage, and I'm sure Miss Cardiff will lend you an umbrella or a cloak." They had not gone far when sounds of horses' feet and carriage wheels came behind them. "They have sent for you," said the curate. "I'm so glad," answered Dorothy. "I hope you won't catch a cold," said Mr. Haynes, as the machine was hoisted into the waggonette. Dorothy held out her hand. said. "Thank you so mach." The curate just touched the friendly little hand. "Good-bye," he answered. "Let this be a lesson to you not to cycle on Sundays." "On the contrary," said the girl, "I shall come again next Sunday in the same way." The following Sunday was dry and sunny, and Dorothy cycled over as she had said she would. But the curate was not at church. He was suffering from a bad attack of neuralgia. If one member of the congregation sat through- out the service with a preoccupied air, it was nothing to do with anyone else; if she went home through the village it was only because she wanted a longer ride back to Dane Court; and if she stared up at all the houses as she passed, it was, of course, only to admire the thatched roof and gabled windows which were the chief beauty of the village of Vering.
"Good-bye," she

Cyril Honeywood, the heir to the poverty-stricken estate of Dane Court, and Dorothy's cousin, came home that week. It made no difference to the village, except that it meant two bicycles flashing about instead of one.

It happened that on the first day Mr. Haynes took up his clerical duties again he met them both in the village, and such meetings were frequent afterwards. The curate was never surprised to hear two bicycle bells close at his heels, and would stand aside to allow Miss Lee and her cousin to pass,, always acknowledging Cyril's salute, but never once encouraging them to dismount and speak. But because he was getting used to seeing them together so much, it did not follow that he liked the state of affairs. Indeed, he frowned in a most marked way when one Wednesday evening on his way to take the five o'clock service he saw the two machines reclining against the churchyard rail- ings and wondered what freak had caused this week-day appearance. The following afternoon saw him bound for Dane Court, not through any wish of his own, but by the vicar's instructions. "It is time Mrs. Honeywood received her parochial visit," Mr. Cardiff said. But as he himself didn't relish the thought of a hot five-mile walk, he assured Mr. Haynes that on such a glorious afternoon the walk would be beneficial.

It certainly was a glorious afternoon, although when the sun is scorching down on dusty roads, a walk along them is not so inviting; but the curate departed willingly. He was hurrying on when, as he turned a bend in the road, a very woeful spectacle met his gaze. Seated on a bank was Dorothy Lee, an expression of great pain on her face, and with the bicycle lying in the road beside her. She looked up appre- hensively at the curate's footsteps, and then as abruptly hid her face in her handkerchief. "Miss Lee, is anything the matter ? " Down went the handkerchief and up came a very indignant face. "Of course there is! Should Ibe sitting here like an idiot if I were all right ? " she demanded. "I had an accident, and have sprained my ankle." "I'm sorry. is it very painful ?" He knelt down in the dusty road beside her and gently touched the pretty shoe; but Miss Lee pushed him away. "Don't," she said; "it hurts dreadfully. I don't know how I shall get home." "Where is your cousin ? " Alicia voice was cool and almost indifferent again. "He hasn't come with me, and I must be at least four miles from home." "You are two miles from Vering. Couldn't you walk if I helped you ? " " Walk ? Did you ever hear of anyone walking with a sprained ankle ?"--hesitatingly, as if she herself were not quite clear on that point. "I tried to get on my bicycle, but I couldn't. It was awful when I put my foot to the ground." "Will you stay here while I go for help? Perhaps I may meet someone." "Wait here, alone, while you walk two miles? Oh, no, I couldn't!" "I will be very quick." "You couldn't be back in less than three-quarters of an hour "—with conviction—"and anything may happen in that time. I can't walk a step." "Couldn't you sit on the machine if I wheeled you along ?." Miss Lee's eyes flashed scornfully. "Let you wheel me into Vering ? I couldn't. Never mind; leave me alone. I shall have to wait here till Cyril comes to look for me." The curate rose to his feet. "You think he will come soon ? " he asked, stiffly. "He may come when it gets dark, not before. Oh, go away and leave me!" Her face went down into the handkerchief again. Mr. Haynes looked sorely perplexed. "You cannot sit here until it gets dark," he said at last, decidedly. "Perhaps I could carry you ? " "Carry me? Two miles?" Dorothy blushed scarlet and cried all the more.

A ick felt lie had been brutal. "Don't cry," he said presently; "that won't mend matters. Try to think what is to be done." "There is only one thing you can do," said the girl, in a muffled tone, "and—and you would never consent to that. No; I must stay here, I suppose." "1 would consent to anything that would help you, Miss Lee," answered the young man, im- pulsively. "Tell me what it is." Miss Lee shook her head, but after much persua- sion looked up. "Why, the only thing is for you to ride my bicycle back to Vering for help, and I know you won't do that, but you would make me tell yon— there ! "
Dorothy screwed her handkerchief into a ball and looked miserable.

"No, I couldn't do that." The curate's voice was rough and startled, and he turned away with dignity. Dorothy sighed. "Of course, I knew you wouldn't," she said. "You must go and leave me. Good-bye," and she turned her head away resolutely. Mr. Haynes did not move. He told himself he would never ride •a bicycle. But to leave her alone ? No, he could not do that. "I have never ridden a bicycle in my life," he said, more to himself than to the girl. "It's very easy. You have only to stick on and— and there you are," said Dorothy, dismally. "But you won't go, so there's an end to it all. 7, Alick hesitated. "Is there no other way, Miss Lee ? " He looked at the objectionable bicycle and back to Dorothy's tearful face. Her blue eyes .salmed to say "Coward" so plainly. Ha bit his

lip and meditated. and fro. "Miss Lee—Dorothy." The curate's face was pale, but she smiled encouragingly. "Please don't cry. lam going." Dorothy's face was a study as she held out both hands to him appealingly. "Don't go—oh, don't go!" she said. "I —l'm so ashamed of myself, Mr. Haynes." "Please don't say that," he answered, cheerfully. "I will not be long." He took one of her hands and pressed it reassuringly, then tried to mount the machine. At another time Dorothy would have thought it very funny, but now she sat in agony while he floundered about, only keeping his balance by dogged determination. "Mr. Haynes—oh, come back!" cried the girl. "If you only knew that I—oh, come back!" But the curato was too far away to hear, and presently the bend in the road hid him altogether. Dorothy sprang to her feet and paced up and down the grassy patch, wringing her hands. "He will never forgive me; oh, why did I do it ? " It was Cyril's fault, she told herself. Had he not said he was certain that she could not make Alick ride a bicycle, the idea would never have occurred to her, and the bet would never have been made. Now that the triumph was hers, what was it worth? She had made him break his word,
Dorothy rocked herself to

and perhaps he would never forgive the deception.. "Oh, he must, he shall," she said, aloud. "It was only fun, he will not mind when I tell him —he can't, he mustn't." But those hopes are com- fortless which are built on doubtful foundations. It seemed ages before the waggonette appeared in sight with Cyril's well-known form on the box- seat. Mr. Haynes was not there, to the girl's great relief. "Well," said Cyril, as he pulled up, "I didn't think you had it in you." "Neither did I, said poor Dorothy, "and I wish I hadn't." "You are sorry you did it ? " he asked, curiously. "Yes, I am." "Well, I'll be hanged!" said Cyril. The following afternoon Dorothy paced nervously up and down the drawing-room at Dane Court, for i Mr. Haynes was. coming to call. She was longing, yet dreading to see Alick ' • so when he appeared at the end of the dusty road, she would fain have escaped.

She decided to greet him still under her false colours, thinking it would be so much easier to explain by degrees. It seemed but a second before the door opened, and the curate came in. Dorothy half rose, then remembered herself, and

flushed sCarlet as she held out her hand. "Don't try to move," said the young man, hurriedly. "I am going to sit beside you. How is your ankle? Not very painful to-day, I hope?" "No," she said; "no, it's not very painful. It is very good of you to come such a long way to ask after me, and I want y thank you too for—for, , well, for breaking your word and riding the
"It was nothing; please

bicycle." The curate coloured. don't mention it again." "Oh, but I must," said the girl, hurriedly. "You don't know, you " "I understand perfectly," Mr. Haynes inter- rupted, gently, but with a look of suppressed eagerness in his grey eyes. "We have both been rather hard on each other. You thought I was very narrow-minded to object to cycling. I thought you—well, never mind what I thought. Let us start again as " "Yes—yes," interrupted Dorothy, trying to appear unconscious of the eager eyes bent on her. "But I want you to know, I want you to let me tell you something first. Mr. Haynes, will you go across to the window? I want to shew you some- thing." Mystified, the curate walked to the bay window. Dorothy jumped up and went across to him. "There!" she said. "Now you know. It was —it was all a horrid pretence to make you ride the bicycle." "A pretence ? " the curate echoed, blankly. "Yes; I'm very sorry," said Dorothy, humble entreaty in her voice. "I wanted to make you give in to me."

"You have made fun of me ? " he said, turning away and looking out of the window. "I didn't make fun of you," answered the girl, in a low voice. "I thought it would be so splendid to make you break your word, and all the rest of it; but I don't think so now." "I understand," he said, quietly. "You did not consider my feelings, or care about them." "I didn't—them. You made me so angry by always lecturing me for biking to church. I wanted to chew you that I didn't care in the least. But I do now. Won't you forgive me, Mr. Haynes?" raising two mournful blue eyes to the indignantly erect figure. "I am mor3 disappointed than I can say. should never ha rq thotTlit it of you." "At any rate," said Dorothy, beginning to fed rather tired of eatiu. htunble-pie, "I am no worse than you thought I was at first. You always thought me a horrid girl, and now you know it." "I did not say I thought so," said Mr. Haynes, uneasily. "Words are not the only way of shewing one's feelings." "Supposing I did think so, need you have paid me out in such a way ? " "There was no paying out' about it. I should not have been so mean. I did not care sufficiently to want to pay you out'." In trying to clear herself, Dorothy was only making matters worse. "You have made me understand only too well, Miss Lee."
"Have I? "—gladly. "Then you will forgive me, and let everything go on as if that bicyclo affair had never happened ? " "I don't see how I can do that I"—stiffly. .

"Not?" echoed the girl. She had expected he would be very angry, but she had been so sure he would forgive her afterwards. "And yet the most eloquent sermon I ever heard you preach was on forgiveness," she continued, desperately. • "No one knows better than I how hard it is to practise what one preaches," he answered. "I forgive you for the joke itself, but you told me untruths."
"I only told you one untruth, and that was when I said my foot was hurt. But I never was a tame sheep, and I know I am the black one of your white flock."

"That is absurd," he said. "I have no white flock, so there I tan be no black sheep." • "No? Well, anyway, I shan't worry you much longer, as I go away to-morrow. I wonder if this deviation from the path of monotony has been a welcome change ? " Alick did not answer, but he winced at her words. Was it possible that she was going out of his world to-morrow, perhaps for ever? "You are going away ?" he said, weakly. One word would have brought him to her feet; but Dorothy gazed with interest at the buckles of her shoes.
"They want me at home.

"Yes," she answered. , Cyril is coming too." 1 Mr. Haynes checked his wandering thoughts. Although a curate with scruples, he was a man capable of jealousy. ; 'Then I will say good-bye now," he said. ' Dorothy stopped swingincr her feet, and a cold band seemed to take hold of her heart. He was going without forgiving her, and she would never see him again. "Good-bye, Miss Lee." Dorothy summoned all her pride or perversity, and looked up. . "Oh, good-bye, Mr. Haynes." She did not raise her eyes. above the white clerical band round his throat, until she became aware that he was holding her hand tightly. How dared he! She looked up, the blue eyes and the grey ones met, and each read the secret that both were too angry and proud to admit. Then Dorothy pulled her hand away, and hiding her face,womart- like, burst into tears. "Dorothy!" said Mr. Haynes. "Go away," she sobbed. But for once Alick, knew what she meant, and he stayed. ._ THE ENb.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The Smallpox Outbreak.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The Smallpox Outbreak.

A meeting of the Warrington Board was held on Wednesday morning, Mr. A. Brooks presiding. There were also present :—Mrs. Clay, Rev. Father Wilson, Rev. T. R. —atthews, Dr. Murray, Messrs. J. W., Knowles, A. J. Jolley, G. Pilling,J. Billinge, A. Jolley, T. H. Ashcroft, William Hickman, R. Forshaw, William Houghton, J. Backhouse, J. Turton, G. Mather, Thomas Ritchie, and Messrs. j, C. Sutton (clerk),- J. F: Awbery (workhouse master). and A. Wright (superintendent Padgate schools).
CHRISTMAS BEER FOR THE INMATES.

The House Committee resolved to give the officers and inmates the usual extra allowance of Christmas fare and allowance as hitherto, including the usual supply of beer, and to those who preferred it mineral waters. Arrangements were made for getting the wash- ing done outside the workhouse during the alterations to the wash-house. At a subsequent meeting held on the 29th November, the committee recommended that the tender of Messrs. Bradford, of Liverpool, for £537 10s. be adopted for the new machinery required for the wash-house and the re-arrangement of the existing machinery. The Master submitted a report on the nursing staff, stating "That it has become imperative to engage some qualified nurse to have entire charge of the hospital by night, and I would recommend that Nurse Bray be appointed to carry out these duties. To fill the vacancy caused by. Nurse Bray's preferment, I suggest that we should advertise for a nurse with three years' training at a remuneration of .£33 10s. per annum ; and to fill up the vacancies caused by the resignations of Nurses Perry and Irwin by the appointment of two proba- tioners. "The Committee adopted the report. Mr. PILLING moved and the Rev. Father WILSON seconded the passing of the minutes.. Mr. HICKMAN moved as an amendment that beer be not allowed at the Christmas treat. Mrs. CLAY seconded the amendment. There was no discussion. _ - _
On a vote being taken, orily three voted for the amendment, namely, Mrs. Clay, Rev. T. R. Matthews, And Mr. Wm. Hickman. The minutes were then passed.
- THE 01,TTBREAK OF SMA LLPDX. RE-VACCINATION STATIONS TO BE OPENED,

The Clerk read the following letter from Dr. Gornall, Medical Officer of Health : • Acting on behalf of the Health Committee of the Warrington Corporation, I have to call the attention of the Guardians cs vaccine: tion authority to the rapid spread of smallpox in the Orford and St. John's Wards and to say that in their opinion it is highly desirable at once to take measures, for securing rapidly the re-vaccination of persons not recently vaccinated in those neighbourhoods. To that end it is suggested that (1) all children in the public elementary schools most endangered namely St. Anns, Silver street, (Wesleyan), John street (infants) and St. Benedict's R. C. be re-vaccinated. I may say here that the Education Committee are prepared to grant facilities for the purpose to the public vaccinator or vaccinators. (2) That public vaccination stations be opened in the wards in question for the vaccination or re-vaccination of adults. For this purpose there will be no difficulty in securing schools. I am sorry to say that a reply to this letter is requested without delay as the Health Committee will at once take action to secure the object desired by them unless the vaccination authority do so at once, and that it will be only hours and it days that they will wait." Mr. HOCFORD vaccination officer, asked for the sanc- tion of the Board to open stations for re-vaccination in Orford and St. John's Wards. - - - _
On the suggestion of Mr. Knowles it was decided to open stations in various parts of the town at the dis- cretion of Mr. Holford. .
The Rev. FATHER NN, ILSON expressed the opinion that t was not advisable to use schools for the purpose:

With regard to the visiting of inmates fn the Work- house and at Padgate Schools, it was decided, in view of the health of the town, to allow no visiting for the present. This was all the business of public interest.

div.head: FASHIONABLE TOQUE
div.p: A FASHIONABLE TOQUE

while tne wearer be possessed of a slender waiss the band might also be of the same colout. Anyone, however, Who is not pos- sessed of a particularly slender -vaist should content themselves with a fitted waistband of the silk 'sewn over with sequins. The sleeves fall loosely from just above the elbow, in a deep frill to the ,wrists. In white or cream silk a gown of this description would look charming trimmed with some pearl or silver sequined embroidery, and with tur- quoise blue as a note of contrasting colour A lace collar or berthe can always be easily addedif desired, and if of good lace would look well.

Toques this winter are worn projecting well over the face in front and fitting closely to the head at the . back. A specimen of what I mean is depicted in my third sketch. It is made of a brown felt, which has such a woolly rough surfacq that it can easily be mistaken- for fur. The sole trimming is a smartly-arranged aigrette, held in place by a cut steel buckle. ~ Some women are exploiting the somewhat quaint idea of selecting their headgear to match the colour of their hair as nearly, as possible. Personally I confess that the mode, although it possesses novelty, does not find much favour in my eyes, as a 'con- trasting colour will often bring out un- expected light and shades of coloar in the coiffure. The kind of felt that I have described has a great vogue at present, and is more comfortable .wear than a heavy fur hat or toque, while the general effect is quite as good. Sometimes they are trimmed by a little bunch of parma violets and leaves or a dainty nosegay of geraniums, both of which flowers go excellently with any shade of •brown or grey. Black and white felts are also much in demand. Coo MUTE.

div.head: CONQUEST OF
div.p: THE CONQUEST OF
THE CURATE.
By RUBY M. AYRES,
Author of "Love ftir a Year," "Number Four," "The Right Sort of Love," "A Ballroom Confidence," "An Endless Lane," &c. •

There she was, more than half-an-hour late again! The gentle face of the Rev. Alick Haynes bore a gravely disapproving look as his eyes rested on the slim, girlish figure which had created such a disturbance on the previous Sunday evening, and lie looked at the girl for the blush which he felt ought to appear, or for some other sign of embar- rassment at the obvious distraction of the congre- gation. But no. She reached the top of the aisle ,and seated herself with perfect self-possession in the very front pew near the vicar's wife. ,The church door was open to admit what air there was to be had, and the curate was not slow to notice a lady's bicycle leaning against the churchyard gate. He sighed, for he hated bicycles; and as he always did his best to instil the same feeling into the minds of his flock he was hardly likely to make allowances for one who did not get to church at the proper time. Yet as he glanced ar her he did make every allowance possible. She was very young and perhaps had been carelessly brought up, he told himself. He was getting quite brotherly in his feelings towards the girl who sat regarding the vicar with quiet attention, when suddenly she turned her head and a pair of blue eyes disturbed his soliloquy. He experienced a shock, and there was something of the "naughty boy" look about him as he flushed with consciousness and fixed his attention on the pulpit. He would not look again. How dare any self-respecting girl come to church on a bicycle and smile at strange curates! During the last hymn the wardens began to take the collection, ladies ftimbled in their pockets, and the curate's attention was wandering again. Crash! Something hard fell into the aisle. . .

Every neck in the church was craned to see what had happened even the vicar peered over his glasses. The curate's head went round with a jerk and he saw in the aisle in all the bravery of its nickel plating a bicycle spanner! No need to ask whose it was, for the girl in the front pew was actually blushing, though she looked as if she badly wanted to laugh, toO I The vicar and curate looked terribly shocked. What an example for the Sunday-school children I Some of them were giggling already. It was very demoralising, and the Rev. Alick Haynes had hardly recovered his composure when the hymn was finished and the choir filed out.

About ten minutes later he was walking leisurely down the little churchyard ruminating on an inci- dent which had put the spanner out of his mind. A large pearl button had been found in the collection bag, and to the curate it seemed that someone had put it there as a practical joke. The button was reposine, in his own pocket for the future conviction of reposing culprit, and he was mentally parading all the mischievous boys of the parish. If it were Jim Danks, he would make a point of calling at the school and telling the head- master to keep him in half-an-hour every day for a week; if it were Harry Smith, he should lose his ticket for the annual Sunday-school treat; if it were- But he got no further in his musings, for a slightly imperative hand was laid on his arm. "Excuse me," a voice said, in a tone that im- plied that its owner had already said the same words several times before and received no attention.
The curate looked up with a start. The erring occupant of the vicar's pew that evening stood before him.

"I beg your pardon," he said. "Oh, pray don't do that, it is I who must apolo- gise for troubling you," answered a sweet and relined voice. "I was at church, this evening, as I fear you know, and that spanner jumping out rather flurried me. By mistake, it was quite by mistake, really, I put a—a button in the bag. It was one that came off my coat just before I started, and as I cannot match them anywhere round here, would you, would you mind letting me have it back? I will give you sixpence instead. I can't afford more."
She spoke with such utter simplicity that the curate was astonished. She was of a type quite unknown to him.

"Won't sixpence do ? " she demanded, a trifle impatiently. And the curate, awaking to the fact that he had been silent some seconds, answered humbly: "1 wasn't thinking of that." ' He wasn't. Ile was wishing he had left the button in the vestry as the vicar had suggested. "I—l will let you have it, certainly, he said, hurriedly, without making the least movement to do so.

"Will you go back and fetch it?" she said, tapping one foot on the gravel path. "It is getting late and I haven't a lamp." She evidently thought he had left. the button in the vestry. "Here it is," he said, producing the button. "Only I would rather you kept the sixpenae, 1 mean until you have an opportunity to put it in the offertory bag yourself." "I may not be able to come over again for some time. lam staying at Dane Court with my aunt, and because it is five miles away and I can gat home quickly I cycled over." "Is there no other way of t getting here?" asked Alick.

"I could walk," she answered, with a puzzled glance at the grave face which had not once relaxed into a smile, "but there is no one to come with me and I can't very well walk back alone after dusk. There is the waggonette, of 'course, but we never use the horse on Sunday." They had reached the gate now. "I don't know that I altogether approve of Sun- day cycling; in fact, I am quite sure I do na," began the curate, not quite certain how to speak the words in season to do good to so frivolous a mind. "Perhaps you don't approve of cycling at all ? " she suggested, smiling. "No, I disapprove of it entirely, especially for ladies," he said, with conviction; "and as a clergyman I try to keep it out of the village as far as I can. It think it is my duty. But when--" The girl was beginnng to understand now. "But you would rather I came to church on a bicycle than stayed away altogether ? Really, I have no patience with such scruples. Good

evening." • She rode away, leaving the curate only conscious of a flash of wheels and sixpence lying at his feet. Another man in his place alight have been seriously disturbed at her anger; but Alick simply wondered a little, hoped he had not been over earnest, stooped to pick up the sixpence, and walked home, again ruminating. The next Sunday anyone more wideawake than the Vering congregation might have seen that, especially during the sermon, the Rev. Alick Haynes started at the least sound, and glanced nervously towards the door.
- It was not that, he wanted her to come, but because he feared he had been the Means of keep- ing her away. But all that Sunday no bicycle-bell startled the peaceful village from its lethargy.
_ "Mr. llaynes—Miss Lee." • It was in the vicar's drawin.(r-room that the inevitable meeting took place. The curate broke the silence.
"It is very warm." "Yes, very," absently. "Quite ideal weather for July:" _ .
_ "Quite." —"I envy those by the sea to-day." "So do I." • "You are still staying at Dane Court ?" "Yes. . By the way, I lost•that button after all." "Indeed.
The curate's hand went to his pocket, and he found, with a guilty flush, that the sixpence was still there. - -
"Yee," she went on. "I must have dropped it when I rode off. I missed it directly I turned the corner.'

"Really." "I need not hive troubled you, after all, as it did no good and only detained you unnecessarily." Alick raised his eyes. "It did not detain me," he said, quietly. "It is very tiresome—about that button mean. I can't get any in the least like it." The curate knew nothing about such matters; and did not look particularly interested. "You did not come to church last Sunday,"
Ii a said. "Did you look out for me ?" she said, naively. The curate blushed. "I thought you were not there," he said, severely, "because we had no dis- turbances during the sermon."

WOMEN'S CHAT.

The King and Queen are to go to Chatsworth early in January, on a visit to the Duke and Duchess of Devon- shire. Last year immense preparations were made for the expected visit of their Majesties, but at the last moment the Kinp was unable to go owing to indisposi- tion, and the visit next month will be the first the King and Queen have paid to Chatsworth since their accession to i the., Throne. The shooting will be reserved for the Royal visit,and there will be a theatrical performance in which Miss Muriel Wilson—who is to be one of the honseparty—will, as usual, take a leadinn, part. Lord Iveaglr's Seat.—The King's visa to Lord and Lady Ivaggh at Elvedon Hall, near Thetford recalls the fact that', when the estate was sold in 1862 it was thought his Majesty—then Prince of Wales—would purchase it instead of Sandringham. It was bought heweverj by the late Maharajah Dhuleep Singh, who converted it into a vast game preserve, and it passed into possession of Lord Iveagh about seven years ago. Since the King was last at Elvedon. Lord Iveagh has had a magnificent marble hall built there. It is a domed chamber some 80 feet long, 40 feet wide, and 45 feet high, and is constructed throughout of carrara marble. The design is oriental in character, but it is considered a gem of architectural beauty. It has taken five years to complete, during the whole time between one and two hundred workpeople have been, constantly at work, and the new hall cannot have cost Lord Iveagh less than £lOO,OOO. Well-deserved Honours.—Madame Curie, to whom the world is greatly indebted for the discovery of radium, was associated with the honour which the Royal Society conferred the other day upon her husband. Madame Curie is a native of Poland, but she has already received many distinctiens from France, of which country her husband, M. Pierre Curie in a distinguished citizen. Their joint researches into the wonders of radium have not only opened up new theories of science, and of the forces that govern the universe, but they also seem likely to lead to new and valuable methods of medical treatment. There is a great hope that radium will prove to be a cure for cancer, and it is now being applied for this purpose at the Cancer Hospital in London. The radium which has the appearance of a few particles of grey i powder, is enclosed, in a metal box, with a glass face. /t, s only applied to the patient for about five minutes every 48 hours, and there is strong hope that the change it brings about at the seat of the disease, are of a permanently remedial character. Spider Waists.—The letters written by girls barely out of the schoolroom in favour of spider waists, and which have lately been appearing in some of the London newspapers are, many of them, deplorable productions. Some misguided writers tell us it is possible to reduce the waist several inches and "feel no inconvenience whatever." One 'girl says she sleeps in corsets laced a half-inch tighter than is the rule by day—seventeen inches,—in gloves very closely fitting, and shoes a size too small for her—and she feels no discomfort what- ever! Such letters can only shock all rightly-minded girls and women, who must know if they have any common sense left, that tightly-laced corsets mean, sooner or later, impaired if not ruined health. Corsets should fit comfortably, and give support to the figure, but there should be no pressure anywhere. A first-class corset-maker will, apparently, considerably reduce the size of one's waist by means of the cut andfit'of corsets, and the skilful dressmaker can also accomplish much by the same means. But tight lacing should never be thought of by the _girl or woman who values her health and appearance, for who really admires a waist that is out of all proportion to the rest of the figure. A Special Christmas Post.—The experiment of mak- ing a special delivery of the Christmas post ,is to be tried in Manchester, and several provincial towns this year. The public will be invited to hand in their Christ- mas cards and letters over the counter' and they will be specially stamped and put aside for delivery on Christmas morning. That is the time when most people would desire their Christmas greetings to arrive, but there is always the official appeal to post early "and the uncertainty of time of delivery owing to the dis- organization of the service. The new plan is designed to meet the convenience of the public,and of the Post Office servants, to whom Christmas is a period of slavery, and there seems no reason why it should not prove a success and be generally adopted. Christmas Cards.—Pic to rial postcards ada pte d to Yule- tide greetings will largely take the place of the ordinary Christmas card this season. They partake of more originality in design, and present opportunities for variation from the old hackneyed form of greeting which has been somewhat done to death in the ordinary Christmas card of recent years. They also have the advantage of being inexpensive, and the fashion of send-, lug costly and elaborate Christmas cards has happily quite gone out of date. Those people who used to buy half-a-crown cards for their very special friends now see the greater wisdom of sending an inexpensive or private greeting card, and spending the money on a gift of some household trifle, or article of personal adorn- ment. Christmas It ifts.—Christmas present choosing has been made much easier fOr us of late years. We can now offer our friends the useful as well as the orna- mental without fear of giving offence, and as almost ' everybody nowadays is possessed of some fad or hobby, the task of selection is a still more simple one. A motor veil, or gloves, suitable for this particular idea of ' covering the ground, are always acceptable to a woman' motorist, and these items are particularly charming and inexpensive just now. Again almost everyone dabbles in photography, and very delightful gifts are exhibited at all establishments given over to this particular art. Something can easily be found for the athletic woman too. Dainty Presents.—The new lace and chiffon" tops intended to convert a low gown into a high one, will rank among the most popular gifts. The method is a new one, as instead of slipping under the bodice, the " top "or" cover "is fixed over it. This is inade pos- sible by reason of the sloping shoulder, and the inevi- table" fall" of chiffon or lace.—Many women are wear- ing a" top "edged with lace, or chiffon frills—which they can retain or throw off as they choope—under their evening cloaks, and in draughty restaurants and theatres, these little additions are very acceptable .

div.head: BULLET-PROOF MAN.
div.p: THE BULLET-PROOF MAN.

A young German from Leipzig named Max —Meyer is now in London with a bullet in his heart. He is in perfect health, and is the centre of interest to medical scientists. Meyer visited the Middlesex Hospital some days ago, and asked to see the house surgeon, to whom hc handed a document from a Leipzig scien- tific society stating the facts of his case. Na- turally the doc- tor was Aur- prised, and alter putting several questions invit- ed Meyer to the "light-cure" de- partment ,where he was examin- ed by Dr. Lys ter, the famous specialist. Strip- ped to the waist, Meyer was placed under the Rontgen rays, -which revealed a bullet imbedded in the apex ,of his heart. The bullet was covered with muscle, and its presence did not seem in any way to impede the action of the heart. The case excited the greatest interest among the scientists present, and Meyer was subjected to every test to ascertain the exact position of the bullet. Each test proved that it re- mained in the apex of the heart. Some two years ago Meyer was out in the country, near Leipzig, with a friend, who was playing with .a revolver. An accidental explosion caused the bullet to enter Meyer's heart. The extra- ordinary part of the whole affair was that Meyer suffered little, and was able with the assistance of his companion, to reach a local doctor. The bullet was eventually discovered 'by means of the Rontgen rays by a professor at Leipzig University, and Meyer immediately became famous.
it roTATO SPIRIT MOTOR.

The public motor cab in England is, in -spite of the rapid advance in motor con- ,struction, still a thing of the future. No -reason except the universally applicable onE that old traditions die hard, can be given for -this backwardness, especially when it is con- sidered how long motor 'buses have been common in London and large provincial towns. These 'buses are often run in competition .against horse vehicles, and carry their passengers at the same fares and a much -quicker rate. Surely, if the running expenses of a motor 'bus do not prohibit its compet-

• THE NEW GERMAN MOTOR CAB, ON WHICH THE FARE IS RECKONED BY THE TAXAMETER. ing against such a cheap means of transit as -the horse 'bus, the motor cab is a profitable :possibility. Germany, strange to say, has -talcen the initiative in this direction, slow -though she has the reputation of being in -street traffic matters. German provincial towns have for some time had a very pass- -able service of electric cabs, and it was the intention of Berlin, to which, strange to say, is the last to move in the matter, to follow .the example of the provinces implicitly; that is also td have an electric cab service. But a 'Cologne firm has saved Berlin from such ignominy. This Cologne firm has made a motor to run by potato spirit, which can be cheaply manufactured in Germany, and on a. large scale. So successful have the experi- ments been with this car that all German municipal benzine cabs are in future to -abandon that spirit and be altered to run by -potato alcohol. All German ;cabs are on the taxameter system. The indicator points to six pence when the journey is commenced, and marks an extra penny for every co many _hundred yards traversed. The number varief with the number of passengers carried.

div.head: VENERABLE JOURNALIST.
div.p: A VENERABLE JOURNALIST.

Few journalists have done in the past, ano -fewer will do in the future, what Mr. R. Quittenton has done. He has held the posi- tion of editor of a general weekly newspaper during the past 40 years. To illOse outside ttbe newspaper sphere such service may not seem anything to boast about, but to the jour- nalist it is a record. Jour- nalism is such a rapidly moving kaleidoscope, having during the past 30 years passed in- to a distinctly new epoch, re- sulting, as was perhaps to be expected, in an almost univer- sal demand for youthful energy rather than the wisdom of ex- perience, that the old man who could adapt himself to the MR. R. QUITTENTON. revolution ana successfu Hy ,compete against the strong prevailing odds, .merits more than a passing thought. The paper Mr. Quittenton has edited for the past .40 years is the "Weekly Budget." Forty- -two years ago Mr. James Henderson started -that paper at Manchester a city that has been the scene of the establishment of many a journal which, leaving it to seek better luck from production in the metropolis, has made its name a household word and its owner a millionaire. Mr. Quittenton was at that time a printer, and he was engaged as foreman on -the Weekly Budget." He had, however, -the indefinable journalistic instinct almost as stron6ly as Mark Lemon had it, and Mr. Henderson, luckily for himself, saw it. When -the 'Weekly Budget" was removed to Lon- -don Mr. Quittenton was made editor, and has gokne from literary stiength to strength ever siince, until now he has . reached the evening of life, and has left his post to be filled by another. Under the nom de plume of *4 Roland Quiz" he has written many serial stories which, especially in the north of Eng- land and Ireland, have won a great popular- ity. He is, perhaps, best known as the author of a series of wonderfully ingenious tary stories descriptive of the. thrilling and interesting career of "Tim Pippin." These series, the motif of which is to emphasise the triumph of right over wrong, display a re- markable degree of imaginative power, and have been ranked by eminent critics among the best contributions to fairy literature. At the present day, perhaps, the taste of our juvenile population does not incline .towards the mythical, but the repeated demands for volumes of "Tim Pippin," "King Pippin," and Giant Land" from parents who read the stories in their boyhood's days—and they belong to all classes of society—shows that the works of "Roland Quiz" were appreciated and regarded as sound .mental food for the young. Mr. Quittenton's success as an edi- tor largely. depended on his intimate know- ledge of printing and time, allied trades.: When he entered the field such a qualification was a sine qua non, for the editor was often ex- pected to take in hand duties now exclu- sively left to the foreman printer and the professional maker-up. The public is un- doubtedly the *airier in this modern special- OD. for &Alt the editor a yesterday had

Ms faculties largely devoted to journalistic technique, the modern college-bred editor can devote almost his whole attention to the more congenial literary side, and rest assured that his friend the printer will look after the com- posing-room details better than they were at- tended to in the days of the combined editor- manager.

div.head: KWILECKI CASE.
div.p: THE KWILECKI CASE.

It seems that Germany will never have had enough of the Kwilecki sensation; certainly the case has excited and sustained more public interest than any other that has ever engaged the German courts. Though a fort- night has almost passed since the decision was given, the _ _ .

little Count is still the chief ..-- - —..,,....--..-..„ topic in gossip- ing circles. Con- ~&ifi sidering _ the ro- mantic details, l's•F,„., there is little to ~_. wonder at in this. The Count k ~ and Countess Kwilecki up till , ....42"... ..,., 1897, when the Countess was \\ fifty- one years son and heir. Then one was \if C, , born in rooms in Berlin. The question that occupied the Court was whether this THE LITTLE COUNT.
child, the little.

Count, was real or supposititious; and Count Hector Kwilecki, the brother and next heir to the title and estates, claimed that no birth took place. Of the sensational evidence given in the case, none was more dramatic than when the supposed brother of the little Count, the son of a German officer and his mistress, and the little Count himself were brought into court side by side. When, after about an hour's deliberation, the jury returned to the court there was the silence of the 'graveyard, though every nook and corner was crowded with spectators. The police had been unable to keep back the hundreds that thronged the corridors and pressed right up to the Judge's desk. The eyes of all that mass of people were rivetted upon the face of the foreman of the jury as he cleared his throat. Then slowly and distinctly fell from his lips the words, "The jurors have found the defend- ants not guilty. A moment of breathless silence followed these words, then with the suddenness of a thunderclap the wildest kind of applause broke out, in which high and low joined, despite the Judge, who tried to check it by beating on the desk with his baton. In an interview the Countess has explained that she does not attribute her troubles to Count Hector Kwilecki and his father, at whose instance the public prosecutor took action against her, but to the wives of these gentlemen, ladies of the other branch of the family, who were annoyed at the prospect of losing the estates which would have become theirs if the Countess had no son. The Countess also says that during the nine months which elapsed between her arrest and the commencement of the trial the examin- ing judge .` repeatedly urged me to acknow- ledge my guilt, and throw myself on the Kaisers's mercy." '

div.head: WONDERFUL MONKEY.
div.p: A WONDERFUL MONKEY.

The London Hippodrome has just enagged, itt a salary of A-200 a week, the most intelli- gent chimpanzee ever discovered. His name is Consul, and it may truly be said of him that he does everything but talk. He plays the piano, drinks, eats, and behaves himself like a man. He is very fond of smoking, and finishes his cigar to the end. Lighting his cigar is no trouble to him, as he thor- oughly understands the use of matches. Stranger still, he understands practically everything that is told him, and he does his best to reply. He utters a mumbling kind of sound which it is evident he intends for replies to questions put to him. At his home in New York he has a suite of rooms, which are divided into a gymnasium, dining- room bedroom, reception room, and a boudoir. An adventure he had at a New York dentist's
CONSUL IN ONE OF HIS FAVO
ATTITUDES

shows to what a pitch of civilisation he has arrived. Consul, by means of signs, made his keeper understand that he was suffering from the toothache. He was forthwith taken to a dentist, who found that three teeth were decayed. Anticipating some trouble, his keeper employed eight men to hold him down in the chair preparatory to the drawing of the teeth. Contrary to all expectations, he neither struggled nor cried, and when the teeth were• extracted he got oil the chair and shook the dentist by the hand, evidently endeavouring to thank him. He is very fond
of children, and has as a companion a- little

_ negro boy, who is .always with him and to . whom he is deeply attached. His manners at table are perfect, and at a dinner recently given in his honour at Paris he occupied the place of honour. He remembers people after year's of absence. He has strong likes and dislikes, but so civilised has .he become that instead of uttering cries when he is annoyed, he simply becomes quiet and puts on a dig. nified air of boredom.

div.head: NSW CHILD COMPOSER.
div.p: THE NSW CHILD COMPOSER.

Max Darewski, eight years old, a sweet- natured child, with a wide Eton collar, large brilliant black eyes, and hair that is dark and curly, promises to go down to posterity as a Mozart. In his brain tunes are always find- ing birth. Only the wisdom of his parents and his doctor prevents him from spending half his time in putting his compositions on paper. Because of that wise restraint "La Reve" is the only one of his compositions which has reached com - pletion. "La Reve " has come to light in England by being played by the late Mr. Dan Godfrey's band at Bourne- mouth, a week' or two ago. The son of a well- known professor of singing, little Max breathes at home the atmosphere of music. Born in 1895, he began to show signs of musical pre- cocity before he knew his alphabet. At five, without having had a lesson, he had composed "La Reve " and a few months later was able to play it on the piano from memory. It was not until he was twelve months older that he was placed under Mr. Carl Weber.for in- struction: At Christmas Max is to conduct a performance of his waltz by Mr. Dan God- frey's band, which now plays it regularly as part of its repertory: Next spring if every- thing goes well, he will appear at _West kEnd goncerta as .a pianist A at
MAX DAREWSXI.

Councillor THORN"I'ON: £3OO ?- The MAYOR : It is an. estimate. Councillor WILK LNSON pointel out that C )uncillor -Thornton was one_of the deputation appointed to in- spect the land and to see whether it was worth the while of the Council to ask Messrs. Hadgkinson to remove the building. He came back. Two of the three agreed, but the other, when the matter came before the committee, changed his mind. Councillor TRORNTON : Who did? Councillor WILKINSON: You did. Councillor THORNTON: I did not change my mind. Continuing, Councillor Thornton said Councillor Wilkinson knew nothing about the matter. As a business man he wanted to know the cost of the scheme before he voted for it. The Tows CLERK (addressing Councillor Wilkinson): No amount has been named. You mentioned £3OO. Councillor WILKINSON: I estimate it at that myself. Councillor PEACOCK said he had been one of the deputation to visit the spot, and he considered that the Corporation were making a very good exchange. He did not think that the extra cost owing to buildings being proceeded with would amount to £3OO. They were entirely in the hands of one man, but he had con- fidence in leaving it with him that the Corporation would not have to pay too much. Councillor TINNION said it seemed to him that the Council should know its own mind, and when a matter was decided at one monthly meeting they should not allow anyone to come there like the proposer and seconder of the amendment to interfere with their transactions. It would be fatal to any business man if he were to conduct his business in such a shilly-shally- ing shifting way, and he hoped the Council would put its foot down once and for all, and, reject . the amendment. _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _

Cauncillor BROUGH said that although he had voted twice against this scheme he could not support Coun- cillor Pemberton's amend nent. it seemed to him to be mere child's play to keep ptssing resolutions and then rescinding them. Councillor DODDS said he agreed with Councillor ! Brough, and he was quite preptrei to acqnise e in the adoption of the minutes. Councillor Wilkinson had,he thought thrown too much heat into the matter, and though he would not vote against the resolution, he thought to blame then for the extra cost of £3OO was hardly fair to those who had voted for the amendment. It was hardly fair also to say that those who had voted fo4he amendment had incurred an extra expense of £303 unnecessarily. If they had carried the amend- ment they estimated that they woald have saved the town £lO,OOO. Having fought the matter out five times and the scheme having been carried by 17 votes to 10 he was quite prepared to acquiesce. Councillor PEMBERTON rose to make an explanation "with regard to what Councillor Brough had said." The MAYOR ruled him out of order. Councillor PEMBERTON continued but was not heard owing to repeated cries of "Chair." Alderman SUTTON, replying, said that he felt that the nail:had been hit on'the head when it was stated that this extra expense in having to recoup Messrs. Hodgkinson and Co. for the money they had expended in the interval was entirely due to those who had opposed the scheme. (Cries of "No.") The MAYOR:—Please save all that. ; Alderman SUTTON, continuing, said thqse who had continually brought forward amendments were entirely I responsible for the extra cost. Tney had obstructed the carrying out of the work, and the cost of the property j that had been erected in the meantime must mow he paid. He did not know, however, why one memher of • the Council should make a statement that the cost was so much, when he could know nothing about it. Councillor PEMBERTON said, having heard the ex- pressions of the Council, he would withdraw the amend- ment. _ _
Councillor THORNTON withdrew his seconding, but still expressed the opinion that the Council should know the cost. Several matters touching the lighting of certain streets were mentioned.

Councillor JAMES Ev .NS said the members should make their suggestions in writing, so that they might reach the committee and the Gas Engineer. The whole of the lighting of:the town was being revised. The minutes were then adopted.

At it later stage of the meeting, Councillor PEMBERTON said he would withdraw the following resolution, of which he had given notice : "That the resolution of the General Purposes Com- mittee, as passed on October 6th, 1903 ; 'Resolved, that the proposal contaihed in the following resolution of the Street Improvement Committee be approved. A proposal from Mr. R. E. Garnett to add 20 feet in width co-extensive with his premises to the proposed passage behind the new premises in Bridge street,and to give the scheduled property belonging to him,containing an area of 316 square yards, in exchange for land in the Eagle and Child yard, containing 531 square yards,' be rescinded." •

over-work and anxiety to do his duty. He had been working 581 - hours per week, hard at it from morning I to night, which was too much for a man of 40 years of age. At present they only taught the scholars of 5 elementary schools out of 23 or 24, but the extension of the teaching to all the schools was what they desired. The committee would seriously have to consider the advisability of appointing more than one assistant. Councillor JOHN EvAxs seconded, and the minutes were approved. ELECfRICITY AND TRAMWAYS.
RESIGNATION OF THE ENGINEER- ADVERTISING FOR STORES.

Aldermin SNIRTRUAST proposed the confirmation ef the minutes of this Committee, and alluded to his elec- tion to the chairmanship. He found it difficult to follow in the steps of his predecessors, and he hoped the Coun- cil would give him all the support and assistance pos- sible. They would see that the resignation of Mr. I Grimsdale had been received. In him they were losing I a most valuable servant—(hear, hear)—and one who had come there and superintended the erection of an elec- tricity station second to none in the country. They I had been going for something like two years and had I never had an accident which also spoke well for Mr. Grimsdale's management. He only wished he could have stopped. Councillor WILKINSON seconded and said, as deputy- chairman, he should endeavour to do what he could towards fathering the good government of the town of his birth. He woald like to appeal to the Council to turn their minds round, from opposing every little improvement which mightle brought forward. He had been accustomed to spending large sums of money in , his own business and he should spend it with the same efficiency for the Corporation of Warrington. 1 Councillor PEMBERTON alluded to a resolution that 1 an advertisement for ducts, coal, stores and other sup- plies be issued annually. He hardly thought it carried ' out the ideas of the committee. The point was that a lot of goods to the extent of thousands of pounds, had I been purchLed without advertisement. " Annually " i would be rather a mistake, especially in regard to coal contracts. and he proposed that the word "annually " be deleted.

Councillor JAMES EVANS thought the resolution was quite unnecessary. The committee should do their buy- ing according to the standing orders of the Council. Councillor TINNION said he thought that committees made a mistake in buying their stores annually. With reference to Mr. Grimsdale, Warrington was losing one of its most capable officials. He had always found him obliging, courteous, and in every way equal to all his duties. He did not hesitate to say they would have very great difficulty indeed in finding a man with all his qualifications and parts. It had often been asked, "how is it Mr. Grhus dale does not carry out the works without a consulting engineer?" It was not his fault. He had not been asked to do so.

Councillor DODDS : Why? Councillor PEMBERTON : He was asked! Councillor TINNION : He was not asked, because many members of the committee thought it was unde- sira`-)le that he should be occupied in running about inspecting new appliances and advising the committee upon them, when there was plenty to fill his time in Warrington. Alderman Smethurst and himself had argued the point many a time, but the majority of the committee were against Mr. Grimsdale dispensing with a consulting engineer. It was absolutely untrue to say that he was incapable of taking these duties. The MAYOR: One reason was that Messrs. Preece and Cardew, being the engineers from the commence- m.nt were responsible for the plant for some time, and the committee thought it better to employ them. I think the standing orders sufficiently meet the resolu- tion brought up. Alderman SUTTON: I think it should tand.

Alderman BENNETT was proceeding t•t argue that there was a good deal in the resolution when he stopped to protest against Councillor Tinnion interrupting. Councillor TtssroN: I-Only smiled, Mr. Mayor. Alderman BENNETT : Mr. Tinnion smiles so broadly that it is equivalent to an interruption. (Loud laughter). Councillor WILKINSON said the resolution on the minutes was Councillor Pemberton'sand he was wasting the time of the Council.

Councillor TINNION said they had frequently asked for quotations, which was equal to asking for tenders. Councillor Pemberton misrepresented almost every matter he brought forward, and he should not charge other people with misrepresentation. Councillor LORD: Councillor Tinnion is a stranger to the truth. (Laughter). Alderman SMETFIURST said the resolution was put on to satisfy Councillor Pemberton. There were at it in committee for two hours and why he brought it up again he did not know.. _ - -

He added that in all his experience of *workingmen's meet- ings he had never seen so much time wasted as there had been that night. _ _

div.head: LATE MR. SHAW GREEN
div.p: THE LATE MR. SHAW GREEN
A letter was read from Miss Shaw Green. thAnking the Council on behalf of her mother and sister for their expression of sympathy on the death of her father.
THE LATE COUNCILLOR BROPHY.

The M %NOR annomiced that since the last meeting of the Council one of their number, Councillor Brophy had pissed away. He had, therefore, a- very sad duty to parfortn. Mr.' Brophy had only been a member of the .Council for one year. but during that period he had been most attentive to his duties in a , quiet and unostentatious way. (Hear, hear.) He Moved a resolution to the effect that the Council receive with very great regret the announcement of the death of Councillor Brophy, which took place on Nov. 19th, and that the expression of the Council's sympathy be con- veyed to the members of Mr. Brophy's family. Councillor DODDS, in seconding, said he could not refrain from giving expression to what he hoped was the unanimous sentiments of the Council in regard to the tragic sadness of the fate which had befallen their late respected and deeply regretted colleague, M r.B roph y. It was his privilege to have a long talk with their late friend on the last occasion of his attendance the-e, and he should never forget with what heroic calmness and fortitude Mr. Brophy had anticipated the critical opera- tions he was about to face, and their probably fatal results. He was an honest man, true to his word and to his religious and political convictions. Such men could ill be spared, and he was sure that his widow and his family had the deepest sympathy of every member of the Councif in the trouble and the concern of their heavy and irreparable loss. (Hear, hear). The motion was carried.
aPPOINT,gENTS ON THE EDUCATION COMMITTEE.

The next business was the appointment of represen- tative members of the Education Committee in place of the late Councillor Brophy and Mr. J. C. Parr, who has ceased to be a member of the Council. Councillor FORSHAW seconded,and Councillor JAMES EVA.NS, supported, the motion being carried unani- mo u sly. The Council hid next to appoint a co-optative 1113111- ber of the committee on the recommendation of the Association of Rom in Catholic Schools within the borough. The Maxoa announced that the association had re- commended two names, namely, Mr. Charles H. Uns- worth and, the Rev. Michtel Ryan. Councillor RodEus moved that Mr. Unsworth be elected.

Councillor TisSroN secondad, and the motion was carried without discussion. The minutes of the Education Committee were con- firmed on the motion of Alderman Bennett, THE NEW POLICE BUILDINGS. REGISTRATION OF MOTOR CARS.

The minutes of the Watch Committee contained the report of the architects on the new police buildings. It was resolved that of the works included in the con- tract the following be carried ont.—(l) the armoury to be removed ; (2) the single men's quarters to be coth- pleted ; (3) one inspector's house, instead of two, to be erected; (4) the parade room to be completed, and that all other nnexecuted works be omitted from the contract, and that it be referred to Mr. William Owen as arbitrator, to decide all claims of the builder under the contract.—lt was further decided that the Town Clerk prepare draft bylaws under the Employment of Children Act, 1903; that the Chief Constable be ap- plinted the registration officer under the Motor Car k Registration and Licensing Order), 1903, and that he be authorised and empowered to perform any duty or exercise any power of the Council for the purpose of carrying the order into effect; and that the office of the Chief Constable 1;e appointed the office for the registration of motor cars and for the issue of licences under the above order. The IVlavoumoved the adoption of the above minutes, and in reading the recommendation with regard to the new police buildings interpolated the remark that at present incomplete state of the buildings was not satis- factory. Alderman HEATON seconded, and the minutes were adopted.

div.head: MONEY TO BE BORROWED.
div.p: MONEY TO BE BORROWED.

Mr. Halton, the tenant of the " George " Hotel, attended a meeting of the Finance and Estate Com- mittee with his solicitor, Mr. Arthur Browne, with res- pact to his tenancy of the hotel, of which he was under notice to quit, and certain arrangements were come to, the committee, upon Mr. Halton giving up possession. to take over the tenant's fixtures at a valuation, &c. It was resolved that the Town Clerk be authorized to apply to the Local Government Board for sanction to borrow £24,000: being the amount agreed to be paid to the County Council in the financial adjustment between the county and the borough; £11,505, being the amount of the deficiency under the Education Act, £21,393 street improvements, and £12,296 for private street works. It was resolved that the resolutions of the Council of the Ist September, 1903, with reference to the proposed borrowing of £lO,OOO for private street works be rescinded. Alderman Fairclough was appointed overseer in the place of the late Mr. Shaw Green.
The DEPUTY-MAYOR , moved the adoption of the minutes of the above committee.
Alderman BENNETT seconded, and they were adopted without discussion. THE NEW STREET. COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON AGAT.N IN OPPOSITION.

At a meeting of the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee it was resolved that so much of the resolu- tions of the 11th August and 6th October, 1902. as pre- scribe building lines through the Eagle and Child yard be rescinded; that the plan showing the line of frontage in the street adjoining the Royal Court Theatre from Rylands-street to the Eagle and Child yard be signed and deposited; that the sum of .£3OO be paid to the Misses Carmen for the purchase of premises at the corner of Orchard-street and School-brow, A requisi- tion from the owners of premises in Irlam-street (Howard-place; to dispense with the name of Irlam- street and to substitute Butterrnarket-street, or in the alternative, Howard-place, Buttermarket-street, was read. It was resolved that Irlam street be re-named Buttermarket-street.—.l further resolution was to the effect that,the new street behind Bridge-street be con- tinued through premises belonging to William Hodg- kinson, Limited, the Corporation giving a plot of land in the Eagle and Child yard equal in area to the plot required for the new street. The Corporation to repay to Hodgkinson's, Limited, the cost of all works and other expenses incurred or necessitated by the altera- tion of their buildings and plans. Alderman SUTTON formally moved the adoption of the minutes. Alderman BENNETT seconded. • In answer to Councillor Pemberton Alderman SUTTON said the present arrangement *as that the new street should ba 40 feet wide. Councillor PENIBERTON said he would move an amend- ment that the minutes of the Committee be confirmed with the exception of the ptragraph.referring to the new street behind Bridge-street. He stated that when it wasproposed to make the street 40 feet wide instead of a2O feet mssage, several members only voted in favour becauge they' were assured that the extra cost would be a very sin ill am )unt of money. They had no approximate figures as to the cost. It might cost £3OO or it might cost £l,OOO. He then pointed out that the prescribed building line went through Greenall's Dis- tillery in such a way that the Council might as well take the whole of it. Then, Mr. Hepherd's property at he bottom would also be within the prescribed 40 feet, aul to ask the Council to pass such a scheme wit4out 'urther explanation was not quite fair. Councillor THORNTON seconded. He said he objected in the ground that th 3 cost of the scheme warn not .'orthcoming, and h 3 • thon;ht they should not plunge the ratep tyers into any scheme of the kind without having some idea of the expense. (Hear, hear.) Councillor WMICENSON said he was certain that Coun- cillors Pemberton and Thornton must be well aware that it was intended months ago to complete this street and to take a piece of land from Messrs. Hodgkinson that came on tout, giving them in exchange it piece of their own land on the other side. Through the con- tinual proposing of amendments by Councillor Pember- ton the matter lay in abeyance. Messrs. Hodgkinson had conseauently gone on with their building, never thinking that this street would go through. The Council had now by a majority decided to go on with the street and now they had to deal with Messrs. HodgkinsOn. Through the opposition of Councillor Pemberton and other people, who could not or would not understand, they might have to pay perhaps £3OO to Messrs. Hodg- kinson' That was all through the opposition of Coun- cillor Pemberton and others, who came there and opposed things they knew nothing whatever about. (Laughter.) That was a thing the public should know, and not be misled by men who came forwardat meet-

div.head: STREET PAVING AND THE COST.
div.p: STREET PAVING AND THE COST.

A letter was read at a meeting of the Paving and Sewerage Committee from Mr. H. J. Longton, solicitor, in regard to the paving of Albert-street. It was re- solved that the forming and paving of Albert-street be proceeded with forthwith, on condition that the owners of property in the street agree to the work being done without the necessary notices being served, and to enter into an agreement to pay the cost thereof. Alderman HEATON moved the adoption of the minutes.
Councillor TINNION seconded.

Councillor CRAM said Mr. Longton's letter seemed to have awakened the committee, and he complained that Icertain other streets of which notices had been given !long ago had not been paved. After a short discussion, Alderman HEATON explained that in matters of street improvement certain legal pro- cesses had usu Ally to be observed, and until this I was done progress could not be made. In this case, how- ever, the owners had set an example by coining to the committee and saying to the Corporation "Go on with • the work and we will pay as soon as it is done." Instead of doing that, many owners did not want to pay either at the time or ever. (Laughter.) In fact, it was necessary for the borough to borrow £20,000 in order to pay other people's debts. i The minutes were carried. BOWLING GREENS.

Councillor PEMBERTON asked the Mayor what was being done with reference to public bowling greens. The MAYOR replied that they had given instructions i for the work of constructing a green n Victoria Park to be carried out as quickly as possible.

div.head: GAS COM NIITTEE.-SLO AIRTERS.
div.p: GAS COM NIITTEE.-SLO AIRTERS.
The minutes of this committee were of a routine ' character. _ _ _

_ • The DEPUTY-MxYort moved, and Alderman HEATos 'seconded the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor WILSON drew attention to the fact that users of slot meters paid their money before they got the gas, and they also paid more for it than those con- sumers who had it on six month's credit. Could not the Gas Committee arrange that the slot meter users could have some disc omit? The MAYOR informed Councillor WILSON that he was really out of order, but it he would bring the matter directly before the committee they would give it their consideration.
The minutes were approved. THE SHIP CANAL COMPANY AND 'ME CORPORATION. DELAY THROUGH THE SWING BRIDGES. CONFERENCE OF MANUFACTURERS.

The MaYOIt moved the adoption of the Rivers Com- mittee minutes, and observed that they were doing everything they possibly could in the Rivers question. It would not be wise to discuss it publicly. Alderman PIERPOINT said he would like the Rivers Committee, while they were making arrangements with the Canal Company, not to lose sight of the present irregular method by which the swing bridges were opened and left open. The other morning' when he was trying to catch an important train, the Latchford Swing Bridge was open for a !quarter of an hour. They could easily have managed in half the time, and he , would then have caught his train. The bridges being ! kept open such a long time often made matters very inconvenient, and he hoped the committee would make some arrangement whereby it could be defined how long the bridges could be kept open. (Hear, hear). I The MAYOR: We have taken this into consideration and will not forget it. But you must also not forget that these bridges are out of the borough. Alderman HEATos: Is not a time flied by the Act of Parliament?

The MAYOR: Yes. • Alderman PIEnPorYr : But there is no penalty. The M.IYOR : There is a penalty, and you can sue the Ship Canal Company for loss and damages.. (Laughter) Councillor PfERPOINT: The minutes were agreed to. _

He (the Chairman) had taken upon himself to engage one of their old pupils. Mr. Mottram,.at £2 ss. per week, to take Mr. Kinsley's place for a time. Mr.. div.head: PROPOSED WOIIEN'S LABOUR BUREAU.
div.p: PROPOSED WOIIEN'S LABOUR BUREAU.

On the recommendation of the General Purposes Committee it was agreed that the following members be appointed to consider and report upon the proposal to establish a Women's Employment Bureau : Mr. Alderman Pierpoint (convenor), Mr. Aide, man Smethurst, Councillors Ashcroft, Lord, and Peacock. Alderman PIERPOINT said he was mainly responsible for the recommendation. Perhaps a little explanation was due as to the reasons why he had introduced it A body of philanthropic ladies in Warrington felt that there was a large number of poor women in the town who wanted employment but did not know where their services were required. The object in view was to establish some kind of organisation whereby these poor women who desired work as charwomen and washer- women, may be brought into touch with ladies who might require occasional help in their respective houses. (Hear, hear.) Councillor MAGISN'S resolution in regard to the inquiry was then debated. The report will be found elsewhere.

div.head: SHOCKING CRUELTY TO CHILDREN
div.p: SHOCKING CRUELTY TO CHILDREN

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Satur- day, before Mr. T. Birch,/IL and other justices, Robert Burke, 7 Edward-street, was charged with having neglected his four children in a manner likely to cause them unnecessary suffering and injury to health.—Mr. A. Browne, who prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C., said that this was one of the most shocking cases ever brought before a bench. The children's heads and necks were 'one mass of corruption." The prisoner was a forge labourer, earning a weekly wage of 235. Since January he had been warned,and everything done for him by the society's inspector. The previous day inspector Hackett visited Edward-street, and found the daughter Kate in a filthy condition. Her head was one mass of corruption, the stench from which was horrible. Dr. Peacocke was called in, and fotind that the other chil- dren were in a similar state. The doctor ordered all four children to be removed to the Workhouse.—Dr. Peacocke said he not only found the children in a filthy condition, but the rooms they occupied conta' ed practically no bedding.—lnspector Hackett andP.C. l Hamblett corroborated, the former adding that drink was the cause of the neglect.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for six months—the maximum period.

div.head: SOLDTER-MURDERER EXECUTED.
div.p: SOLDTER-MURDERER EXECUTED.

Bernard White (21), of the 2nd Battalion Essex Regi- ment, was executed at Chelmsford on Tuesday for the murder of Maud Garrett (20), at Warley Gap, in May. —The girl was an old sweetheg.rt, but on his return from South Africa he found her engaged to another man.—At the trial Mr. Jtistice Lawyance said the murder was one of the foulest and most cruel he had ever heard.
