div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
As the Parochial Committee was so much to blame in the first instance it was recommended that no action be taken.

The Chairman said the report revealed an extra- ordinary procedure on the part of the Parochial Corn- mittee. There was a definite breach of the byelaws—in fact the property seemed to have been built without. any reference whatever to the requirements of the bye- la .vs. He moved that the attention of the Parochial Committee be called to "this very gross breach of tha- byelaws" and that they be requested to adhere closely to them in future. If he byelaws were to be broken systematically they might as well be done away with altogether. Mr Wright seconded.
After so-me discussion the motion was agreed to. FINANCE. _ _ _
Mr. Wright presented the financial statement froni which it appeared that the cheques drawn that day amounted to £363 5s lid, leaving a balance in the hands of the treasurer of £Bl5 16s sd.

div.head: Isolation Hospital.
div.p: The Isolation Hospital.

The monthly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Distigct Council WM held at Dutton Workhouse on TueWy morning, Mr. S. Woodward presiding. There were also present :—Messrs. G. Pilling. C. E. Linaker, T. Baxter, J. Moseley Williams, T. Wright, A. G. Guest, J. T. Collier, J. B. Chadwick, J. Spruce, J. L. Jones, T. Clarke, J. Lewis, J. Edwards, .1. Whitlow, T. Darlington' H. Mawdsley, J. Mounfield, with Dr. Adams (medical officer of health), Messrs. W. Diggle and J. Swinton (surveyors). W. Farrington (inspector of nuisances), G. F. Ashton (clerk), and W. E. Hough (assistant clerk).

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH PRIVATE STREET WORKS.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH PRIVATE STREET WORKS.
The Local Government Board wrote under date 21st November sanctioning the borrowing of £650 for the purpose of the making of private •streets in Stockton Heath.

div.head: TIJBERC (7LO 17S M ILK.
div.p: TIJBERC (7LO 17S M ILK.

The Clerk read a letter dated 12th November from the County Council enclosing copy of a letter received from the County Medical Officer of Health in regard to tuberculous milk at Mr. Thomas Morris' farm, Marsh House, Little Legh and urging that effect be given to the suggestion in .the last paragraph. In the enclosure Dr. Vacher intimated that on the 29th October he received a letter from the Liverpool Medical Officer of Health stating that a sample of milk consigned from Mr. T. Morris' farm had been found to be tuberculous. Dr. Vacher visited the farm‘on October 30th in company with Mr. Eaton Jones, veterinary surgeon, and Inspector Quinton of the Liverpool Cor- poration they efamined the premises and found that the ventilation and lighting of the smaller cow house were imperfect. The veterinary surgeon examined all the dairy cattle and picked out three which appeared to be diseased. Samples of milk were taken from two of these animals for the purpose of being tested, and the farmer was instructed to keep all three apart from the rest of the herd and dry them off for slaughter. The letter concluded with the suggestion that the farmer , should be requested to improve the lighting I and ventilation of the smaller cow house.
Mr. Farrington reported that the building was not in accordance with the bye-laws, and Mr. Linaker said the work would be carried out as required by the owner of the estate.

div.head: PRODSHAM-DELAMERE ROAD.
div.p: THE PRODSHAM-DELAMERE ROAD.

The Cheshire County Council intimated by letter dated 16th November, that they were not prepared to declare the highway between Main-street, Frodsham, and Delamere Station to be a main road. Mr. Baxter said one of the reasons for the decision of the County Council was that the volume of traffic on the road was local. It would have cost the district .£6,000 if the road had been taken over, and the Rural Council could keep it in repair for that amount.
THE ISOLATION HOSPITAL

The Local Government Board Wrote udder date 11th November with reference to the application for sanc- tion to borrow £B,OOO for the erection of an Isolation Hospital at Dutton intimating that they were not pre- pared to sanction the borrowing of .000 for acetylene gas plant etc. Subject to that deduction they were prepared to comply with the application and formally sanct:onibd a loan of £7,700. The Board expressed regret that the Rural District Council/ had not seen their way to make a reduction in the anticipated cost of th Hospital. The Clerk said the Board wished the Council to cur- tail the size of some of the rooms in the administra- tive block but they decided that they could not do so to any advantage. The Council had now to consider whether to advertise for tenders at once or to wait until the water supply was extended to the site. He had had an interview with the engineer of the Liver- pool Corporation and he promised to bring the matter before the Corporation and obtain their decision as to the proposed extension of the mains to Dutton and Preston-o'th'-Hill.
The Chairman said it would not he advisable to pro- ceed with the building during the winter. It was decided to defer the matter for the present.
NORTH-WESTERN ELECTRICITY AND POWER -GAS RILL.

The Secretary of the Association of Clerks to the District Councils and Guardians of Cheshire wrote stating that as the result of the opposition by 25 com- bined Cheshire Local authorities the County of Chester was excluded from the area of supply covered by the North-Western Electricity and Power Gas *Bill. The costs of the opposition amounted to £62513 s., which will be divided among the 25 Cheshire authorities. The Clerk said the Council in the first instance promised to contribute £5, and aMrivards agreed to consider a further contribution of £5.

The Chairittn said the Council had to help to pay the costs of a petition which was so successful as to obstruct their desires. (Laughter.) A committee was appointed to attend a conference which will be held with a view to an equitable arrange- ment being arrived at.

div.head: STREET I PROVEMENTS.
div.p: STREET I PROVEMENTS.

Mr. Pilling moved (that Cawdor-street arid Birch- street, Stockton Heath, be levelled, paved, metalled, &c., and that the Surveyor be instructed to prepare specifications, estimates, and provisional apportion- ments. He also moved that application be made to the Local Government Board to invest the Council with the power of the Street Works Act, 1892, in respect of Bedford-street.

Mr. Mountield seconded and said the making of Cawdor-street and Birch-straet would open out a very valuable road which was now blocked with posts by the Bridgewater Canal Company. The result would be that the distance between Walton and London Bridge would be shortened by a quarter of a mile. The resolution was agreed to;

The Council also decided to apply to the Local Govern- ment Board for power under the Private Street Works Act in respect of streets at Weston. The Council approved the minutes of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee which included a recom- mendation that the footpaths in Chapel-lane be paved with concrete slabs at an estimated cost of £llB.
PROPOSED VILLAGE CROSS AT HALTON

A proposal that a village cross should be erected at the cross roads at Halton was consitlered by the Ilighways Committee. The Clerk was instructed_ to inform the Parish Council that the committee con- sidered a cross placed in the position suggested would be dangerous to the travelling subject and therefore refused the application. The minutes were approved. . THE PROPOSED NEW SHOPS AT STOCKTON HEATH.

Mr. Linaker reported that at a meeting of the Build- ing Committee plans were submitted by Mr. Thomas Williams for twenty three shops and dwelling-houses at Stockton Heath, but the committee did not feel justi- fied in passing them until they had been before the Parochial Committee. This decision was confirmed. "A GROSS BREACH OF BYRLAWS.'

The Clerk read the report of a sub-committee appointed to inspect cottage property erected by Mr. J. Crosslansl Taylor at Helsby, which, it was alleged, was not in accordance with the byelaws. The committee considered that the plans had been contravened in re- gard to the walls at the rear of the premises, hut they were of the opinion that if the walls were set back to the line originally approved by the Helsby Parochial Committee there would be no material improvement.

div.head: CHICKEN rox AT HELSBY
div.p: CHICKEN rox AT HELSBY
Dr. Adams reported that chickenpox had become epidemic among the infant children of Helsby and he suggested that the infante school be closed for a fort- night.
this was agreed to. HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.

The Medical Officer reported a case Of. diphtheria at Walton Inferior. He had received an intimation of the death of a cow from anthrax at Aston. The carcase was cremated and no human beings had been affected. A complaint had been made as to the sewerage arrange- ments in Fairfield Road, Latchfotd Without. . The Surveyor was instructed to attend to the matter. Dr. Adams informed the Council that smallpox had broken out in Warrington and over twenty cases had been reported. It behoved the Council to be in a. position of preparedness for any epidemic that might occur in their district.

A request by Mr. Dodd, who had charge of removal work &c., during the last epidemic, for permanent employment in case of another outbreak was referred to the Smallpox Hospital Committee. Mr. J. L. Jones was elected a member of this com- mittee.

div.head: BAD ROAD.
div.p: A BAD ROAD.

Mr. Baxter complained that the road passing under the arches at Lower Walton was in a wretched state and was really dangerous. Mr. Mounfield said the road was in a terrible con- dition. The soft material that had hitherto been used in repairing it was useless. The Clerk was instructed to call the attention of the Ship Canal Company to the complaint.

div.head: MARIE CORELLI AS LITIGANT.
div.p: MARIE CORELLI AS LITIGANT.

The forthcoming actions for libel at the Birming- ham Assizes in which Miss Marie Corelli is concerned are creating a great amount of interest. There are two actions, one against Councillor Winter, of Stratford- on-Avon, and the other against Mr. G. Boydon, the proprietor of the" Stratford-on-Avon Herald." Mr. Winter made the allegation that although Miss Corelli protested so strongly against the proposal to devote a certain site in Stratford to the proposed Carnegie Library, she herself had tried to buy the same site for a similar purpose. This Miss Corelli characterised as untrue, and demanded an apology, but it was not forth- coming, so she is bringing actions for libel against the two persons named.

A FEW SUMS.
MR. CHAMBERLAIN and his adherents

are faring badly in the war of statistics. They produce a new set of figures every day,signifying woe to our industries, and the following day sees it demolished. Mr. BRAILSFORD, who is in the steel trade, bewailed the incapacity of the Welsh manufacturers to re- tort against "dumping" by shipping their products to the United States. The American tariff, he said, made this impossible. But next day came a row of figures to prove that the United States, in the last three years,had imported greatly increased quantities of iron and steel. The tariff had not kept them out after all. Foreign tariffs, indeed, formidable as they appear, are not impenetrable. Protectionist countries must import something They cannot carry on their foreign trade by send- ing us goods and taking nothing in return. UP to the end of October our exports of manufactured goods for the present year show an increase of £8,000,000. That does not look like stagnation. Meanwhile,some of Mr.CHAMBERLAIN'S friends are dissatisfied, on reflection, with his plan for getting our food supplies from the Colonies. Mr. W. H. Mara.ocK points out, in the "Fortnightly Review," that the plan, as it stands, is of doubtful advantage to the Colonies, and no advantage at all to the British farmer. Why not protect him while you are about it? A two shilling duty on foreign wheat, and the admission of Colonial wheat duty free is not likely to stimulate British agriculture. So Mr. Mard,ocx suggests to Mr. CHAMBERLAIN a duty of sixteen shillings on the foreign producer and fourteen on the Colonial producer. This scheme would make an appreciable difference in the price of bread. Econor_nists of Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN'S school have persuaded themselves that duties may be clapped on pretty freely witnout raising the price of anything. Mr. Mar.a.ooK has workel out a little sum to show that his proposal would involve nothing more than "a poll-tax of fivepence-halfpenny a month," for which trifling cost we should gain the "restoration of British agriculture, an iccrease in the rural population, a rise in agricultural wages, and the ability to feed from the soil of our own country some 12,000,000 more persons than we are able to do at present." It reads likes grotesque travesty of 31I.CHAMBER• LAIN'd promises• to the electorate ; but Mr. MaLLook would not jest on this, or .any other subject, for untold gold. Experiments with the Fiscal system do no great harm, and contribute to the harmless gaiety of the nation, while they are confined to paper. It is as good as a new Christmas puzzle to write letters in the " Times" like those of the gentleman who signs himself "Tariff Rsformer," and who under- takes to show that " a low protective duty may not raise prices, or may even lower them, and yet benefit the protected manufacturer." And yet the manufacturer in countries where people apply the beautiful principles of Protection, instead of writ— ing about them, has been known to complain that' low duties are no good to him, and to agitate for increasing theta. Everyday we are favoured with the assurance that retaliation is what our coin- merce needs, the power of "hitting back," or, as Mr. BALFOUR puts it in his gentle academic way, "freedom to negotiate." Sir HENRY CaNfr- BELL-BANNERMAN ridiculed this panacea in his Newport speech. In the "Fortnightly" Mr. SHAW-LEFEVRE gives us a few in- structive cases of its possible application. Russia has the champion tariff of the world. n would be nice to retaliate on her manufactures for her disobliging treatment of our own. But in our imports from Russia, which are manufactures and not raw material, Mr. SHAW-LEFEVRE discovers • total of only £3lo,ooo,including paper,which stall° at £214,000, and may be itself regarded as rs 7 material, "looking to its general use and necessity. Indeed, some people may doubt whether paper eon be set down as a manufacture until the arguments of "Tariff Reformer" are printed on it. But how are we to shake the Russian tariff by retaliating on a trade which amounts to a total of £310,000? Our imports from America, which would lend themselves to retaliation, exclusive of food, raw material and necessary machinery, allow

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: a total of about a million sterling. They include caoutchoue and cotton manufactures, chemical products,watches, and glass. "Is it to be believed that a threat to impose duties, say of 10 or 20 per cent., on these articles, or even to prohibit them altogether, would have any effect whatever in inducing the American Congress to depart from its settled policy of Protection?' True, Mr CHAMBERLAIN does propose to tax food from America; and it is extremely probable that his policy would force him into the taxation of raw material all round, though he demurs to that soft impeachment at present. But making every allowance for possible developments of the great retaliation plan, does it really commend itself to a comwunity which has not thrown prudence to the winds?

We publish a somewhat remarkable letter in another column from the Secretary of the Labour Representation Committee, Mr. Buckley, in which through his committee, he charges " Liberal leaders," Conservatives, and the Licensed Victuallers' Association, with conspiring together to defeat Mr. Stott in Orford Ward, at the same time warning trades union delegates against this alleged organised opposition to "independent Labour." Mr. Buckley will, we hope, forgive us for very gravely doubting the accuracy of his statements. It is all very well for the Labour Representation Committee to make such a sweeping assertion, but can they prove it? We are so sceptical that we venture to assert that they cannot, and we challenge them, through their Secretary, to give chapter and verse for the allegation made in such condemnatory language. Who formed the 'power- ful organisation supported by Liberal leaders and the Licensed Victuallers' Association ? " We demand the names of these " Liberal leaders," for it is within our Knowledge that many well-known and staunch Liberals worked hard for Mr. Stott. This is a matter we shall not allow to rest where the Labour Representation Com- mittee has left it, and it is incumbent upon Mr. Buckley—and Mr. Stott also—if ,they are the men of honour we believe them to be, to prove the serious charges made with such a show of authority.

The Town Council was in its most talkative mood on Tuesday evening, and the consequence wad that the proceedings dragged along for nearly -lour hours. Almost every subject that came up provoked a lengthy discussion and several members spoke as often as they could without going outside the standing orders. They are getting rather into the habit of doing this sort of thing and if they do not reform we shall be compelled to pillory the chief time-wasters. It would be as well if they could realise that no man's opinions are counted very weighty if he volunteers them on every possible subject. The escape of gas was so great on Tuesday that even Councillor Stott, not- withstanding the blushing shyness of the new member, called attention to it in a comparison with meetings of workingmen which was not at all nattering to the Town Council. There is no doubt that when once the ball had been set rolling the Warrington councillors would take a lot of beat- ing in a talking competiti"n. 'Tis a great pity some of them do not become as weary as their auditors!

As usual, the business of most importance was -reserved for the end of the meeting, and once more the inquiry question figured largely. Councillor Maginn had a brand-new resolution on the agenda, which he proposed—and made no secret of the fact —in the interests of "the accused." After an hour's discussion it was withdrawn and this alone saved it from defeat. The Council is fairly-well convin- ced of thef act that a public inquiry is neither prac- ticable, nor likely to achieve the object aimed at by a thorough investigation. Then, too, the basis of inquiry has definitely been decided upon after a struggle lasting about a year, and there is not much desire to tamper with it again, even at the instance of Councillor Maginn. The latter made a powerful plea, nevertheless. He has all the typical Irishman's natural assurance .and eloquence—and a bit more—and if words and gestures could have turned the scale then Mr. Magma had carried his point. Earlier in the 'evening Councillor Tinnion had raised a very proper protest, on the new street question, against the absurd passing and rescinding of resolutions. He is, too, one of the original framers of the pre- sent basis of an inquiry, and yet he was so carried away by the eloquence of the hon. member for St. John's Ward as to make a speech which sug- gested that he was in favour of Councillor Maginn's motion. This does not seem quite consistent, anst there is no greater stickler for consistency in others , than Councillor Tinnion. The matter really stands adjourned for a month, and in the mean • ' time it is hoped that the Commissioners will be able 'to adjust their little differences and get the inquiry going again. Councillor Pemberton seemed fairly robust on Tuesday, and he will have a 'difficulty in convincing people that it is his state of health alone which prevents him taking his place alongside Mr. Norbury Williams and Councillor Horrocks. Once the inquiry makes progress and the useless- ness of Councillor Maginn's proposal will become more and more apparent. We can hardly con- ceive the Council seriously considering a public inquiry, seeing that it would possess none of the privileges of a legal court and, consequently, there would be absolutely no protection for either the witnesses or the press. The question of publicity does not affect, in the slightest, the thoroughness efficiency, or even all round fairness of the inquiry -and we hope the Council will have none of such inspired suggestions.

By-elections have been almost weekly events in Warrington of late and we are not finished with them even yet. Monday's contests in Orford and • Bewsey produced close struggles, supremacy being -eventually gained by Messrs. Stott and Gough with majorities of 80 and 50 respectively. We are glad to have the opportunity of at last con- • gratulating Councillor Stott on becoming the first representative of Labour in the Town Council. He has fought hard and fought long for the lionour,and we have confidence in his proving him- self worthy of the trust reposed in him. There are few more enlightened worgingfuen, and his complete knowledge of trades union affairs and the needs of the workers should be applied to advantage in the government of the town. Coun- cillor Gough has earned his prefix by perseverance and it says much for his determination and the strength of the Non-Trading eause that he was able to defeat the Liberal nominee, Mr. Owen Toole. The latter has no cause to be disheartened. He made an excellent "first attempt."

The Bewsey electors will be required to go to the poll again on Monday next, when the vacancy caused by the death of Councillor Brophy will be 'filled. Liberal and Non-Trader are again opposed, though the former, Mr. P. Peacock professes Non- Trading principles. It is one of the greatest triumphs of the Non-Trading cause, in our opinion,' that nearly every candidate of whatever political complexion, avows himself in sympathy with the Principle of no trading between members of the Council and the Corporation. With two candi- tlates of very similar views before them the electors must have considerable difficulty in cast- ing their votes. Personal considerations doubt- less weigh heavily, and what those are worth in t.he forthcoming struggle we have no meanstof 3udging. Though our prediction was falsified last Monday, we again favour the chances of the Liberal nominee in Bewsey Ward. Mr. Peacock is, in our view, the better man.

A peculiar legal point has been raised in con- nection with the impending election in Bewsey Ward, ard one, we believe, which has never been decided. It appears that the nomination paper handed in on behalf of Mr. James Dickenson, the Non-trading candidate, was subscribed to by a certain " Ann Eliza Williams." That name ap- _pears on the new burgess lists and at the time When the lists were made out, it was accurate in every detail. Since then, however, Ann Eliza

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: Williams has married and is now the wife of Joseph Bradbury. On Tuesday, Mr. Peacock lodged an objection to her signature on Cis nomination paper on the ground that Mrs. Bradbury, being a married woman, was not en- titled to sign it. The Town Clerk held the view that the nomination was bad, as " Ann Eliza Williams" did not exist in law, and as a married woman living with her husband could not vote,she therefore could not nominate. No such point, so far as we can learn, has been raised before, and one can well sympathise with the Mayor in not taking the responsibility of depriving the electors of making a selection. Nevertheless he held that the nomination was bad, and in proceeding with the election, Mr. Dickenson is running the risk of any legal proceedings which may eventually arise.

We have been asked to draw attention to the needs of the suffering Macedonians, for whom a relief fund has been opened in Warrington. So far, the subscriptions have come in but slowly, and the Committee urgently appeal for more generous help. Warrington, as a rule, is not behindhand in charity, and some splendid efforts were made, daring the war, for the benefit of the relatives of absent soldiers. The inevitable re- action seems to have taken place,and it is difficult to stimulate the response that is generally relied upon from Warrington. We believe that our towns- people have only to realize the terrible condi- tionof things in far-off Macedonia for the re- lief fund to be handsomely augmented.:Mr. Brails- ford, honorary agent of the Ma3eclonian Relief Fund Committee, reports from Kastoria that pleurisy and pneumonia, the result of exposure and weakness, are working terrible havoc among the population. The mortality is appalling. The peasants need clothing and food, for which m )nev is necessary, and unless help cornea from Eagland, Mr. Brailsford concludes, thousands will die this winter.

Our local Scotsmen celebrated in a manner be- fitting the occasion, the anniversary of St. Andrew the Patron Saint of Scotland. The Warrington Caledonian Association has had a chequered career during the fourteen years of its existence, but at the present time it is in a stronger position than ever, and Mr. Monro, the president, is entitled to take a fair meed of praise for the rrogress made. The dinner on Monday evening was a successful function and there was every indication that Scotsmen can thrive well on Warrington soil. Reference was made to the wandering propensities of Scotsmen, of which evidence is afforded by the fact that on St. Andrew's Day similar gatherings of Scotsmen were being held in all parts of the world in honour of Scotland's patron saint. In ascribing one reason for the Scotsman's success, often far away from his native hills, Mr. W. B. Roberts alluded to the superior educational facilities which Scotsmen enjoyed and which were taken full advantage of, England has lagged behind in educational matters. far too long. To-day more attention is being paid to higher education than formerly and now that the matter has been placed in the hands of the municipalities greater progress may be looked for. Meanwhile the Scotsman is entitled to some credit for showing us the way.

div.p: LOCAL NEWS.
Personal. We are pleased to learn that Major F. Mc T. 'Roorne of the South Lancashire Regiment, the late adjutant of Warrington Volunteers, has passed for promotion to a lientenant-colonelcy.

_ The Bishop of Chester collated the Rev.F.A.Screeton to the church and benefice of St. Thomas's, Hyde on Saturday. Mr. E. E. Lowe, formerly assistant curator at 'War- rington, and now curator of the Municipal Museum at Beaumont House, Plymouth, is delivering popular scientific lectures fortnightly at the Plymouth Corn Exchange during the winter months. Mr. Lowe's action in giving the lectures is purely voluntary, and at a recent meeting of the Museum and Art Gallery Committee hearty appreciation was expressed at the educational services he is rendering to the town, and a vote of thanks was passed. Crowded audiences have attended the lectures which are illustrated with lantern slides.

Colonel W. H. Moberley, formerly of the "Fighting Fortieth," South Lancashire Regiment, retired on Tuesday, under the age rules after over 37 years' service. He has had two tours in India with the 40th, of which he has been instructor of musketry. He has had command of the 37th Regimental District since 1899. The Rev.J.Gardham Reed occupied the -pulpitat Legh- street Primitive Methodist church on Sunday evening and referred to the death ef the Rev. Walter Graham, formerly minister of the circuit, who was deeply re- spected. The organist, Mr. Fred Podmore, played Chopin's " Dead March" as a mark of respect to the memory of the deceased. The choir sang "Gloria" (Mozart) with precision.

Screton, who entered upon his duties at St. Thomas's hurch, Hyde, on Sunday, was the recipient of a han some gift from the congrega- tion of Christ Church, eatchford, on Saturday evening. The presentation took lace at the annual sale of work in the Parish Room, there being a crowded attendance. Mr. John Fairclough, who was accompanied on the platiorm by several of the church officers made the presentation and said it was his pleasant duty to pre- sent to their late highly-respected Vicar a beautiful salver and a purse containing £lOl. (Applause.) Iff r. Screeton suitably acknowledged the gift

Longford Depot. At the meeting of the Rural Council on Wednesday, the Inspector reported that the nuisance arising from Longford Depot had been very bad during the past month. On Tuesday he visited the works in company. with the Surveyor but no further alterations had been made. He was given to understand that the Sanitary Works Committee met on the previous day and de- cided to make further alterations with a view to having the nuisance abated.—Mr. Knowles said that during the past month the, smell had been as bads as ever it had been. Tt could not be worse.—Mr. Forshaw said he thought the Corporation were as anxious as that, Council to abate the nuisance.—Mr. Longton: Nonsense. If they were they would have done some- thing long ago.—The Inspector was instructed to make further observations during the ensuing month with a view to definite action being taken.—The Clerk said he had always been convinced that the Corpor- ation were anxious to abate the nuisance.

Teachers' Annual Gathering. The members of the Warrington Certificated Class Teachers' Association combined business and pleasure very effectively on Friday evening last, when the annual meeting was held in Fairfield Schools. Mr. I. Bowen presided over a full attendance of members and an encouraging report of work done was given by the Secretary, Mr. S. W. Jeffery. The Association has only been formed this year, yet all certificated class teachers (except those quite recently appointed) within the County Borough of Warrington are in- cluded in its membership-12 new members being elected at this meeting. The following were appointed officers for the ensuing year : President. Mr. I Bowen ; vice-president,Mr. J. Pinnington ; treasurer Mr. 'l'. Edden ; secretary, Mr. S. W. Jeffery ; com- mittee : Misses E. Brookes, N. Fowler, E. Shaw, E. Pickavance, Messrs. F. H. Longshaw and J. Arm- strong. Business over, the remainder of the evening was devoted to enjoyment. Songs were pleasingly rendered by Miss N. Fowler, Mr. L. A. 'Puke and Mr. Dagnall, after which dancing was indulged in, Mr. F. J. Ernsom officiating at the piano in his usual able manner. Refreshments having, been served, the majority of the members took part in a whist drive which proved most interesting and enjoyable. Vote; of thanks to all responsible for the arrangements brought to a close a most successful evening. PUBLIC BENEFIT. UNDER. the CLOCK: for Bs BOCTS in LANCASHIRE.—Advt.

" Club Night" at the Academy. There was a very good attendance at the Old Academy on Thursday evening when I. Naden read a most interesting and thoughtful paper on "Types of Character: Hamlet and Lady Macbeth." The lecturer could hardly have selected two more " contrasty " characters from the whole realm of literature, and his study of the subject was an intellectual treat. Lady Macbeth was typified, of course, as an ambitious, designing and forceful female, while Hamlet figured on the contrary as one of those !invertebrate vacillating individuals who are always going to do something but never reach the point of achievement. Towards the close Of his paper—which was enlivened by many pithy allusions and Shakespearian readings—Dr. Naden drew deduction's from these two characters and applied them to phases of modern exist- ence in a manner which compelled individual thought and considerable dissent. The discussion which followed must have been highly gratifying to the lecturer, whose object it had been to provoke a debate on character; as exemplified in • Lady Macbeth) and Hamlet. Interesting, and widely diverse opinions, were expressed by the chairman (Mr. F. R. R oberts , Alderman Bennett. Mr. Sherbum, Mr. E. J. Hall, Mr. H. S. Page, Mr. J. M. Murray, Mr. Ti. G-reening, • Mr. Hill, and Mr: H. M. Ashton.—Votes of thanks to the Lecturer and Chairman concluded a very enjoyable evening. ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASs MINERAL WATERS.—Advt.

The Danger of Crossing Railway Lines. At Crewe County Petty Sessions on Monday, Thomas Ford, farmer, of Latchford, Warrington, was summoned for trespassing on the London and North- Western Railway, at Crewe Station, on September 20th. Mr. Lambert, of Enston, who prosecuted said notices were posted up and down the station warning passengers against the offence. ,Only the day before the offence a man was killed by crossing over the line at the same spot. The practice was very dangerous, and although warnings had frequently been given to passengers, this was the first time legal proceedings had been taken. The company were desirous of putting a stop to this sort of thing, not only in their own interests, but in the interests of the public. In the course of a year no fewer than 500 persons were killed in the United Kingdom whilst trespassing on the railway.—Detective Oliver and George Dale, porter at Crewe station, spoke as to seeing defendant cross the line, and a minute or two later an express dashed through the station.—Defend- ant said he did not see any notices against the offence and it was usual at stations near Warrington where he lived for passengers to cross the line ; in fact, there was no bridge. Notices should be posted up saying that persons trespassing on the line would be prosecuted.—Defendant was ordered to pay the costs. LADIES BEST GLACE BOOTS and SHOES, UNDER the CLOCK, BRID GE-STREET.—Adyt,

Master Willie Williamson, son of Mr. W. Williamson, of 10, York-street; Runcorn, won the first prize in pianoforte playing last S Lturday at the Warrington Eisteddfod. The test piece was " Warblings at Eve" by Brivley Richard, Mr. C. Lewis Jones, Mis. Ban. A.R.C.0., the adjudicator, spoke in the highest terms of Master Williamson's performance, placing him first out of the 24 competitors who playea. It will be remembered the same boy wn the first prize at the last Widnes Eisteddfod out of 32 competitors. Master Williamson's teacher is Mr. William Cooke, F.R.C.0., of 45, Waterloo-road, Runcorn.

Appointment of an Assistant Congregational Minister. At the annual business meeting in connection with Wycliffe Congregational Church on Thursday evening, it was decided to invite Mr. Harry Wall, of Notting- ham Institute to accept the appointment of assistant minister. If Mr. Wall elects to come to Warrington his work will be chiefly confined to the charge of Wycliffe Cockhedge Mission. Prior to entering the ,Nottingham Institute, Mr. Wall lived at Kirkham, near Preston. ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINERA. WATERS.—Advt. Riding Accident. A serious accident Mel Mr. Harry Bolton, late of Warrington, and now residing at Llandudno, on Friday afternoon, as he was returning from a ride in the country. When passing over the level crossing at Wilderspool, his horse, probably owing to the slippery state of the road, rolled over, throwing Mr. Bolton violently to the ground. Mr. Bolton sustained a broken collar bone, and his right leg was also badly bruised. He was conveyed to the Patten Arms Hotel. H. M. Good Work by a Warrington Firm. An excellent specimen of wood-carving is at present on view in the window of Messrs. J. M. Greenhalgh and Company's handsome and commodious premises, 138 and 140, Bridge-street. The armorial bearings of the Lancashire County Council have been carved on an oak panel and the work is considered to be a masterpiece of its kind. The firm have undertaken the pannelling in oak of a room and the armorial bearings will ppear above the centre of the mantel- piece. Such a piece of skilful workmanship reflects great credit upon Messrs. Greenhalgh and Company. Animated Pictures at the Parr Hail. Warringtonians vill have an opportunity of seeing some of the latest triumphs in animated photography at the Parr Hall next week, when, by means of the new imperial micrograph, a series of 10,000 pictures will be presented. This is the first visit of the com- pany to Warrington and the attraction will doubtless be great. Mr. Lester King, the oelehrated baritone, direct from the Alhambra Llndon will render songs illustrated with lantern slides. inrther particulars appear in our advertising columns. The Outbreak of Smallpox.

Warrington is once avin suffering from a revisita- tion of small-pox. Within the last three weeks over 40 cases have been isolated at the Sankey Sanatorium Fortunately the disease is of a mild type and there no necessity for undue alarm. The disease was intro- duced into the town by a tramp who stayed here for a short time undetected. The disease is chiefly located in the Orford Ward district, and the officials of the Corporation, under the able guidance of the Medical Officer (Dr. J. Guest Gornall) are doing their utmost to restrict tbe outbreak. Stations for re-vaccination have been opened where the public vaccinators attend at specified hours.

Liverpool and District Devonian Association. Our townsman, Mr., W. H. J. Jenkins. at the recep- tion held at the Bear's Paw, Restaurant, Liverpoel, on Thursday evening last, on the occasion of the annual banquet of this Society, had the honour and the pleasure of presenting General Sir Redvers Buller, V.C., G.C.8., the principal guest, with a copy of the 'first volume of the " Dawn," containing a sketch from the pen of gr. Jenkins, of the death of Jailor Takeman, an old Dartmoor worthy and sports- man; a keen forhunter nad naturalist, whose life was spent in close touch with na3mbers of the Buller family, and who tlok a deep interest in its welfare.

A hearty welcome, was accorded to the Re;.. Charles Harvey Cook,•the newly-appointed pastor of Cairo- Street Chapel, and Hrs. Cook at a meeting of the Congregation held in the schoolroom on Monday evening. An excellent tea was serftd and afterwards a largely-attended meeting was presided over by Mr. F. Monks, J.P.--Speeches of welcome and congratula- tion were delivered by the Chairman, Mr. William Long, J.P., Mr. J. R. Young, the Rev. J. C. Roberts, of Liverpool, the Rev. J. F. At Runcorn, on Thursday, before Messrs. F. J. Norman and E. Imison, William Henry. Johnson was sentenced to a month's hard labour for allowing his wife and children to become chargeable to the guardians of Run- corn Union.—Mary Ann Rose, a well-known character, was charged with stealing a shawl from Martha Alice Crank, and she was committed for fourteen day—John Carney, apprehended in Widnes by Detective Motters- head was remanded on a charge of stealing a box of "Cabinet" cigars from the Holyhead Harbour beerhouse on Wednesday. LOCKS FATALITY AT RUNCORN.

Mr. It. Dobson, district coroner, conducted an inquiry at Runcorn on Saturday into the circumstances attend- ing the death of John Santley, of Albert-street, Run- corn, who died on Friday from a spinal disease caused by an accident at the Bridgewater Locks about twelve months ago. Mr. J. Evans attended on beh tlf of the Ship Canal Company. Ellis Clarke, 4, Wyvern-place, night watchman in the employ of the company, said he went to Santley's cabin on the night of the accident, and saw him sitting in front of the fire. He told witness that he had fallen down some steps, and could not walk. There was a lamp a few yards from the steps near the pierhead. Dr. MacLennan said he was called in to deceased,and found him suffering from severe bruises on both legs, sprained ankles, and an injury to the middle of the spine. His legs were much discoloured and swollen. Witness had constantly attended him since the accident. A disease of the spinal cord deve- loped, and was the cause of death. The jury returned a verdict in a.ccordmice with the medical testimony. HEAVY FAILURES OF A HAT,TON FARNIER.

At the Warrington Bankruptcy Court yesterday before Mr. Registrar Ridgway, JosephiWalker of Hallwood Farm, Halton, near Runcorn, came up for his public examination. Mr. Johnson, assistant Official Receiver„ conducted the examination. Mr. Bancroft, solicitor Northwich appeared for the debtor and Mr. Willett solicitor, of Warrington, for the creditors. Mr. C. J. Hughes of Northwich appeared as a trustee. The state- ment of Affairs showed the gross liabilities were £2,085 18s. ss. The assets were estimated to pro- duce .£706 10s., levying a deficiency of £1,379 Bs. sd. He alleged the causes of failure to be" losses of cattle, colts and pigs; bad trade, bad weather; and heavy interest on loans." The Official Receiver in his obser- vations said that the bankrupt commenced business in February, 1895 with £2OO cash and horses, carts, &c., worth about £lOO. In April 1895, his wife gave him £l5 and five cows, but not having kept any books of account whatever, he could not file the prescribed defici- ency account. He first became aware of his insolvency about twelve months ago and had since contracted part of the existing liabilities.—The examination was ad- journed.

div.head: CO-OPERATIVE CONFERENCE AT RUNCORN
div.p: CO-OPERATIVE CONFERENCE AT RUNCORN

A conference ofthe `6Cels'iiii;3 and North Wales District Co-operative Association was held in the Run- corn Co-operative Hall on Saturday afternoon. Mr. W. Millington. chairman of the Runcorn Society, pre- sided over a large attendance of delegates. The quarterly report of the Executive Committee was read and approved.—A discussion followed upon the diffi- culties of store management and the question was raised as to whether the manager should have the power to engage and dismiss employees. The general opinion was that the power to suspend only should be invested in the manager and that the larger question of engage- ment and dismissal should be left to the committee.— Mr. T. IL Priestley, of Runcorn, read a paper on "The comparative merits of high and low dividends."—About fourteen delegates took part in the discussion.—Mr. Robert Wright,secretary to the district, moved a resolli- tion re-affirming the conference resolution that there should be a fixed dividend of 2s. 6d. in the I.—Mr. J Johnson (Manchester) seconded.—Mr. W. E. Dudley (Runcorn) moved an amendment, which was carried, that the question be left to the individual societies.— It was, however, the general opinion of -the delegates that a dividend of from 121 to 15 per cent should not be exceeded.—lt was decided to hold the next confer- ence at Mold Junction.—The delegates were afterwards entertained to tea.

There is a great difference between. becoming a party-man and taking a part. I think I can shew Mr. 0. Buckley in a sentence or two that he is the Azrty man whilst lam only takin,ra part. The latter denotes only such an occasional or sub-ordinate interference .in party affairs as is consistent not only with due attention to one's private concerns but with a preserva tion of the ordinary intercourses of s)ciety and civility between righteous and fellow-citizens, th)ugh of opposite opinions. The former, on the contrary, signifies such an attachment to party as influences the whole character, and gives the tone and colour to a man's conduct through life. It is the ruling passion. and like all other passions scorns the control of good sense and moderation. Mr. Buckley's present position is one of selfish isolation. lie is bound down to sup- port a Trade Unionist wh .tlier he is a worker or not and the problem of the labour question must receive his undivided sympathy and support: If that is not being a "Party.man" perhaps he will explain to us what he Understands by the term. I trust, therefore, that Mr. Buckley will see that my intentions are quite as honourable- as his undoubtedly are, and whilst he calls me black a little thought should be given to his own condition.
THE MADNES OF MANY FOR THE GUN OF A FEW.

It has long been a favourite maxim that all parties are fundamentally alike, and that, however they may be discriminated by adverse denominations, their principles of action are essentially the same. The doctrine is a very convenient one and may apply to those whose interests are practically the same,namely, self. Why; the whole structure of party is built upon that foundation and unless we, individually, see to it we shall earn for ourselves, and which ought to be placed over the entrance to all our societies, that well deserved maxim" the madness of many for the gain of a few." Why cannot we determine to push forward representatives who will pledge themselves to work for and earnestly support ' such measures as will bring happiness into the homes of every individual,.—whether he is a Trades Unionist orinot,rather tha.n allow our- selves to quarrel over some side issue? Such persons would greatly enhance the spirit of the ballot-box and instead. of being canvassed and cajoled into voting, the electorate would see to it that their support was given without such undesirable methods being resorted to. There would then be no necessity for the hope that someldav canvassing would b 3 made illegal. People are shouting out for "reform, reform, reform," and yet when the opportunity preSents itself many of them outrage their own consciences by being bought over to vote for the candidate who can treat their stomachs the most.lt is debasing to know that the some- what vulgar maxim readily applied by the foreigner to us as a nation, viz.," the way to an Englishman's heart and mind is through his stomach" has so much that is true in it. lam not writing against the working- man's candidate. G-od forbid. My objects in writing are to have the whole subject thrashed out; to sift the chaff from the corn; to know that there is no selfish motive in a man's candidature; to get a representa- tive for the people; to create a desire in the minds of those who have hitherto held aloof, or have been led by the neck like a beast, to utilise that power which was given to them after a hard struggle, and vindi- cate their character and desires by taking a keen interest in the forthcoming election which will mean so much to the country and the common good.

div.head: LIBERAL AND LABOUR.
div.p: LIBERAL AND LABOUR.
Mr. Osborne and His Critics.

I have been honoured with replies to my last letter from the President of the Trades and Labour Council, Mr. Joseph Podmore, jun.., and the Secretary of the Labour Representation Committee, Mr. 0. Buckley and I thank them .both for the kindly interest they are taking in this controversy. I would again point out that it is not my desire to misrepresent the Trades Council; and I would further implore my friend, Mr. Podmore, not to iniirmate that I "have been imposed upon by some mischief-maker." He has replied to my friendly criticism twice; as he has used the ex- pression on each occasion it is getting tiresome., I have already proved beyond any question of doubt that a certain society of workingmen was prevented from being allied with the Trades and Labour Council on account of "the revolutionary character of the debates at its meetings." Whether such debates took place "in Mr. Podtnore's tim3 " or not I do not know, nor does it really affect the argument, because as a matter of fact that Society is still outside the influence of the Trades and Labour Council. I hope, therefore, Mr. Podmore will admit that my authority for stating my facts is as honourable as his own, and that he will drop that unnecessary blatant exprassion, If the Trades and Labour Council has improved so much, as he would have Us believe, under his con- ductorshiP and.l have no reason to doubt it, I con- gratulate him most heartily and wish him joy in his achievement. There is still hope that before long they will see that by their hastily contemplated action in bringing Mr. Wilkie from Newcastle and caosing his masters and himself to entertain expecta- tions which, at present, cannot be realised, they are allowing themselves to be hurried into an unfortunate position which will do the object they have so mach at heart incalculable damage.
SO-CALLED SOCIALISTS

I have previously stated that there ought to be some " giving and taking" in the matter of represfintation of the people and, of course, quite naturally, I have been accused of asking for more than is due to me. Somehow, some so-called socialists imagine that the distribution of this world's gifts should be left entirely in their hands and those who are at heart socialists must be satisfied with the crumb that fall from the s3-called socialists' table. If you ask for a little you may depend up mit you will ask for too much. Ido not wish to descend to the depths of socialism, as it is evidently understood by some of its ranters, but I would most earnestly implore those who are anxious to see a brighter side to the deplorable c3ndition of things which we are lab3uring under at present to think this matter out 'carefully and rati wilily and realize that no good can come of accusing others of asking for too much when their own dispssition is to keep everything themselves. Surely, it is better to acquire our objects one at a time and be sure of them than to ask for them all at once and get none.
.1. SMALL OPEN SPACE.

I have already, in a previous letter, replied to Mr. Podmore, so for a moment, I would like to turn my attention to the criticism of my remarks made by Mr. 0. Buckley. He asks" The Editor" for a small open space and then stands on his head in one earner of it whilst he breathlessly refers to the question of La- bour representation. His remarks coupled with his uncertain actions are altogether too much for him and becoming exhausted he gradually drops from his uncomfortable position by appealing to me to desist from dealing with the subject whilst looking through " party spectacles." It has been said, and perhaps there is sOna.e truth in the remark. that there is no man ". so blind as he who won't see:" Probably, ram placed in that category; and, whilst I am so selfish in my motives: he is ram- pant on an " individualist " platform. If he is the Secretary of the Labour Representation Committee, as , he says he is, I imagine, that his Committee will int altogether be pleased with the confession that he is not a party-man, and that they will no doubt soon , find a Secretary who will look after their interests. Really, it is surprising how a p irty-m in condemns another man because he is taVng a part in current events which, as a young citizen, he is fully entitled to do—even if he was not born .when Mr. Wilkie began his labours. I wonder how long Mr. Pod.more has been working!
`! PARTY-MAN" AND " TAKIKG A PART."

div.head: PROPOSED PUBLIC MEMORIAL TO FALLEN SOLDIERS.
div.p: PROPOSED PUBLIC MEMORIAL TO FALLEN SOLDIERS.
The Mayor (Alderman William Bolton) has written the following letter to townsmen likely to assist in the above scheme :
Town Hall. Warrington. 4th December 1903. SOUTH LANCASHIRE REGLUENT

Dear sir,—The proposal to erect a public memorial to the officers and men of the above regiment who lost their lives in the recent war in South Africa has been brought to my notice with a request that I should take steps for forming a committee to carry out such a proposal. The officer commanding the 8/40th Regimental Dis- tricts and the officers of the Sauth Lancashire Regi- ment whom I have consulted cordially approve of the proposal and have agreed to merge the handsome sum already raised by them regimentally towards the cost of a public memorial. I have ventured to call a meeting to be held at the Town Hall here on Wednesday afternoon next at 3 o'clock and I shall be glad if you will favour me with your attendance to consider the proposal and to appoint a committee to take such further action as the meeting may decide.

The Rev. W. J. Spriggs-Smith, Vicar of Terringtoa St. John's Wisbech. Norfolk, delivered a lecture on " Chamberla,inism," in Providence Schoolroom, Stock- ton Heath, on Tuesday evening. The meeting had been arranged by the Stockton Heath branch of • the Knutsford Division Liberal Association and was largely attended. Mr. Thomas Birchall, J.P., pre- sided and there were present on the platform the Revs. J. S. Hughes and H. Dannico, and Messrs. Joseph Mounfleld, A. H. Dann, W. J. Brown, W. H. Sherburn, and E. Lloyd Jones (hon. secretary). Mr. E. Lloyd Jones said he had received letters of apology for non-attendance from Mr. A. J. King, Ghe prospective candidate for the Knutsford Division, Alderman Pier- point, and Councillors Tinnion and Brough. THE CHAIRMAN AND THE TARIFF QUESTION. The Chairman said he was very pleased to be there that night to meet so many young men who were now engaged in that district, and one, he was goiag to say, of the nests of Toryism, to uphold the old flag. (Hear, hear.) Let him tell them for their encouragement that he began his political career sixty years ago in the Market-place. He was then an enthusiastic young Radical of thirteen, and it was in the Market-place that he heard Richard Cobden. Ha should never forget that scene, for he could see Cobdea then as he stood on an extemporised platform near the old Barley Mow with two stalwart Warrington gentle- men whom they had all learned to honour—John Gordon McMinnies and Peter Rylands. (Applause.) It was from these man he learnt his political alphabet, and since that time he had never had occasion to regret his Radicalism. (Applause.) He had a firmer faith in it to-day than he had then. He never founded his Liberalism on expediency,bu'; on principle. (Hear.hear.) They could take his word for it that if a political faith or creed would not stand the simple test of Christianity it was not worth having. (Hear, hear.) By simple Christianity he meant a verydifferent thing from a'great deal that was going on just now—asort of decorative business that ha was afraid the Master would not know if He saw it—a kind of Christianity that did net mind riding rough-shod over the consciences of Nonconform- ist brethren. He saw they had been having a Tory meeting at Stockton Heath. It was one of the old kind with a great deal of "Rule-Britannia" and not much argument. (Laughter). Their friends were very good at that. There was a great deal- of sentiment but when he examined the speeches he found they ware very disappointing. It was unfortunate for their Tory friends that the Blue Books of the Government had only to be looked up to show how false and futile their arguments were. If they could suppress the Blue Books they would do a good thing for themselves. Then there was- that singular letter from their good old friend Mr..Menks. who said their workmen were playing one or two days a week. This he gave'as a sort of reason for changing our present Free Trade system to Proteetion. About that time, the New York correspondent of the "Daily Telegraph" wrote stating that the bar iron makers in America had come to the conclusion that they must drop their pro- duction :50 per cent which meant three days a week in which the workmen would be idle. If two days a week were an argument for Protection he should think three days a week on the other side were a stronger argument for changing from Protection to Free Trade. He (Mr. Birchall) could tell them candidly that he 4id not want America to adopt Free Trade. He dreaded such an eventlThey werehaeging a millstone round their necks. by Protection. They had the cheapest iron and coal and all .sorts of advantages and yet they could not build an iron vessel within 40 per cent.of the cost that the making of such a vessel would incur in England. That was because they had made everything dearer by Protection. Mr. Edwin Woods, who was a Tory of the old kind—something like the man who always wore blue spectacles and saw nothing that was not blue—told him some time ago that he had been buying rods from the Germans at 2s. Gd. per ton cheaper than they could be bought in England and he did not like it. He therefore advocated Mr. Chamber- lain's remedy which was to put a 10 per cent, duty on the rods. The result would be that he would have to I pay us. 4d. per ton more for the rods. Of course, English rod-makers would advance to the same price, and how would that help Mr. Woods? They had met that night to hear a lecture on that interesting subject " C'namberlainism." Not Arthur " Chamberlainisrn," but Joseph" Charnberlainism." There was a great difference between those two men. Arthur was a man who could see straight; Joseph could, but did not. He had watched Mr. Joseph Chamberlain's career for a Igood while, but he had been a most disappoint- ing man to him, for he once had had great hope,s of him. It was not a mere inconsistency. He could understand a man advancing from narrowness Ito breadth like the late Mr. Gladstone but he could not I understand a man with the training of Mr. Chamber- Jain going back from breadth to narrowness. Mr. Chamberlain was brought up in the most Liberal of ' religious sects and yet he stood by the injustices inflicted on the Nonconformists by the Education Act. Although he had not had much to say about it he had consented to it and was equally guilty. They used to hear a great deal about the terribly-oppressed Outlander who was only getting 21 adayoccasioually andsuffering greaewrongs which Mr Chamberlain was going to redress Did they ever hear of the Outlander now? He heard much about packing South Africa with Chinamen and niggers because they did got give trouble With trade unions. (Laughter). They could be easily managed—A whip was perhaps useful occasionally (Laughter). Mr. Chamberlain was once a temperance reformer but he now stood by the trade and would give them almost unlimited licence. He would limit magisterial control and deprive them of their present indefeasible right to consider the wants of the community. Mr. Chamberlain had played many parts and one could only think what a man with his great abilities might have done for the nation had he taken up the cause of the people. (Aapianse.) In calling upon the lecturer, Mr. Birchall said it was really pleasant to find a clergyman who had some fellow-feel- ing for his Nonconformist brethren. (Applause.) THE LECTURE.

The R3V. W. .1. Spriggs-Smith commenced his lecture by defining man's duty to himself and to the State. He then invited his hearers to join with him in a practical consideration of Chamherlainism from a citizen's, a parent's, and a teacher's point of view. As a citizen he considered from a national point of view they were living in cloudy and dark days. He had no hesitation in saying that there was no man or woman in that room who ha.l passed 50 years of age, who had seen darker or cloudier days than they saw tolday. He might say they were days which their forefathers would never have dreamt of as possible at the beginning of the twentieth century. The Govern- ment of to-day was not; ashamed to trespass and deprive them of their civil rights —taking the education question as an example. (Applause.) He much regretted that their Anglican bishops—with one noble exception—were not ashamed to speak and record their votes in the House of Lords to rob them of their religious rights and to invade the domain of conscience. Conscience was sacred to Gad and man, and it was a sphere which admitted of no intrusion on the part of bishop, priest, or statesman. (Atmlause.) The Arch- bishop of Canterbury recently said the Bishops had no more to do with the Education Bill'than the people he was addressing. He (theaspeaker) had copies of seven resolutions passed in Convocation in 1901, drawn up by a Joint Committee of York and Canter- bury, and six of them were contained in the. Bill. (Cries of "shame.") He had no hesitation in saying that what the Archbishop of Canterbury had said was outside the bounds of truth. (Applause.) He said as a clergyman, and he had no fear of being truthfully contradicted, that the Church had trampled upon the rights of citizens. The Education question was not a question for Archbishops or Nonconformist ministers to settle. The communicants of the Church and the members of chapels were not a third of the nation and the nation must settle the question. (Ap- plause.) Alluding to the compensation question the lecturer said thatliMessrs.Balfour and Chamberlain had their way the liquor traffic would become a heavier yoke upon them and upon their children. Could any man stand still in the face of that? Chamberlainism was a national suicidal mission. He did not belie ye for one "moment that the fiscal proposals were the result of conviction. One of the main factors of Mr. Chamberlain's propaganda was to hide up the South African War—(applause)—and the WarCarnmission report. The very fact that he was so absolutely sileet on the subiect proved that. Another lobjeat he had in view was to shunt the Education ques- tion. if he sueceede I in that, their children for generations w mild suffer from the unhappy divisions in religious bodies. (Hear. hear). They hai no right to burden the children's minds and to divide them into little sections. \Viten a child cante of age, let him decide that for himself. in the mtantime the parent could train up his child in the religioas belief he em- bracedandthe Sunday sehools existed to heln parents in that respect. Another idea of those who brought forward the fiscal proposal was to steal a march on passive re- sisters. He said fearlessly that the action of the passive resisters had saved Flagland at the present moment. !(Apolaese.) Tao first meanie who expected to benefit by Protection were the Itn-low ism as their anticipated an increased rent roll. Some parsons would also benefit as tithes would be increased. The speaker painted out that whereas the price of wheat per quarter iw.l-;11,1 I ,at %4 275. 64., in Germany under Protection, it was 355. 6d. The wages per week for skilled labour in England averaged 42ss. 6d.. in Ger- many the amount was 255. 6d. The hours of work in England were 48 per week, compared with 72 in Germany. Mr. Chamberlain told them that the con- sumer would not pay the tax on corn, but that it would be paid by the foreigner. That was deception all along the line. Referring to the state of affairs in Protection- ist countries the speaker said he spent eight years in Spain and as an instance of the price of goods, there he had to pay 4s. 6d. for tea which cost him is. 6d. in England. Mr. Smith concluded his address with a criticism of the Educat!on Act. • He also eipressed himself in favour of labour represen-

tation, the restoration to trade unions of the rig hts which had been taken from them, the holding of all elections on one day, and the stoppage of the sale of intoxicating liquors on that day. (Applause).
"THE GOOD OLD TIMES."

As instancing the state of affairs before the introdu9- tion of Free Trade the chairman pointed out that In his younger days a good joiner, if he could get any work earned £1 a week, a bricklayer 18s. and a labourer 11s. The hours were long and children of seven and eight were sent to the factories. THE GOVERNMENT'S POLICY CONDEMNED.

The Rev, H. Donnie° moved the following resolu- tion: "That this meeting, in tne light of the revela- tions contained in the report of the South African War Commission, and in view of the enormous increase in the national expenditure, considers the continued con- duct of public affairs by the present Government to be a gross d 'tiger to the State. In particular this meeting condemns the Education Act of 1902-3, and expresses the conviction that the education question can never be settled save by legislation, which will place under general popular control elementary schools maintained out of public funds. This meeting also condemns the proposed reversal of our fiscal polfcv by Mr. Balfour and Mr. Chamberlain, and calls upon'all who are inter- ested in our commercial prosperity and social con- dition of the people, to resist by every means in their power pia*fosals which if adopted will raise the price of food and all manufactured goods, reduce trade by increasing the cost of production, endanger our relations with our Colonies and threaten the stability of our Empire. (Applause.) All he would say in regard to the War Commission report Was that such a piece of crass ignorance and criminal incompetency had never been revealed by any other modern Government. Of the Education Act let him say that it was not an Education Act but a priests' Act and an endowment of Popery. A more outrageously iniquitous measure had never been placed on the statute book of the realm. They, the Nonconformists, would not allow the matter to die. They intended to keep it to the front; and the only condition that they would agree to was that all schools should be placed under popular control. In regard to the fiscal question, Mr. Chamberlain had distinctly said that his proposals were not put forward in the interests of the country but in the interets of the colonies. At the same time, Mr. Chamberlain ought to • remember that the United Kingdom was just as large a part of the empire—and a more important part—than Canada, Australia and South Africa. He must not • jeopardise the in- terests of this country in the interests of our colonies. We had already sacrificed £150,000,000 and thousands of lives for a country that was not worth a. snap of the fingers, If our empire could only be main- tained by such sacrifices on the part of the mother country, let the empire go. It was not worth retain- ing. Only 12 per cent of our total trade was done with the colonies. Oar total exports amounted last year to 293 millions the colonies took 53 millions and the foreigner 2:35 millions and were we to jeopardise 88 per cent. of our trade for the sake of that 12 per cent? The idea of a self-contained emnire was not only irreligious but it was immoral. God had made alI people one physically, and Gods purpose was that they should all be made one morally. God endowed different coun- tries with varied soils and climates, and had done it in order that all the people of various countries should reap and enjoy the advantages of those countries. A preferential tariff would prevent that. In conclusion the rev, gentleman urged his hearers to fight to the death the fiscal policy, the tax upon the poor man's table, and the fiscal fetters which would ruin our coun- try, and to stand up for Free Trade—the cause which rested upon the glorious double foundation of the beneficence of God and the brotherhood of men. (Applause). Mr. J. Mounfield seconded and said that Chamber- lainisin to his mind, meant expediency. He remembered the time when Mr. Chamberlain thought it expedient to catch the vote of the agricultural labourer and he pro- posed three acres and aCow for every agricultural labourer. What had been done to redeem that promise? Nothing. What had he done to give the old age pensions which he promised? He knew well that they were not within the range of practical politics, and he also knew that his fiscal policy was not a practical thing. Mr. Chamberlain promised the workingmen a rise of wages. Were the work- ingmen in highly protected countries better off than they were in England? When he was in Ger- many he saw workingmen going for their wages at one o'clock on Sunday. He should be very sorry to see the working classes of this country come down to the level of the highly-protected countries. Thousands of old horses were shipped from England to Germany,Holland and Belgium and he had seen them hung up in the shop windows in those countries. The working classes fed on them. He hoped the English people would not be so foolish as to exchange the many privileges they enjoyed for a phantom. The new policy was not for the benefit of the workingmen but of the manufacturers and land- owners.
The resolution was carried without dissent. THANKS.

div.head: CHAMBERLAINISM.
div.p: CHAMBERLAINISM.
REV. W. J. SPRIGGS-SMITH LECTURES
AT STOCKTON HEATH. Mr. B!rchall, J.P., and the Days of Protection.

Mr. W. H. Sherburn moved a vote of thanks to the Rev. W. .1. Spriggs-Smith and the Chairman. He re- marked that it needed some courage to come out from the Church of England and speak so plainly as Mr. Spriggs-Smith had done. His hearers should read some of the old Lancashire poets if they wished to learn something about life before Free Trade was introduced Protectionist countries, he continued, made million- aires and poor people. Mr. Longland seconded. To his mind the education question was as important and probably more important than the fiscal question. They ought to have the school managers properly elected and that was the only thing which he, at any rate, would be satisfied. He felt a very great deal stronger on that matter than on the fiscal question. In putting the motion to the meeting Mr. E. Lloyd Jones observed that there were Free Traders in Stockton Heath who would be prepared to debate the matter in public with Mr. H. J. Westbrook. The priloosition was heartily carried and the Rev. W. J, Spriggs-Smith and the chairman having acknow- ledged the compliment the meeting concluded.

div.head: WARRINGTON CALEDONIAN ASSOCIATION. Concert by the Glasgow Select Choir.
div.p: WARRINGTON CALEDONIAN ASSOCIATION. Concert by the Glasgow Select Choir.

The annud "gathering of the clans" in Warrington on St. Andrew's Day has for a second time been followed by a concert in Parr Hall, in which the singing of the Glasgow Select Choir, under Mr. J. Millar- Craig's conductorship, has been appropriately made the feature.

The audience on Tuesday evening, though not crowded, was fairly numerous in all parts of the hall except the first reserved seats. But it made up for its - comparative sparcity in numbers by an evident deter- mination to find both edification and enjoyment in a musical programme, the strong national flavour of which has clearly yet a potent charm for Warring- tonians. Ti) the more discriminating, however, it was clear that the singing of the choir did not quite reach the high standard attained last year. Whether well- founded• or not, one received the impression that, collectively, members were not up to their usual form. Some little slips and lapses pointed rather to lack of concentration arising possibly from the weariness of much travelling than to any innate shortcomings in the choir itself. The failure of the male voices to rise to the occasion, as they certainly did at a former visit, in "The Wedding of Shon Maclean" may be instanced as a case in point. Nevertheless there remained much that was undoubtedly excellent in the ensemble singing of the choir. "Blow, gentle gales," "The March of the men of Harlech" and "'The Cruiskeen Lawn" had all many meritorious points in their interpretation; while in "Ye mariners of England "—probably the most exacting of the choral items—there was so obvious a. determination to "go for" the sentiment, as resulted in a most artistic presentment of this rousing part- song. The Choral Ode " Sennacherib (Patterson) proved somewhat monotonous in the dulness of its note against note setting. Something more varied in musical treatment in the middle of the piece would have been both grateful and enlivening. But if, as we hive said, the male voices proved unequal on Tuesday to the exigencies of "Short Maclean's Wedding "the united choral forces attackedthe kindrei theme portrayed in "Barney Brallaghan " with such ' spirit and zest as fairly aroused the audience's enthusiasm; "Macgregor's gathering " and "Scots wha ha'e" being the encore numbers given here and after the "March of the men of Harlech" in response to well- deserved and long continued applause. It occurs to one as taco much to expect that, having done conscientious duty in the choir individual members should be expected also to undertake the burden of solo singing, and one feels that some other means might be found of gaining desirable relief and contrast in the programme of these concerts. In spite of such difficul- ties, however, Miss Galloway, Mrs. Laurie, Mr. Macfarlane Brockett and Mr. George Watt filled the breach bravely in the singing of some songs embodying it is to be regretted, sentiment and reminiscence too pronouncedly Scotch in character to answer fully their obvious purpose. Mr. Brockett is endowed with a light and pleasing tenor voice but he is too unemotional in his style to do full justice to such a love-song as "The Lea Rig." Miss Galloway in a sweet and clear soprano (Teak daintily enough with " The bonnie banks o' Loch Lomon," while Mrs. Laurie sang so sympathetically of the" Auld Scotch Songs" as to gain a well merited encore. Nor was Mr. Watt's "Border ballad" less admirable or less successful, his manly declamation of the martial feeling of this fine song marking his possession of distinctly artistic instincts. Mr. Nelson Jackson was in exceptionally good form and, catching the prevailing contagion, he hit at the onset the audience's humour in that drollery of his "A Scotch coon song," following up a most unequivocal success with anecdote, parody and mimicry,all of which while hugely funny in recital and performance, were never tainted with vulgarity. Mr. J. Millar Craig wended the baton during the singing of the Glasgow choir with rare skill and judgment, while Mr. Herbert Cross's accompaniments to the songs &c., were in excellent taste.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

IMPUDENT ROBBERY AT WARRINGTON. At the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday Mary, Ann M`Carthy and Edward Nl`Carthy, last from Wigan were charged on remand with stealing from the person of Richard Clare in the yard of the Queen's Hotel, Sankey-street, at eight o'clock on Monday last week a silver watch and rolled gold chain, valued £2. They pleaded not gnilty.—The Chief Constable said the prosecutor who was a Northwich youth, and a moulder Caine to Warrington from London to take a situation. He arrived about 2:30 on Monday week, and outside the station mot the female prisoner who offered to find him lodgings. Prosecutor foolishly gave her a 'sovereign and his portmanteau, containing articles of clothing, &c. She went away, and later in the day she again met him, and introduced the male prisoner and another man as her brothers: They went to the Queen's Hotel, and had drinks together. The woman then induced Clare to go I into the yard of the hotel, and the two mew followed. They hustled and jostled the prosecutor whilst the female prisoner's hand 3 were " going about his cloth- ing." As soon as they went away Clare missed his watch and chain, and, along with a youir, man named Hallows, followed the female prisoner. *They caught her in Castle-street, and Clare demanded his watch. She -first denied having it, but subsequently said, "-Don't get me pinched. I'll get it for you." She then returned to the Queen's Hotel, where the male prisoner was. A large crowd had now assembled, an d the male prisoner crouched behind du counter where he apparently handed the watch to the female prisoner, who then returned it to Clare, minus the back. Prisoners were subsequently arrested by Superintendent Monaghan. The woman was a notorious character, and the male prisoner cohabited with her.—After several witnesses had been called for the prosecution, the two prisoners denied having committed the theft. They said the prosecutor had given the watch to them. They were all in drink at t'ae time.—The bench ..decided to send the female prisoner to gaol for two months, and the male prisoner for one month.

div.head: Warrington Borough P3lie.l Court.
div.p: Warrington Borough P3lie.l Court.
Minor Cases. MONDAY —Before the Mayor (in the chair), Alderman Smethurst, Councillor Thornton, Messrs. Birchall, _

, Hayward and Wright. AN IMPUDENT THlEF.—James Taylor, who is well known to the police was charged with stealinr, a pair of boots of the value of 7.3.11 d. the property of sYressrs, Scales and Son, Bridge-street.—The Chief Constable said the boots were hanging at the entrance of the shop, and prisoner actually walked into the place with the boots wrapped in a coat which he carried under his arm. On being questioned prisoner said he knew nothing about the boots, and when they had been taken from him he was allowed to go. Constable Clough, who had been watching the man, took him into custody. Prisoner had been before the magistrates 13 times and he lived by theft.—He was sentenced to three months' imprisonment. OBSCENE LANGUAGE.—James Htlitley was, on the information of Constabie Lewis, fined ss. and costs for making use of obscene language in Erwood-street on Saturday afternoon. TITESDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton (in the chair), Dr.

Fox and Mr. J. R. Young. &BEGGING- IM POSTER.—Thomas Parkinson, last from Bolton, was charged with begging in Mersey-street at two o'clock on Monday afternoon. Police-constable -dough stated that he received information on Monday of two men going about with begging letters, and he kept a watch for them. He saw the prisoner go into the shop of Mr. Carter and present the following letter :—"Dallam Forge, Novemly,r regret to state that part of our works (No. 2 side) has been stopped this last live weeks owing to a breakdown. The bearers; Thomas Parker sad James Hampson, two of the unemployed, are married men, and are in needy cir- cumstances. I have assisted them myself, and I can recommend them to the charity of others.—(Signed), John Higson, foreman." From inquiries witness had learned that the whole letter was a fraud. The prisoner did not work at Dallam Forge, No. 2 mill had not been stopped, and there was no foreman named Higson. Prisoner was arrested, and on the way to the -police station he admitted that the whole thing was a fraud. Superintendent Monaghan said the prisoner was before the bench two years ago on a similar charge, but it was Monks's Forge which was stopped then. He had recently been committed at Lytura, and in all he had been thirtytimes before di fferont courts. Prisoner was -sent to gaol for one mouth with hard labour.
