div.head: INQUIRY.
div.p: THE INQUIRY.
CERESPONDENCE WITH COMMISSIONERS.
AlOth.lr DiSCIISSIOII in th?. Chambgr.
COUNCILLOR MAGINN INTROOUSES MOTION. •

The Qaestion of a Mlle or Private Inquiry. The subject of the inquiry into the trading transac- tions of the Corporation was ag tin under discussion at the meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tues- day evening. In the first place the following correspondence was read :—" Town Clerk's °lice,- Warrington, 23rd November, 1903. Dear Sir,—l am instructed by the three Commissioners appointed by the Corporation. to inform you that they are prepared to meet the Commissioners appointed by the Non-trading Association, and to make arrangements for proceeding with the ineuiry on the lines indicated by the recent resolution of the Town Council, with rezard to the reporting and printing of the proceedings. The Corporation Commissioners are prepared to meet you on Monday or Tuesday, the 39th November or let December, at 11. o'clock in the forenoon, in the Town Hall, and they instruct me to roiliest that you will be good enough to favour me with a reply to this letter on or before Saturday morning next.—Yours truly, J. LYON Wiarrrra.;." The above letter was sent to Councillors Horrocks and Pemberton; and Mr. S. Norbury Williams. "S. Norbury Williams, 71, Shakespeare-street C-on-M. Manchester, November 27th. The Town Clerk, Town Hall, Warrington. Dear Sir.—l have this afternoon been over to IVarrington, and had an interview with Councillor J. Pemberton,who informs me that his medical adviser prohibits him, for the pre- sent, from resit fling his attendance at the sittings of the Commissioners. He hopes shortly to receive per- mission to attend, as we are wishful that our regular sittings should be resumed at as early a day as pos- sible. Until he receives the requisite permission, he is willing to be present on one:day,say Tivirsday next, December 3rd, ateleven o'clock, at the Town Hall, when we may be entbled to arrive at an agreement as to the reporting of our proceedings. Please inform me whether this arrangement is agreeable to our colleagues.—Yours faithfully, S. NoRetTRY WELLIANIS." "Warrington, November 39th. To the Mayor. Sir, —Oa November 23rd we asked the Town Clerk to offer the Non-trading Commissioners a choice of dates for the resumption of the inquiry. Instead of an acceptance of one of these, we have received, through the Town Clerk. from Mr. Williams; apparently acting for the Non-trading Cetnraissioners, an offer to engage in a further discussion, as useless as those by which five sittings have already been wasted, and a suggestion that the inquiry shall be postponed until such time as Mr. Pemberton's medical adviser may certify that he is fit to attend. We decline to allow our time to be wasted in any further aimless discus- sion, and we further decline to wait for such an indefinite period as is suggested. We wished to know whether the Town Council desire Ili to conduct the inquiry on the lines laid down in our letter to the .11:tyor on October sth, in the absence of any or all of the Non-trading Commissioners.—We remain, Sir, yours respectfully, ALL, AL FRED J. JOLLEY, Lis. GRP:ENING." The MAYoR, stated that at that period of the meeting there could be no discussion ripen the question, but he thought it well to take the Council into his confidence, and that was why the letters had been read. Councillor MaorelN moved the following motion of which he had given notice.-1.) That the proposed In- quiry into the alleged trading by members of the Council with the Corporation be proceeded with, with all snood, and that the Commissioners he requested forthwith to proceed with the Enquiry an-1 to complete the same without delay. (2) That so much of the resolution relating to the said Thriiry passel by the Council on the 11th August, 1913, be varied so as to en- able the Inquiry to be held with open doors, and that the rateptyers and the Press be admitted to OACI.i sitting of the Commissioners," Councillor Maginn moved the resolution without any'feeling of enmity, either to one party or the other. He was not present that evening as a member of the Council to represent any party, but to give his views upon the unseemly delay of the inquiry so long talked about. He hid told his electors that the inquiry was needed and demanded it in the interests of certain gentlemen who belonged to the Council who had been accused of dishonesty. He demanded an in- quiry into their conduct,and if they were found guilty A Voice : "Hang them "and laughter. The-Maxon; Order. Councillor Maxus,: : Well, let public opinion be their punishment. What should they do with the accusers in case the accused were found innocent? A VoicE : " Hang them "arid ine,r3 laughter. Councillor liAorxat (continuing) said the shouting of "atop thief" had gone on for two years, and they had got no further than shouting" stop thief." The matter had been advertised all over the town, and every child knew about it ; all Engle td knew of it, and it was said that this town had the most in-met-al and dishonest Council. He heel the heneer of being a member of the Council,but he refused to allow.any one-to call him dis- hpnest until he had been proved guilty of dishonesty. He therefore asked the Council to vote for his resolu- tion with a view of bringing the matter to an end— (hear,hetr) —so that the town might begin to do some business. For two years it had lost its time through these unseeml v recriminations, intimidations and scandal-mengering. The poor ratepayers had been gulled into voting for one mte or other. With regard to trading he was bound to take it to mean what the Act of Parliament said about it, but there were some wiseacres in the town who would pot a rider to 'Wand. say , it meant so and so. If a man accumulated waalthhe wanted an investment, aud would he prefer to invest his money here or income other town? In Warrington any man who had any ability in his business was condemned whilst those who had no ability were to be 'called ueon to conduct the affairs of the town. They were told that limited liability companies must not trade with the Corporation unless a member of the Council had not more than ten per cent. of the capital. Then in the name of goodness if that were so a certain section of the Council had only to put in ten people and call it a limited non-trading company and it would then be quite legitimate to supply the town front bricks to a tripe supper. (Laugh- ter.) Did it not seem ridiculous night after night, and day after day, to keep on haggling about the-Non- trading ? A certain numher of members had been put out of the 'Council who were innocent, and they had been treated most unseemly and most cruelly. ROBERTS, a vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman and speakers. A programme of vocal and instrumental music was given at intervals by Bros. A. Egerton, J. Sheath, J Stamford, and A. C. Walmsley. Mr. Jackson was the pianist. SUNDAY'S SERVICES. On Sunday Good Templar services were preached by Mrs. Lee, P.D.V.T. (Liverpool). The members of the order appeared in regalia and presented a pleasing appearance. In the morning Mrs. Lee spoke of the various stumbling-blocks in the way of Christiaa life. Among them were love of pleasure, love of money, Superstitious ceremoriy,doubts and fears,and the greatest of all,strong drink. Sheath sang" The Holy City" and a duet entitled" Down in the valley" was rendered by Sisters J. Hughe and D. Cook. 0A good congregation assembled for the evening service when Mrs. Lee spoke on" Charity," giving an excellent definition of the parable of the Good Samaritan. The choik very creditably rendered the anthem" T will lift up mine eyes," Bro. C. J. Sheath singing the bass solo. Mr. W. Birch presided at the organ with his customary ability. The collections amounted to 14s. 6d. OPERETTA BY THE CHILDREN. On Mon ay, a very successful operetta was ren- dered by dthe members of the Juvenile Temple. The title "The Right Little Island " and the plot of the . WaS invadelnece was laid in Temperance Island, which was while, by bY Lord Brewer and his followers. After a , Quee.:,Lord Brewer falls in love with Clara, one of the pled u s attendants, and she induces him to sign the exa.ge and live among them. His followers follow his L i mple and, of course, all ends happily. Miss Ada ttlewood played the part f Queen Teetolia with true egal dignity. She was attended by two diminutive maids of honour, Misses Alice Egerton and Minnie Broughton. The parts of Lord Brewer and Clara Miss excellently portrayed by Master Sam Hugh es and Jane Hughes. At the close Mr. F. Merlin presented books to Master Hughes and the Imes Littewooe and Hughes. The children had been admirably trained by Mrs. Sheath and Messrs. Walmsley and Jackson, the last-named also acting as pianist. During an interval a very clever ventriloquial sketch was given by Bro. 3lai dment

div.p: OF INTEREST TO WOMEN.

The case of Mr. J. R. Parry, Morn TAM, Moss Side- road, Cadishead, Manchester, is one which will be read with interest and profit by scores or woman who may be suffering in the saute way. Mrs. Parry suffered for over ten years. She had Scarlet Fever, and a chill, which seemed to settle on her Kidneys. She describes her symptoms in this way : "I was subject to heart fluttering andpains in my back and cramps in my muscles. My eyes were swollen and I was often dizzy and had occasional attacks or neuralgia. I became low-spirited and depressed. My memory failed me and had difficulty in collecting my thoughts. I was extremely nervous and my limbs would swell terribly. I as always tired and languid and any exer-. tion fatigued me. "I made up my mind to try Dodd 's Kidney Pills and - lam very glad I did so, for they saved my life. From the very first they ga,vo the relief, and so I persevered with them and now I ani pleased to be able to say that I am quite cured. "Tenn earnestly and heartily recommend this medicine Ito women who may be ailing as I was."

But many have said to themselves, "I really must use Vi-Cocoa," and have failed to do so. Why? There is no more agree- able and inexpensive cocoa on the market. A 6d. packet or a 9d. or is. div.head: NOVEMBER EVENING.
div.p: A NOVEMBER EVENING.

O'er yon hills, now dim and lonely, Slowly passed the orb of day; Leaving streaks of amber only Wn.are his waning glory lay. Saorn of all their spans and gladnass Bleak the flelds around us lie; Waite a ton3h of tender sadness Tunas the sympathetic sky. M anrafully the winds are sighing Through the hedgerows and the trees ; And the sere leaves round us lying, Rnstle in the passing breeze. Far away the woodland singers, Unto brighter skies have flown ; And but ens sw N3t, voice still lingers— Robin sings his song alone. Waero their kindred ones are sleeping La the ground all cold and bare, Fading flowers, their vigil keeping, Band in silent sorrow there.

Ram] toilers, homeward wending, ' Pass along with cheery will ; Ere the 5p311 of twilight ending Lives their path more sombre still. An-I trot) 5C31139 all dtrk awl dreary, With their wand'rings tired and worn, Wild birds pa3s, on wings all weary, To the nests they left at morn. Thus in gloom and silence holy, All her light and labour fled; , N Wire waits the midnight slowly, • Surely gath'rino•' round her head. J. H. W. CLiTNOINNING.

" SPECIAL"

Dr. T. J. Macnamara. M.P., is to " contribute onr special article next week, and he will take the War Report as his subject. The doctor is a Cmadian by birth, though he came to the Mother Country in time to have part of his educa- tion at St. Thomas's School, Exeter. He began life asa school teacher, and steadily worked his way up in that great profession till, in. 1893, he became President of the National Union of reachers. A year later he enterel the politi-cal arena ; he joined the Eig'atv Club, an took an exc3edingly active part on the Liberal side. The same year he contested Dept- ford without success ; but such a man does notlremain long outside Parliament, and at the last General Elec- tion Dr. Macnamara won North Camberwell. For recreation he ,writes books, plays golf, and catches fish. Dr. I.Vfacnamara is known psrhaps best of all for his splendid work in connection with the London School Board.
MIEN WELL COAL GIVE OUT?

It app3ars that there is coal in the United Kingdom to a depth of 4,033 feet, sufficient, at the present rate of output, to suffice for 371 years. but that this period will be considerably extended seeing that there is every probability that mining can be cirried on to a depth of 7,000 feet, though at this depth there will not be any- thing like the area of coal that there is at the former limit. And it further seemsreasonable to expect that this period of supply may be still further extended by the more economical use of fuel, due to the establishment of central electrical supply stations, and the utilisation of Mond and other gas-producing processes, and of gas- driven engines, as well as other means of obtaining a higher percentage of the heat value of the fuel.--Prof. R. A. S. Redmayne in "The Engineering Magazine "for December.

div.head: SHORTHAND STUDENT'S SOLILOQUY.
div.p: THE SHORTHAND STUDENT'S SOLILOQUY.

We are pleased to notice in the current number of the "Reporters' Journal" (which is printed entirely in shorthand) that Mr. Walter Crompton, "Sunrise" Office, Warrington has been awarded first prize for the best eccentric contribution on shorthand (not to exceed 500 words). The following is a transcription of the successful parody: Scene: The Class-room. PUPIL To learn, or not to learn,—that is the question : • Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer The slings and arrows of outrageous ignorance Or to take up pen, and phonographic text-book, And, by earnest study, end it?—To read,—to learn,— No more; ..but by that application so to end The heart-ache, and the thousand painful shocks Ignorance brings about,—'tis a consummation Devoutly to be wish'd. To read,—to learn,— To test !—perchance to fail !—ay, there's the rub ; For with that failure dread what dreams may come— Humiliation worse than death itself— Must give us pause: there's the respect That makes calamity of so long life; For who would bear the scorn of non-success— The jeers of those possess'd of greater merit— When he himself, by absence from the class, May learn no more! Who would o'er lessons, pore And with mysterious hieroglyphics fight, But that the dread of something later on— When youth is pass'd—puzzles the will, And makes us rather work the text-book through , Than risk a future dire—calamitous? I Thus, conscience is the truest friend of all ; I And, by it. guided in our resolution To succeed, we banish sickly thought Inert; embrace the aids flll'd with intent , To spur us on to action. Soft, here comes I The Teacher!

div.head: WESLEYANS AND TEMPERANCE. Society Formed at Bold-street, Warrington. -- – THE COMPENSATION QUESTION.
div.p: WESLEYANS AND TEMPERANCE. Society Formed at Bold-street, Warrington. -- - THE COMPENSATION QUESTION.

In harmony with the recommendation of Conference mid the expressions of the last quarterly meeting, Sunday last was observed as "Temperance Stmday " in the Warrington Wesleyan Circuit. At Bold-street Church Mr. William Hickman preached on "The gospel of common sense "at the morning service, and in the evening the Rev. G. H. Carnson discoursed on "The force of example." His text was "Be ye followers of tae, even as I also ant of Christ." Cor. xi. 1. The rev. gentleman showed how people's lives were influenced by Uhristian examples and made a direct appeal on behalf nf total abstinence. On Monday evening a circuit temperance meeting was held in Bold-street schools, but there was only a meagre attendance. The Rev. G. H. Carnson presided and was sallported by Mrs. Garnett, Miss Bessie Dutton, Mr. A. Perkins, and Mr. W. H. Sherburn (circuit temperance secretary). The CHAIII,MAN said he had been anxious ever since he came into the circuit to hold a temperance meeting but he had found it very difficult to move people in the tuatter. Still they must not be discouraged, for they believed that they were on the right side. They believed that the consumption of drink was not good for the body, for the family life, nor for the nation. He (the Chairman) had been trying to find someone who would tell hint what drink was good for. It might, in some eases, be useful for medicinal purposes, but he did not ti_hink it was necessary for friendliness, or for trade and Ile was positive it was not necessary at election times. Laughter.) He pointed out that people were very analoUS to reoeive the full value for their money they N3ent in ordinary goods but when they purchased drink they did not stop to consider. The beer trade seemed t„O be the only trade which didnot give value for money. people did not know the value of moral character and, further did not know how to secure that purity of la, orals. He had never met a man who had indulged in liquor, or been in company where it was consumed, who was able to maintain his moral character intact. Further eerne people did not know the value of spiritual life. Old-street Church was going to Inke a step forward and were about to form a tempirance societ y.' Miss DUTTON gave an address of encouragement to temperance workers, pointing out the great need that there was for their efforts in the cause. She alluded to e good work which was being done by the Girls' Club In Silver-street, which was much appreciated in the district.

Mrs. 6ARNETT also spoke, and said the Girls' Club 'WS the outcome of a suggestion of the late Mr. Gar- raett. On coming home one day After he had been on the magisterial bench, he said he wished something could be done for the young women of Warringeon Cases came before the Court, and it was very difficult 10 deal with them. He thought some institution might be farmed to prevent them from becoming worse. The club was formed simply to tkeep the girls off the streets and out of 'the public-houses, which 'were sometimes the only resort for them, as their homes mere not very comfortable. She believed the club was doing a good rescue and preventive work, _Sl:leaking of temperance matters Mrs. Garnett quoted the remarks ,of Mr. Justice Grantham at Durham *Assizes as 'evidencing the trend of opinion. In spite of what had been said by judges and ministers she didnot think temperence work was at present making much Ileadway. She did not want to appear pessimistic but ahe did not feel they were much " forrader." She thought they would have got a little" forrader "in Warrington as the result of that night's meeting and she aalsed them to rally round their minister to further the temperaaace cause. (Applause.) , Mx. PERKINS moved: "That this meeting of Wesleyans of Warrington declares its strong conviction that the number of licences for the sale of intoxicat- ing liquors is far in excess of any supposed require- ments of the people, and that new legislation for reducing the number of such licences upon a large scale is urgently needed. Meanwhile the meeting pro- tests againstany proposals for ilegislation which would lessen the present powers possessed by the licensing jus- tices for protecting the public from the ravages of this mischievous traffic, or which wound confer a vested inter- est in a licence for any period beyond that for which it was granted." They all knew;he said,what was threatening the country during the early part of the next Parliamentary session, and temperance workers must make their voices heard and their influence lett throughout the land. They had been told by the brewers that if a licence were taken away from a house, bompensation ought, in fair- ness, to be granted. For his town part he could not see why (Applause). If they were going to compensate anybody there were a few who had first claim The closing of public houses would throw people out of employment .and they, as well as the publican, might have scene Claim for compensation. He did not, however, see why the brewers should ask for compensation for themselves. Then again if any- one had compensation it shatild be those whose homes had been blasted and who had been made fatherless through drunkenness. What had the brewers done for the good of the nation beyond subscribirw to Parlia- Mentary interests.? They could make theil presence felt and they could make their powers manifest to our states- men who were bowing down to them. If they could find any solid good arising from the £180,000,000 spent annually on drink, they would have one reason why the .brewers should be compensated. There was no solid good, but, on the contrary, _much solid harm. Mr. Perkins alluded to the opinions expressed by leading pedical men that intoxicath' or liquors were neither reds nor beverages, and only in very rare triestances could they be described as medicines. 4-leaPpealed to allalstainers to do what they could to overthrow those who were working for compensAtion.He Predicted that if the proposed 'Compensation Bill was PeAsed, it would threw teniperance work back a hundred sears.( Ap I lame.) _Mr. W. FL SRERBURN seconded, and expressed the rile that 11:ntd of Hope secretaries would help hi.n in 15 work as circuit teraperance secretary by supplying all:r returns he required. He hoped the Band of Hope 1101 d-street would increase in membership. It Was decided on the motion of Mr. J. E. BARLOW I.lsoaded by Mr. DIXON, to form a slciety, to be named 1110 Bold-street Wesleyan Methodist Temperance eeietv." A committee composed of the following was tec,ted :---Messrs. Nelson, Sanders, T. div.p: TRUTH AND TRADE.
MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S DELUSIONS.
STRANGE CONDUCT OF A "BUSINESS
MAN."
Ruined Industries.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S "awful examples" of the evil effects of Free Trade have not been a success. He has set out to prove that certain British manufactures have been ruined by free imports, and that therefore the Free Trade policy has been injurious to the nation as a whole. Even if his "examples" would bear investigation, this argument is no more worthy of notice than that railways have injured the old stage coaches. As the Duke of Devonshire said at the Queen's Hall, London:
I cannot understand his arguments; the ideas at the root of them are drawn from another world than that in which we live.

Dumping Iron. MR. CHA3IIERLAIN informed us, some, time ago, that "dumping" only takes place when the trade of the "dumpers" is depressed. It happens when the "dumpers" are obliged to get rid of their surplus stock at any price. At Cardiff, Mr. Chamberlain tried seriously to argue tile the "dumpers" make a profit by selling goods at a loss! He spoke specially of the iron trade. Said .he-,
For every 1,000 tons of rails imported into this country there is a loss a something like £2,000 in wages and employment, to the people of this country.
Very well; but where 'do our imports of dumped iron come from? Here are the figures according to Mr. Walter McLaren, one of the leading ironmasters in the kingdom:

Germany, Holland, and Belgium combined —. ... 78,615 tons. United States of America._ ... 45,973 „ Canada:— ... 103,202 „ Mr. Chamberlain proposes to "hit back" at the "dumpers." How does he propose to 4' hit back" at Canada ? If be does not hit back at Canada, how can he hit Germany? German and American dumping is the work of individuals, but Canadian clumping is the work of the Canadian Government. The Canadian •Government is actually now pro- posing to vote 2,000,000d01. to help its iron- masters to dump their products on our shores!
Trade and Competition. BUT is the British iron trade in any danger from Colonial or foreign competition? Here are a few figures: 1901.
Iron trade personal incomes ... £2,979,442 £5,380,418 Iron works assess-
ments £2,979,442 £6,600,263 Persons employed in iron works ... 202,000 216,000 Average export of
maeltinery Total exports

5,500,000 8,517,693 It is very difficult to feel depressed about the condition of the British iron trade in' face of the above figure. A very amusing blunder into which Mr. Chamberlain walked blindly at Cardiff arises from the fact that the tin- plate trade lives almost entirely upon "dumped" iron. And yet while Mr. Chambe- rlain is prepared to stop the raw material of tinplate. and so ruin that industry, he tried to show that his scheme would save the tinplate trade. A marvellous business man is Mr Chamberlain. Tinplates.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN keeps up his reputation for contradicting himself in the same speech in a truly wonderful manner. After breathing out threatenings and slaughter on the foreigner for making money at our expense by dumping iron below cost upon our shores, he turned his attention to the sad and forlorn condition of -the tinplate industry. Said he: Owing to the McKinley Tariff, the tinplate trade of South Wales had been greatly endangered, and if we had not been bound hand and foot by our policy we might now have all the American tinplate trade. We have lost, aq compared with ten years ago, 80,000 tons. He desired to impress upon the working classes that their interest in this question was the greatest of all, for they had to depend upon employment, and by this decrease there was a loss of £60,000 per annum.

It wculd be difficult to find a grosser case of false statements and half-truths in so few words as the above. It would require a column fully to answer. In brief the reply is as follows: We used to supply America with tinplate until .1890, when, in order to start a tinplate industry of their own, the Americans placed a heavy duty upon the plates we sent them. In 1892, out of every 100dol. paid in the States for tin, 45d01., was paid for the duty. Thus we see that, in order to set up a special industry for a few people, the rest of the American people had to pay almost double the price for tin. What happened? Sir John Jenkins, the highest authority in the kingdom on the tinplate trade, tells us:

It was estimated that in 1891 those engaged in fruit-canning industries numbered 2,000,000. The interests of all these were adversely affected in order to establish an industry which at the ooside would give direct employment to no more than 16,000 people. Millions of bushels of vegetables and fruits were allowed to rot because it did not pay to can them. English firms took advantage of the situation and exported jams, jellies, marmalades, &c.., into the United States

In considerable quantities. The ,result of all this was to increase the canning industry in England, and to shift the States industry to South America, Australia, Tasmania, and New Zealand. These new centres of the canning trade soon began to demand more and more tinplates from England, and the result was that Sir John Jenkins says last year was the best the .Welsh tinplate trade has ever known. But Mr.' Chamberlain by shutting out cheap iron, wants to kill it. And Mr. Chamberlain tells us be is a business man. wit

div.head: Further Ruin.
div.p: Further Ruin.

WE have no space to deal with the pearl- button industry, which has suffered because the ladies have changed their fashions. Cloth- button makers are now having a trade boom instead. The jewellery trade is affected by the demand for Parisian styles in preference to British, while the excess of imports last year only arose through the forced sales of jewels in Morocco, on the purchase of which large profits were made by the British trader. The watch trade has more than recovered lost around—ground which was lost owing to the reluctance of British makers to manufacture machine-made watches. Similarly with the cycle and other trades, as soon as British makers adopted modern ideas they quickly outpaced foreign rivals, because they were able, through our policy of free imports, to buy their raw material at the lowest possible price. Give the British workman the same intellectual training as the foreigner, and, with the help of free and cheap materials, he can hold his own against the world. _ _

div.head: RETALIATION AS A POLICY.
div.p: RETALIATION AS A POLICY.
BY SYDNEY BUXTON, MP.
Liberal Under-Secretary of State for the Colonies).

We have heard a great deal, in the innumerable speeches which have inundated the country, about the policy of Preference and the policy of Protection, but much less about the policy of Retaliation, which was adopted by the Prime Minister as a means of keeping • his party together, and which he announced at Sheffield two months ago, and reiterated at Bristol the other day.

Mr. Balfour's speeches and Mr. Balfour's policy have, by reason of their very indefiniteness, been fairly suc- cessful in the object he had in view. With the excep- tion of the new Chancellor of the Exchequer—who naturally follows his father—all the members of the Government who have spoken, and more especially the new Ministers, have repudiated Preference and Protec- tion if they are to lead,as they infallibly and admittedly must lead to the taxation of food. But the Ministers, and the Unionist party generally, appear to be prepared to accept Retaliation as a policy, and to follow the Prime Minister—who,as he tells us, is nothing if not a leader—wheresoever and into whatever Protectionist bog this will-o'-the-wisp may lure them. The policy of Retaliation is really, therefore, of greater moment, and more dangerous, thanthat of Pre- ference. Indeed, ifor the destruction of the latter I chiefly pin my faith on Mr. Chamberlain, who has at least the courage to stick to his tax on food. Protection we know, and Free Trade we know, but what is this Retaliation? It is neither fish, flesh, fowl, nor good red-herring. The policy of Preference is clear—the levy of a duty on foreign imports of food- stuffs, while admitting the products of the Colonies free. The specific policy of Protection, proposed for our adoption by Mr. Chamberlain, is clear—a 10 per cent. duty on all imported manufactures, in order to protect the home manufacturer hi his home markets, and to enable him, by some mysterious means, the better to compete in protected foreign markets. But both these plans are repudiated by the Prime Minister —for the present. He proposes instead "Retaliation." But the policy of Retaliation is wrapped in obscurity. ; Mr. Balfour apparently does not know what he wants, though he tells us that he won't be happy till he gets it. Sir M. Hicks-Beach implores him not to explain any further, for if he were to do so Sir Michael might have to disagree with him, and to seek again some other fold.

But the policy of Retaliation cannot be left where it has been put by the Prime Minister at Sheffield and at Bristol. It requires expansion, explanation, and defini- tion. For the worst of Retaliation is that it may mean nothing or it may mean a great deal. Sir M. Hicks- Beach at Bristol put Retaliation simply on a par with the Sugar Convention; while Mr. Balfour has told us that he desires by means of it "to alter per- manently the Fiscal foundation which has prevailed luring the last two generations." Who is right? Which wags the other? What we want to know, what we are entitled to know, but what we have not yet been told, is what exactly the Prime Minister means' • .and how, in a concrete way, he proposes to accomplish lois end. To use his own words at Sheffield, the " guid- ing policy" of Retaliation is "to give the Government of this country freedom of negotiation," so that "we an inform any foreign Government which we thought was treating us with, outrageous unfairness that unless they modified their policy to our advantage we should feel compelled to take this or that step in regard to their eNports to-this country." . _ . . .

So fai so good. And if dis is all he means there is ;little difference of opinion. Each particular case (he : characteristically refrains from specifying one) of '.alleged "outrageous unfairness" must be judged on its merits. It must be carefully considered and cautiously decided whether the policy of levelling the "revolver" at the head of the offending party will be effective; and whether, if not (and the alternative must be faced), the consequence of firing, and the commercial vendetta which would therefore ensue, would not, in the end, be more injurious than beneficial to us and to our trade. But the particular case having been considered, and action having Leen decided upon, there is nothing in the world to prevent a Government, this Government, any Free Trade Government, when negotiating a com- mercial treaty, or otherwise, from using commercial threats, and from biting as well as barking, subject only to the fact that if any alteration in taxation is thereby necessitated, they must get the Assent of Parliament to their Budget and to their Finance Bill, in order to legalise the consequential charges involved. The Sugar Convention Bill of the other day (injurious and mis- taken though I think it was) was an instance in point. It was a case,—more or less legitimate, of ietaliation— retaliat ion against bounties. What more does Mr. Balfour want? Surely in his wildest moments he cannot believe that the country and the House would give a free hand to the Executive to ilea.l, on their own initiative, with questions of trade and of taxation without the necessity of coming to Parliament for its assent? We are entitled to a clear and lucid explanation, and we ought to be told where, when, and how he proposes to carry out his policy of Retaliation. But neither at Sheffield nor at Bristol has one single word been vouchsafed to us dealing with the matter in its practical aspect. We have been given neither light nor leading on the subject. Yet,in regard to the policy of Retaliation, the essential question is whether it is feasible, and how it is going to be effec- tively carried out.

Retaliation, as defined by Mr. Balfour, means that when a particular country, by its prohibitive duties treats any of our trades with outrageous unfairness, or where a trust, syndicate, or combine disturbs our, trade by unfair competitive, manipulations, we are to put duties on the imports from the country in question; and presumably on the particular goods sent here through the action of tho trust or syndicate. Though how these dumped goods are going to be individually penalised passes the wit of man to determine. In order to retaliate effectively on a large scale, we must be able to convince the traders, the people, and the Government of the Protective country that we are in earnest and that we have the power and the will effectually 'so to injure their trade that they will be compelled to agree to our terms. With our big revolver we are to "perwail on them to stop." And by its effect in breaking down the Ameri- can tariff—the Protective tariff that injures us:the most —must Retaliation as a policy be judged. What then is the commercial position as between ourselves and the United States.? In 1902 we imported from the States £127,000,000 sterling of produce. We exported to the States £24,000,000 of Britislf produce and £19,000,000 of foreign and Colonial produce—a total of .Z 12,000,000. Nominally, therefore, as Mr. Chamberlain sees and argues, we are fiscally in a strong position to break down what he calls this" immoderate, unreasonable, and unnecessary "tariff ;for the Americans send us three times as much as We send them ; or, if British produce alone be corsidered, they send us five times as much as we send to them. Nothing more eas: surely than to bring them to their senses by clapping a duty on their imports to us. Ver, pretty in theory, but now it is going to be done? Both Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Balfour, and every speaker without exception, have stated emphatic- , ally that the raw materials of industry are not to be , taxed. As a matter of fact, I think it is absolutely certain that if the policy of Colonial Preferences be adopted, raw materials will certainly have to be taxed. If Australia is to have a fair share, and if the Cape is to I have any share at all, in the advantages of inter-Empire Preference, the raw materials they send us must receive preferential treatment—in other words, foreign raw , mate" ials must be taxed.

'However, be this as it may, raw - materials are ruled out, as far at least, as retaliation is concerned. Then Mr. Balfour, the Government. its new recruits especi- ally. declare by all their gods that the question of the taxation of food isnot before the country, and is not within the limits of practical politics. So, in order to arrive at the American imports, which are open to attack and on which we can retaliate, we must first deduct the imports, of raw materials and of foodstuffs. But .thiS makes rather a big hole in the imports, for out of the £127,600,000 of American imports not less than £62,500,000 are foodstuffs, and no less than £44,000,000 (chiefly cotton) are raw materials. Then tobacco— already heavily taxed—and a few miscellaneous articles, such as books, drawings. plants, &c.. must also be eliminated, to an amount of about £6,000,000. Then, again, there are some . £5,000,000 of manufactured articles, such as leather, pig-lead, cordage, &c., which form the raw material of later stages of manufacture, and the taxation of which wOttidadmittedly injure some of our manufacturing trades here. ..We §tarted with some £127,000,000 of produce from a Protectionist country on which, following Mr. Chamber- lain and Mr. Balfour, we thought we could retaliate. But from these we must deduct, it is c1ear,2117,500,000 made up as above. This-leaves us but a balance of £9,000,000 to £10,000,000 of American imports, much of which -fmight perhaps be utilised for retaliatory pur- poses. And these £9,000,000 to £10,000,000 of so-called "manufactures" are made up from over forty different items of import, some of which. are hardly articles on which retaliatory taxation could profitably oreffectively be placed. How are the mighty fallen! Instead of having, as we thought when we gaily started, £127,000,000 of American imports on which we could retaliate, we find that there are, at the best, a beggarly £9,000,000 open to our attack. The prospects of -Retaliation hardly looked so rosy as they did at first. And then, further, if wo tax these . few millions of imports from the States, the Americans would not for a moment hesitate to re-retaliate, and most effectively to re-retaliate, on All or most of our £24,000,000 of home exports, and on the .£19,000,000 of re-ex•ports that we send to them. The beautiful "weapon," the arm of precision. on which the Government apparently think they can rely appears on nearer examination to be much of the same calibre, and as effective as the ammunition and the rifles on which they relied for the Boer War. The Government ammunition was more dangerous to the man who fired it than to the man against whom it "'was fired; and the Government rifles shot eighteen inches to the right ! PPHow. then, will the policy of Retaliation, if attempted as a policy and on a large scale, work out?
