div.p: -I
LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.

Authors of letters intended for publication must mall cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. Matter intended for publication must be written on one side oatg of the paper and sent in, if possible,not later than Thursday.

A Plea for the Shop Assistants. Sir,—Would you kindly allow one a little space in your columns. The shop assistants are at present con- cerned as to the coming Christmas holidays. In the year 1896 Christmas Day and Bank Holiday came on the Friday and Saturday. the majority of the shops closed irom the Thursday night till Monday morning. A few opened on the Saturday and closed on the Monday; but as little or no bnsiness was done on the Saturday most of them closed by teatime after spoiling the holiday. If the Markets Committee would decide to close Christmas Day and Bank Holiday, and let it be made known the shops would do likewise, and it would end in a satisfactory holiday for shop people. Con- sidering those whose homes are out of town it is far more convenient for them to have an unbroken holiday, than have to remain in town (in apartments it may be) to enable them to-be at business on the Saturday, thus depriving them -of being able to join in the family circle justyat the festive season.—Yours SHOP ASSISTANT.

div.head: Councillor Dodds and Mr. A IL Crosfield.
div.p: Councillor Dodds and Mr. A IL Crosfield.

Sir,—T observe that Mr. A. H. Crosfield attempts to be facetious; I presume, to hide the nakedness of his positiOn. He has also decided to run away; burnot until he had fired what he no doubt conceived to be an effective parting shot. Of course I allude to his characteristically misleading reference to Mr. It. A. Naylor's suggested candidature for the Parliamentary representation of Warrington. As Mr. Naylor has ex- plained, and I think everybody now knows, his idea was to stand independently of the two political parties, and to make his platform, public parity, temperance, and economy. I was disposed at the time to favour such a, candidature, although as I tom Mr. Naylor my prefer- ence was for a progressive Labour Candidate. No doubt the subsequent raising of the fiscal question, in which Mr. NaDor has for years been keenly interested, changed his plans,—l am &c. December 4th.
.1 kIAES DODDS.

div.head: Councillor Stott's Election.
div.p: Councillor Stott's Election.

Sir,—At a meeting IA the Warrington Labour Repre- sentation Committee held ,on ednesday evening, a resolution was unanimously carried congratulating Mr. Stott and the I.L.P. on their srilendid -victory in the Orford Ward Bye Election. The Committee expressed the opinion that great credit is due to Mr. Stott and his party 'for the way they fought that election, seeing they had to face a powerful organization,supported by the Liberal Leaders and the Licensed Victuallers' Association, and the delegates were desired to draw the attention of their societies to the lesson to be learnt from this Victory, where Conservatives and Liberals were joined together to 'defeat Independent Labour.—Yours respectfully, .0. BUCKLEY. (Sec. Labour Ropresentation Committee). '

div.head: WARRINGTON EISTEDDFOD.
div.p: WARRINGTON EISTEDDFOD.
RESULT OF SATURDAY'S COMPETITIONS.
LOCAL SUCCESSES.

Transplanted from its native soil 'the Welsh e istedd- fod has taken root in Warrington and, we hope, will continue to flourish with increased robustness as years go on. It speaks volumes for the energy and enter- prise of the members of the Apollo Prize Choir that they should embark upon the somewhat hazaidous undertaking of introducing an annual muSical festival in this town. Although the general public have not yet rallied as enthusiastically totheir support as might have been expected the venture has,on the whole,been success ful and now that the initial difficulties have been over- come the choir will no doubt peasevere in their efforts to popularize the Eisteddfod among the townspeople. One thing was evident at Saturday's festival—which was the second ,of its kind—and that was that the choir had profited by experience. The numerous competi- tions were carried through far more expeditiously than was the case last year and by ten o'clock the singing of the National Anthem had conclnded the day's proceedings. A. new , departure was the hearing of the preliminary tests in Holy Trinitysehoolroom instead of in the ante- rooms of the Parr Hall, and the arrangement proved convenient to all concerned. The trying duties of musical adjudicator devolved upon Mr. C. Lewis, Jones, Mus. Bac.; A.R.C.0., who was kept busily occupied during the greater part of the day. His decisions—pronounced after a careful weighing of the respective merits and short comings of the competi- tors--appeared to give satisfaction all round. The meetings were conducted by the Rev. Wynn Davies, of Liverpool, whose geniality soon placed him on good terms with the audience. The attendanc6 in the afternoon was disappointingly small but in the even- ing there was a marked improvement tie hall being well-filled in all but the higher-priced seetiona. The chair at each meeting was occupied byNlr. E.Llones, who,at the outset, expressed the;hope that the Eisted- dfod:would in the future be increasingly successfulfrom the educational and musical standpoint. It deserved better support than it had received that afternoon and he thought it was a shame that the attendance was so small

CHILDREN'S CHALLENGE SOLO COMPETITION. This competition, confined to children under 16, w:cs the opening item and the the vocalists were allowed to give songs of their own selection. Miss Carrie Hast- ings of Warrington, had the honour of winning the prize for the second year in succession, the adjudiCator speaking very highly of her rendering of "Come unto Me " from " The Messiah." She had, Mr. Jones said, a very finished style for a girl so young, possessed a very good, equal voice, and sangiwith groat sympathy. He had heard the solo sung much worse by singers with great names. During the latter part her singing was slightly short, but that was in his opinion, entirely due to nervousness. A pupil of Miss M. E. Parry, of Birkenhead, and a young lady from St. Helens were the other competitors in the final test and sang "Lead kindly light " and" Queen of the earth" respectively. BARITONE OR BASS COMPETITION. The test song for this competition was "Guiding Light" (Henry) and the vocalists selected to appear before the audience were Mr. Robert Hamblett, of St. Helens, Mr. Bert Kirkham, of Preston, and Mr. J. Edwards, of Widnes. The adjudicator awarded the prize to Mr. Kirkham, who, he said, sometimes gave one the impression that he was singing out of tune owing to the use of the vibrato. HO had, however, a good voice, style, and words, and gave a good rendering of the song. Mr. Harablett, was sometimes wanting in his words and in one or two places the aspirate was wrongly used. In order to give the dramatic effect which the song required, Mr. Edwards had sometimes to force his voice on tha high notes, and that robbed the song of a great deal of its dignity. MALE VOICE QUARTETTE COMPETITION. Only two quartettes—Southport Orpheonic (Mr. W. H. Martin and party) and Garston—competed, the test piece being "Eileen Alannah" (J. R. Thomas). The prize went to the Southport party, the adjudicator remarking that the voices were nicely balanced, and there was a good finish and attention to detail through- out. The Gersten quartette was not so well balanced and their rendering of the piece might have been much improved by more careful attention to little things. MIXED CHORAL COMPETITION. Mr. J. Gibbins' Choir (Warrington), and Mr. J. Weedal's Choir (St. Helens) competed for the prize of £5 and a gold centre medal for the conductor. Handel's "Hallelujah chorus" was rendered and the adjudicator said both choirs sang very well. indeed. The tone and balance of the Warrington choir were not so good as those of the St. Helens party. In both choirs the tenors were much alike—that was, wantieg much. There was Also a tendency to hurry and when the St. Helens party was singing he thought at one moment that the basses would wreck the ship. They, however, settled down almost immediately and the rendering was very much better afterwards. He awarded the prize to Mr. Weed- all's choir.

PIANOFORTE SOLO COMPETITION. Twentv-four competitors entered, and the piece selec- ted was Warblings at Eve" (Brindley Richards.) The adjudicator said that with twenty-three of the competi- tors the hands were not playing together, and that was the worst fault a young pianist could have. He pointed .out other errors which came under his notice, and said he had decided to award the prize to Master William Williamson, of Runcorn, whose playing was not so faulty as the other competitors.' SOPRANO SOLO COMPETITION. After keen competition,Miss Sumner, of Warrington, Miss M. Hunt. of Preston, and Miss Foster, of St. Helens, were selected to sing "The Swallows" (Cowen) before the audience. Miss Foster carried off the prize, the adjudicator saying that her singing was the most finished. WORKS GT,EE COMPETITION (MALE VOICES). The Eisteddfod Committee are to be congratulated -upon this innovation which proved one of most enjoyable items. The parties competing were Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Company's, (conductorMr.W. White), Messrs. Fletcher, Russell and Company's (Mr. W. Woodcock) Messrs. P. Walker and Sons, (Mr. Arm- strong). The adjudicator said he was sorry he could

' not award three prizes, because the ideaoTf fostering al love of music in that way was so splendid that he would like to back it up as much as he possibly could. Referring to the renderings of "Oh! whb will o'er the downs" (Pearsell) he said. Messrs. Walker's choir was very well balanced indeed, although the singing was a bit rough at the commencement and at the conclusion. 'lt was, however, an excellent attempt at cultured expression in music. Messrs- Fletcher, Russell and Company's party gave a very excellent rendering of the piece. Their singing was crisp,the voices well balanced and the words clearly pronounced. Messrs. Monks, Hall and Company's choir was not so well balanced but the members ftried!their ' very best to sing in good tune. They had the makings of a very good choir indeed. The prize of £2 was awarded to Messrs. Fletcher, Russell and Company's party.
DTA ER AWARDS.

Other awards were announced as follows :—best pair •of men's hand-knitted woollen stockings, Miss Brindleyll Lovely-lane; best fretwork photo frame, Mr. t,John Marsh, Pierpoint-street Warrington best set of d'oyleys, Miss M. Barker, Haydock-street, Earlestown. _ .

CHILDReg'S 6110Ili COMPETITION, A new feature at the evening meeting was the chil- dren's choir competition, the entrants being Widnes Children's Choir (conductor, Mr. A. L. Finch), Sutton. united (Mr. W. Knapper), Garston 'Clifton (Mr.' W. H, Higginson) and Albert Soad Children's Choir (Mr. J. Platt). "The Night bells " (0. Vincent) was the test price and there was a keen coldest for the prize of RS and a gold centre medal for the conductor. The adjudicator gave his decision in favour of Garston Clifton, observing that tkechoir consisted of nice, soft voices, which were well under control, and gave an excellent rendering of the Piece.
CHALLENGE SOLO COMPETITION.

The competitors appearing in the final test were Mr. E. H. Pearce, of Warrington, Miss B. Stott, of South- port, and Miss Potts, of Crewe. Mr. Pearce sang "Why do the nations rage" and the adjudicator said he had an excellent voice and gave a fine rendering of the piece. Certain bars were not, however, sung absolutely correctly. Miss Stott, to whom he awarded the prise sang"ioh! dry those tears" beautifully. Miss Potts, of Crewe, attempted a difficult piece in "Thel heavens are telling," and the adjudicator said it was especially diffi- cult in her case owing to the natural break in her voice.
RECITATION COMPETITION.

Out of nine competitors, Miss Newbold, of liuyton. Mr. Tom Kenny, of Rarlestown, and Mr. T.Robinson' of Preston, were selected to recite "The Rapids" (J. B. Gongh) before the audience. The Rev. Wynn Davies adjudicated and awarded the prize to Mr. Robinson whose recitation, he said, was splendid from beginning to end.

MIXED VOICE QUARTETTE COMPETITION. Hamblett and party, of St. Helens, secured th award for the best rendering of "Good night, beloved" (Pinsuti), the adjudicator commenting upon the excel- lent blending of the voices, close attention to detail, and light and shade.
CONTRALTO SOLO COMPETITION,

"Abide with me" (Liddle) was the test piece and the competitors who sang in public were Miss E. Parr, of St. Helens, Miss J, Williams, of Widnes, and Miss Pats, of The prize was awarded to Miss Parr who, Mr. Lewis Jones said, sang from memory in a very finished and dignified manner. Miss Williams showed peculiarities of pronunciation,an'd Miss Potts appeared at times to be" in a hurry to getalong."

TENOR SOLO COMPETITION. The audieuce had the pleasure of hearipg interpreta- tions of "Mona "(Adams) bt Mr. G. CI. Hughes, of Liverpool, Mr. J. H. Corrin, Of Warrington, and Mr. A. Cheetham, ef Wigan. To the satisfaction of all, the adjudicator declared Mr. Corrin to be the winner, and spoke highly of his free, and at the same time expres- sive rendering. Mr. Hughes, he said, possessed keen musical intntion but did not infuse sufficient spirit into the song Mr. Cheetham wanted a little more of the divine art in his singing.

div.head: CHIEF CHORAL COMPETITION'.
div.p: CHIEF CHORAL COMPETITION'.

The concluding-- item—and certainly the most inter- esting one—was the competition for male choirs of between 30 and 40 voices. The renderings of" Com- rades' song of hope" (unaccompanied) were, speaking generally, thoroughly enjoyed, the competitors being: —Prescot (conductor, Mr. H. Berrey) ;Warrington (Mr. S. Hassan Garston (Mr. Greenwood) ; Liverpool Welsh (Mr. D. Roberts) ; Wigan Harmonic (Mr. (leo. Martlew). The adjudicator remarked that his hearers might go to Wales but they woudd not hear anything better than they had heard from those choirs—in fact, choirs sometimes sung worse in Wales when they had between 70 and 80 voices. To go into details, there was in the singing of the Prescot choir an absence of crispness in the whole production until they reached the last page. when the choir seemed to have awakened out of sleep. The Warrington choir opened in distinctly better tune and kept better time. It was well balanced and of good tone, although there was a slight 'losing of pitch- at the conclusion, and 'mother small fault to which attention was called. Garston Choir. he thought, was a choir with a future. (Laughter.) He didn't want to bully-rag them in any way. Hewanted to admire their pluck. (Applause). Liverpool-Welsh was a well-balanced choir but there were some faults such as want of verve and energy in the attack of the allegro, and an overstepping of the mark towards the close. Wigan Harmonio Choir gave a. fresh, vigorous, and magnificently worked-out produc- tion, and ended dead in pitch. He awarded thofirst prize (£lO and silver cup presented by Mr. J. Finlay- son) to Wigan Harmonic, and the second (£2) to War- rington. PHOTOGRAPHIC COMPETITION. - _
The prize for the best photo (mounted) was awarded to Mr. W. H. Podmore, Warrington.
THE OFFICIALS.

A meed of praise must be accorded to the officials and especially to the General Secretary,Mr.R.W,Cook, who was untiring in his efforts to ensure successful meetings. Mr. E. Wilkes was an able accompanist.

div.head: GLADSTONE : CHRISTIAN, PATRIOT AND STATESMAN.
div.p: GLADSTONE : CHRISTIAN, PATRIOT AND STATESMAN.
Lecture by the Rev. John Yonge.

At the meeting of Wycliffe Young People's Society,. on Monday evening, Mr. Alfred Corney being in the chair, the pastor, Rev. John Yonge lectured -on " Gladstone : Christian, Patriot and Statesman." The lecture was based on the recently published " Life " by John Morley,and the lecturer in describing the magnitude of the task which the biographer had so successfully completed, made his audience realise the hopelessness of either adequately dealing with the three volumes in question in the time at his disposal or attempting more thana.an outline of the life of this great "example ""of a great Christian man" as a political opponent had once described him. Although Mr. Gladstone made his first" after-dinner" speech at the early age of three, being brought from the nursery to lisp " Ladies and Gentlemen "on the occasion of Canning's election in Liverpool, he was not, he tells us himself an interesting child, nor was he religious. He was a child of slow development whose chief characteristic was a wonderful memory. He was educated at Eton under a famous" flogging" master and went from there to Oxford for which he ever cherished a strong love. • When he left the university, laden with honour his first impulse was to enter the church for his early ideals were strongly religious and had he followed his early bent there is little doubt that he would have made his mark even in an age which boasted such names as Maurice, Manning,Newman,and Pusey. But fate decreed otherwise and in 1832 he entered Parlia- ment where he quickly attracted attention and after holding a post in the Treasury he became President of the Board orTrade in 1843. While in this position he became a convinced Free Trader and did yeoman service in the cause. His subsequent career, how he developed front a Tory to a Liberal and a Radical, how he won his way to the proudest position England can give the son of a commoner, is so recent as to be common knowledge. He was a noteworthy Chan- cellor of the Exchequer, his four Budgets marking epochs in English Political History, while as Premier he carried through such reforms as the Disestablish- ment of the Trish Church, the Irish Land Bill, the Ballot Act, the Abolition of Army Purchase bill and a host of others. After the many vicissitudes of his 01 years of Parliamentary life he walked out of the House of Commons in March 1894 with no flourish of trumpets, no valedictory address to enjoy a brief term of retirement and quiet. The old spirit blazed out again. for a brief space when the story of the Armenian horrors thrilled the land and what °lie had done for Bulgaria he tried to do for Armenia,but in vain. On May 19th 1898,in the bosom of his family he passed away, and every civilised nation under the sun bore testimony to the worth of his character by sending sympathetic mess- ages to his bereaved wife and children. In his wedded and home life he was peculiarly happy, for his wife was a convinced and ardent sympathiser with all his plans. He was a man of splendid physique and as a worker his indomitable energy was a continual re- proach to the indolence of his fellows. His master secret was concentration but this was only rendered possible by his strength and steadfastness of will. His dauntless courage carried him through defeat and victory alike while as an orator he had no rival even in a " House " of Orators. But the noblest and best thing about Gladstone was his religion. He was a moral as well as a spiritual force and he ever held that the same rules which govern individual morality should govern national morality. His religion showed him life as a glorious thing, not to be grovelled through but if rightly used leading on to an elevated and lofty destiny.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday December 5, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday December 5, 1903.

another in the sense they did now. Mr. Carruthers contended that Scotsmen did not leave their homes to become Andrew Camegies. (Laughter.) The mere desire, for wealth WU not the guiding star of their existence. Great wanderers like Mungo Parke and David Livingstone did not open out Africa with the iolea of gaining dollars. Scotsmen were wanderers and the existence of the Caledonian societies showed that. Not only wdre they wanderers but they were extremely loyal and patriotic. In the history of the world scarcely any'race of men had been found that were fonder of their native kind; that had more cause to be fond of their native land, or that looked with more desire and hope to see again that land. (Hear, hear.) They were told in history and geography that the races that lived amongOt mountains were always the most patriotic and that was so amongst the Swiss and the Tyrolese and amongst the Scotch. (Hear, hear.) The narrow affairs at home cramped Scotsmen and compelled them to send out their young men abroad to , look out for. themselves. (Hear, hear.) These Caledon- ian societies in various parts of . the world bound together the Scotch from one side of the world to the other in such a manner that they would never forget that they came from that small mountainous country, which in spite of its small size and in spite of its poor natural resources had had such a huge effect on the world's history. (Hear, hear.) It was a country which through all ages had produced great, men, which through all ages had run an extremely straight course, and which through all ages had refused to do anything except what it felt was to its own advantage—(laughter) ' —and which to-day was a partner in the greatest firm that the sun ever set on, rnd,- by thei: leave, was no junior partner. (Laughter and hear, hear). The toast was drunk with enthusiasm, the difficult feat of standing with one foot on the chair and the 'other on the table being successfully performed by most of the Scotsmen present. Piper Sergeant Donald Murray, of the Liverpool City Police then played "Cock o' the North "on the bagpipes. "THE LAND WE LIVE IN."

This toast was proposed by Mr. Skinner in a felici- tous. speech, in which he referred to the great debt of gratitude which Scotsmen in Eliland owed to the Eng- lish people for their kindness,, hospitality and even generosity which was bestowed upon them. "THE CORPORATION AND TRADE OF WARRINGTON." SPEECH BY THE MAYOR.

Mr. MAY, in proposing this toast, said he had just heard the news that two more Non-Traders had been elected to the Council.(Laughter.)There was aScotsman who was troubling the Council at the present time, one who was making his mark—either doing good or doing harm—just as they liked to take it. It was a pity they could not have him with them that eyening, sitting on the other side of the Mayor with a glass before him. (Laughter.) The Corporation of Warrington required their sympathy at the present time in its difficulties. The Town Clerk in his evidence the other day said War- rington would be obliged to spend over £200,000 in widening her streets. That was a large amount of money to spend on such an undertaking, but Warrington had been doing good work in widening her streets. They had a good Mayor in Alderman Bolton—(hear' hear)—and he (Mr. May) had no doubt he would meet the troubles of the Corporation and put things right. At any rate if he did not succeed in putting things right they must get a Scotsman to succeed him.. (Hear, hear.) If they had Mr. Monro or Sir Andrew Walker in the position of Mayor they would have good Scotsmen to fight their' battles. (Hear, hear.) In Alderman Bolton, the town had a Mayor who was straightforward, a man of the right sort. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the trade of Warrington, Mr. May said he had been engaged for the last seven or eight years digging in the earth at Wilderspool and discovering the ancient trades of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) There were iron and blast furnaces in Warrington from 1600 to 1800 years ago. He had also found remains of glass furnaces and there was evidence of spinning and other industries. Mr. May proceeded to refer to his visits to the principal works in Warrington and spoke of the grand order of system which characterised them and the beautiful , products produced. He coupled the name of thQ Mayor with the toast.

The toast was heartily drunk, and the guests sang "For he's a jolly good fellow "and raised three cheers for the Mayor and one for the Mayoress. The MAYOR, in reply, said he did not want all the sins of the Corporation visited upon him, but as long as he had anything to do with Warrington he should al- ways stick up for the "good old town." As far as the Corporation was concerned their predecessors in office had started improvements and left them half-finished. It was for the members of the Corporation to complete them and he had no doubt they would do their best. (Hear, hear.) They did not want to be hampered with all sorts of insinuations that they were not doing things straightforward and above board. So long asjhe had anything to do with the Corporation he intended that it should be straightforward and carried on in a proper manner, and if charges and insinuations were made he would see that they were ferreted out or done away with. (Applause.) Referriug to Scotsmen, the Mayor said those he saw before him seemed to be doing very well. Everyone was good enough to own a dress suit—(laughter)—and that meant that they had made money out of somebody. (Hear, hear.) If the welcome they had extended to him was a sample of their generosity and their way of doing; business it augured well for them. Under the presid- ency of Mr. Monro he felt that the Caledonian Associa- tion in Warrington would prosper in the future. (Hear, hear). With reference to the trade of the town, every Scotsman present seemed to be doing well and it would be superfluous to say a single word. All present seemed to be making money in the town and that was perhaps the best thing they could do. (Laughter.)

, "OUR PATRON—SIR PETER CARLAW WALKER." Mr. W. J. FORSHAW said he certainly aelt honoured in being asked to propose what he considered one of the most important toasts of the evening—that of their patron, Sir Peter Carlaw Walker. He had prepared no brief beoause Mr. Steel was entrusted with the toast, but he was unable to be present. There was no doubt that the name of Walker was a household word in the county of Lancashire and more especially in the town of Warrington and the city of Liverpool. They knew what munificent gifts both places had received at his hands. (Hear, hear.) They could not have a better patron and they hoped Sir Peter might live long to he the patron of the Warrington Caledonian Association. (Hear, hear.) The toast was drunk with musical honours and three cheers were raised for Sir Peter and Lady Walker, and one for the son who was born on St. Andrew's Day. "THE WARRINGTON CALEDONIAN _ _ ASSOCIATION."

The MAYOR pi:OWs-ed—t-ii;simportant toast. He facetiously remarked that until that night he under- stood the Associatiorfwas one that met once a year to eat haggis—(laughter)—to sing Scotch songs—(laugh- ter)—to drink Scotch whisky—(laughter)—and thengo home and get up next morning with a severe headache. (Loud laughter.) He now knew it was not so. (Laughter.) He found it was a useful institution. 1143 hoped they would drink the toast with the usual good- will, and that they would drink it for many years. The Association was a credit to the members and the town too. (Hear, hear).

div.head: WARRINGTON CALEDONIAN ASSOCIATION,
div.p: WARRINGTON CALEDONIAN ASSOCIATION,
Annual Dinner.
INTERESTING PROCEEDINGS.

Scotsmen in Warrington, in common with their kins- men in all parts of the world, celebrated on Monday the anniversary of St. Andrew, the patron •saint of Scotland. Under the auspices of the Warrington Cale- donian Association, the fifteenth annual dinner was held at the Lion Hotel and the function was a complete success. Much of the success was due to the energetic efforts of the President, Mr. Monro, who has done much to give vitality to the local association. About 60 Scotsmen sad personal friends gathered round the festive board, and the catering and general arrange- ments as carried out by Mr. Lee, "mine host of ye Olde Lion Hotel," were in every way excellent and left nothing to be desired. The room had been taste- fully decorated for the occasion. As a background there was a choice collection of plants and banners. On one side was a banner bearing the white cross of St. Andrew, whilst on the other was the Scotchensign. In the centre was the Royal shield, with a lion rampant. An excellent bill of fare was submitted. It was only natural that some Scotch dishes should be introduced and there were several which in name and taste were peculiarly Scotch. There were, for instance, such dishes as Cookie Leekie, Scotch Haggis, and "Haunch, o' Red Deer:" The haggis was brou4ht into the room to the skirl of the pibroch, the piper parading the room in typical Highland dress. The programme was interlarded with appropriate quotations, many of them Scotch. Drinkers of drams were reminded of the familiar line "An his nose is juist a sicht Wl' drinkin' drains," but this warning did not seem to have any effect on the demand for drains. At the conclusion of an excellent repast, a long toast list was submitted and some'interesting speeches delivered. The chair was occupied by Mr. James Monro, who had on his right, his worship the Mayor (Alderman Bolton) and on his left, Colonel Ridgway. The vice chairs were taken by Dr. Ferguson (vice-president) and Mr. B. Shearer (ex-president.) There were also present: Alderman Francomb, Messrs. J.; Hepherd, G. Dakin, G. Carruthers, M.A., W. Skinner, A. Browne, T. May, E. Parry, E. J. Parry (Liverpool), Dr. Leadbetter, Dr. Eades, W. B. Roberts, J. A. Ewart, J. A. McGregor, Councillor Forshaw, Alex. Neil, W. R. Neil, J. Neil, D. R. Hodge; G. C. Miller G. Bowman (hon treasurer), J. Finlayson, W. Chalmers, Carruthers, J. Hunter, W. B. Newman, J. Tennant, D. Reid, J. Farquharson, W. Mitchell, J. Banks, J. McDermid, A. Richardson J. Holt, J. Grounds, J. Whitlow, W. Houghton, J. F. Awbery, H. Singleton, T. Weir, T. J. Lee, A. E. Turpin, W. Gibson, Sergeant B. Williamson (hon secretary), Detective Barlow, Coun- cillor Maginn, J. Davenport. A. Booth, W. H. Payton, J. Podmore, F. Fieldhouse, W. H. Ireland, J. Sampson, W. Dowling, Stubbs, (Bristol), THE LOYAL TOASTS.

The CHAIRMAN, in proposing the toast of "The King," said that night over the whole civilised world there would arise to heaven the sincere and hearty wishes of thousands of loyal Scotsmen for the health and happi- ness of the King and the security of the British throne. (Hear, hear). Nowhere under any circumstances could the toast be drunk to with more cordiality and loyalty than in these little gatherings of wandering Caledonians, far from their native land, but full of a consuming love for it and fond remembrances of it (Hear, hear). Many hours since these St. Andrew's gatherings would have begun in the far east and the toast of the King would have been spoken to,and as the sun's rays reached the earth in the course of its revo- lution it would travel west till it reached us. They must now take up the fiery cross and toast it to the cry of "Here's to the King • God bless him" (Applause), Then when they had done that and that little patriotic meeting dispersed the cry would still go on. The toast would be given on board the Atlantic liners crossing the ocean. It would be heard in Canadian cities, in the cities of the United States, in shanties on the prairies and amongst the snows of British Columbia, until the whole globe had been girdled with shouts from thousands of British throats saying" God save the'King."(Hear,hear.)lKing Edward had already proved himself a worthy successor of his mother, of blessed memory. There seemed a cheeriness, a tact, an intelli- gence and a heart which had not only endeared him, if he might use the term, to the continental nations and to ourselves but had strengthened the respect for him and it must also tend to the security of his subjects and his country and to the whole of the British empire. (Hear, hear.) They all felt sure that King Edward would always exercise his kingly preroga- tive on the side of justice, of wisdom and of progress. (Applause.) The toast was drunk with musical hononrs, Mr. Fieldhouse singing the National Anthem which was taken up by the guests. The CHAIRMAN then proposed in felicitous terms the toast of" the Queen,the Duke and Duchess of Rothesay and members of the Royal Family." This toast was also received with musical honours, Mr. Fieldhouse singing a verse of" God save the Queen."
THE SERVICES.
OUTSPOKEN REMARKS BY COLONEL RIDG WAY.

Dr. FERGUSON proposed the toast of "The Navy, Army and Reserve Farces," and pointed out that at the present time when there was so much adverse criticism of the forces, it was gratifying to find an American officer paying a high tribute a the efficiency of the British navy in one of the' American reviews. Dr. Ferguson pomted!out that recent experience had shown us that we still had the same spirit and thesame quali- ties animating the services and if necessity arose they would carry out their work as they had done in the past. Mr. FIELDHOUSE sang" Reign, Edward Reign' and the audience joined in the chorus. Colonel RIDGWAY, in responding to the toast, said it was one that stirred every British heart. He was sorry that the fiscal question had somewhat overshadowed the question of army reform. That was rather a misfortune. He was not going to enter into politics, but still he wished the fiscal qUestion had been put off a little longer because he felt that the army was one of those burning questions that ought to be settled at once. Dr. Ferguson had spoken about the spirit of the army. There was no doubt the spirit was there, and wherever the Britisher had to fight he would try to do his duty. A book had come out within the last fortnight written by Lord Wolseley called "The life of a soldier." In that book Lord Wolseley spoke very plainly and he was very glad to see it. Lord Wolseley stated that in the whole of his experience, he had only known one good war secretary, and that was Lord Corn- well, who introduced short service, abolished purchase and gave us a reserve—a reserve which was of the utmost use to us in the South African war. The report of the Commission on the war was very sad reading. It showed how-we were deceived. Whilst we were led to think that Lord Lansdowne had got everything pre- pared for war. we now knew that nothing of the kind was done. Colonel Ridgway proceeded to refer to the treatment of General Butler whenhe was recalled from South Africa, whom it was generally supposed was to blame for not giving us information as to the prob. lability of war and what we might expect. The report of the Commission now revealed the fact that General Butler sent to the Secretary of State for War (Lord Lansdowne) a report on the number of big guns in the possession of the Boers, the number of troops, in fact everything that was necessary for us to be prepared. What did Lord Lansdowne do? He did nothing. The Army Service Corps requested that they might be given a sum of money,about £17,000, some three or four months before the war broke out, because they saw that it would be necessary to haul the waggons by oxen. Lord Lansdowne would not give them a penny. Three months later he not only found that he had made a Mistake but the treasury had to give out money in hundreds of thousands of pounds. Not being prepared we could not take the field. We could not attack when we ought to have done, and the delay caused us to require 100,000 men instead of 50.000. Lord Lansdowne did nothing that was right so faros he (Colonel Ridgway) could see. Referring to the treatment of General Buller, who had been given the order of the boot for making a few in- judicious remarks, Colonel Ridgway asked what had been done with Lord Lansdowne who had made many mistakes? The Government had given him a higher position. He had been made foreign secretary. If Lord Lansdowne only made half the mistakes as foreign secretary as he did in the Boer war we should very soon be "in a devil of a mess." (Laughter and hear, hear.) In referring to the strength of ounarmy, Colonel Ridg- way proceeded to refer to Mr. Brodrick's attempt to raise six army corps. Mr. Brodrick was told by.military officers that he could not do it, but he had tried and found that he could not get the men. In the army list four army 'corps were supposed to be raised but as a mat- ter of fact only two of them were at full strength. The staff had not even been appointed for the fifth and sixth He supposed Mr. Arnold Foster, the present secretary of state for war, would try some other means. Mr. Brodrick had failed. He did not know that they ought to blame him. It was a question of men. The army was in a very serious position. He believed Mr. Arnold Foster was going to re-organise it, but oolong as they had the army governed through a civilian he did not believe they would get the reforms needed. (Hear, hear.) •
"THE LAND 0' CAKES." SCOTSMEN GREAT WANDERERS.

In proposing this important toast Mr. CARRUTHERS referred to the tendency amongst Scotsmen to leave their native hills and go into all parts of the world. Wherever man had placed his foot the Scotsman would b a found. He had no doubt that when the North Pole was reached, there a Scotsman would be found and no doubt he would be doing "fairly well." (Laughter.) Scotsmen had been great wanderers through all ages. In an interesting Way Mr. Carruthers demonstrated this from historical incidents. He re- ferred to Shakespeare's lines— "lf France you would win With Scotland begin"
as illustratincr the part played by Scotland in assisting France in the middle ages when unfortunately the English and Scotch people did not understand one

div.head: "OUR VISITORS."
div.p: "OUR VISITORS."

In proposing this toast, lift.: J. L. -DAVENPO Rr spoke of the pleasure it gave the members of the Association to see so many friendspresent. Although Scotsmen had these clannish instincts they did not preclude them from extending their hospitality to their brother Britons. (Hear, heat.) The toast was heartily receiv.ed. and the President sang "Rule Britannia," which was taken up by the guests. Mr. W. B. ROBERTS responded in an excellent speech. He paid a tribute to the work of Scotsmen in helping to build up the British Empire, and in crossing the border to England, the Scotsman, he said, had educated us to things that we knew nothing of. In educational matters England had much to learn from Scotland. We were still wrapped up in denominational principles. Scotland had set us a noble example of educational progress, free from denominational and sectarian tests, and he was looking forward to the day when English education would likewise be free from them (Hear, hear). As Englishmen they welcomed the assistance of Scotsmen, and might the Scotsmen in Warrington live long to give us the benefit of their guiding knowledge and their intrinsic worth.(Applause)

div.head: PRESIDENT.
div.p: THE PRESIDENT.

Mr. SHEA.IZER then responded on behalf of the "War- rington Caledonian Association." It was fourteen years he said, since he and a few others started it. Its early career was a chequeced one and it was four or five years before the As4ociatioh paid its way It was now a very prosperous concern, thanks largely to the efforts of the President. The Association was not started merely for the sake of a social gathering. The main idea was to see if they could not help their brother Scots in adversity. They had succeeded to some extent in doing that. It must not be assumed that Scotsmen were never in adversity. Sometimes they were, and when they found any deserving case worthy of support they gave assist- ance. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion, Mr. Shearer pro- posed-the health of the President, and said Mr. Monro had been able to support the Association financially% and otherwise, and had made it a great success. (Applause.) The twist was drunk with enthusiasm.

Replying, the PRESIDENT said they did not want to make the Association simply a social institution, but they wanted to do good not only to their countrymen, but to those around them. Last year, by means of a concert they were able to make a donation of £l5 to the Infirmary and he hoped they would be able to do something of the kind this year. (Hear, hear.) The speeches were agreeably interspersed with musical items. During the evening a new song was rendered by the President which was much admired. The words are of Jacobite origin—"lt was a' for our rightfu' Kin" and the musical setting is, it is pleasing to note, by our townsdian, Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac. The pro- gramme of music was in charge of Mr. .1. L. Davenport, a rember of the committee of many years' standing, whose musical abilities have always been ungrndgingly placed at the disposal of the Association. Mr. Fred Fieldhouse in addition to ihe songs already mentioned, ,gave a vigorous ndering of "The Wedding of Shon McLean." re . Mr. IA . Ireland was encored for his flue interpreta.

div.head: • THE BY-ELECTIONS. RESULT OF THE POLLING IN BEWSEY AND ORFORD.
div.p: • THE BY-ELECTIONS. RESULT OF THE POLLING IN BEWSEY AND ORFORD.

By-elections to fill vacancies in the Orford and Bewsey Wards took place at Warrington on Monday when the candidates were : Orford, Mr. F. Stott, (Labour), and Mr. J. Rushworth (C), the licensee of the " Horse and Jockey"; Bewsey, Mr. S. Gough (Non- Trader), and Mr.Owan Toole (Liberal). Considerable excitement was displayed in both wards, and the helpers on the respective sides were not only numerous but energetic. Fine weather' prevailed—in fact the dry frost made electioneering quite a pleasant, healthy occupation. The circumstances of the two contests are soon told. In Orford Ward the seat left vacant by ex-Councillor Upson was fought for. Mr. Stottsecretary of the Trades Council, has been the labour candidate for some months and a contested the ward unsuccessfully on November 2nd. Since then he has strengthened. his claims on the electors, and was expected to have a con- siderable pull even over his popular publican opponent. In Bewsey Ward, the vacancy was caused by the eleva- tion of Mr. W. Pierpoint to an .Aldermanic seat. Mr. Toole was an entirely new aspirant to Council honours, while Ar. Gough, the Non-Trading nominee, was in the position of having fought the ward before. The polling booths and officials were : BKWSEY:—For district No. 3, the Mission Room, Hoyle-street ;and for district No. 4, St. Anne's School Dannett-street. The presiding officers were Messrs. A J. Willett and J. R. Williams, and the poll clerks Messrs. W,Sum ler and S. F. Welsby.

ORFORD:—In this Ward there were two polling stations. At one the presiding officer was Mr. W. E. Fowler, and the poll clerk Mr. J. D. Cannell ; while at the other station the presiding officer was Mr. H. Lawrence, and the poll clerk Mr. W. Taylor.

Result of the Poll. Speeches from the Town Hall Steps. The result of the poll in each ward was declared from the steps in front of the Town Hall shortly after half-past eight. The crowd was smaller than usual, but several hundred persons were present, although the weather was bitterly cold. Alderman Francomb (in the absence of Alderman Hutchinson) declared the result of the election in Orford Ward, and Alderman Fairclough the resulc in Bewsey Ward. The figures were:—
_ ORPORD WARD. Stott (Labour) .529 Rushworth (C) 449
Majority BEWSEY WARD.
Gough (N-T) Toole (L)

Majority The results were, of course received with the usual cheers, counter-cheers, hoots and groans. A fair hear- ing was, however, given to the speakers afterwards. Councillor STOTT, who was heartily received, was the first to address the electors, and he did so at consider- able length. He thanked those who had worked for him for the second time, and pointed out that they had had a long fight. He had been before the electors for four months and had fought almost night and day. They had had enthusiasm but, no experience, but he must admit that they had had the assistance of a few work- ing men who were acting as pioneers of the Labour movement in Warrington. They had made a beginning and they intended to go on to the end. (Applause.) Now that they had made a start he asked the working men to stand by them. They had seenktot what could be accom- plished by a few workers, but what could be done by many? A lesson had, in fact been given to the working men of Warrington. A lead had been shown to them, a straight lead, an honest and independent lead, and the result was that the Labour party had at last been successful. Theyhad seen the action of certain individuals who had aspired to municipal honours. Their wavering had been their downfall, whilst the independance and firmness of the Labour party had resulted in success. (Cheers.) He , hoped the present victory would be an object lesson to all working men interested in labour politics. ' Liberalism and Toryism would not effect the salvation of the working classes; that could only be done by a ' united Labour party. (Cheers.) For eight or nine years they had been striving as a Labour party and that *day they had beaten all. He complimented his opponent, Mr. Rushworth, with whom he was on the best of terms. Though he was a Conservative, he believed he would make a better Town Councillor than many who had been returned to the. Council. He was a thorough gentleman and courteous. (Cheers.) Councillor GOUGH, thanked the workers for the noble stand they had taken in upholding the Non-traders. They needed encouragement. He was glad Mr. Stott had been returned because he was a Labour representa- tive. (A Voice : Why did you oppose him last time?" and cheers.) He thanked every worker for his assist- ance that day. "NOT CREDITABLE TO THE NON-TRADERS." Mr. TOOLE was warmly cheered by his supporters. He thanked the 315 electors who had voted for him. Mr. Stott had said he had been in his ward four months but he (the speaker) had only been canvassing four days Yet he had been defeated by only 50, and that was • small margin. (Hear, hear). He contended that the Non-traders had adopted tactics that day that, were not creditable to them. (Cheers, and hissos). He had nothing to say personally against the leaders, but he had against some of the followers, some of the hench- men. He was "going again for Bewsey." He obtained 315 votes in four days; in four weeks he would get three times the number of votes. (Cheers.) i" PURITY AND PURITY ONLY." Councillor DODDS said he congratulated all those present upon the election in both wards. (Hooting and cheers.) He had supported Mr. Stott from the beginning—(hear, hear)—and Mr. Stott was present to say so. He had supported Mr Gough and he (Conn- cillor'Dodds) thankod the electors for the greatest victory they had yet had, because Mr. Stott was a sound Non-trader as well as Mr. Gough. (A Voice : " don't think so" and" What about the last election ?" (Laughter and cheers.)' Well, he did all he could for Mr. Stott at the last election, everyone knew he did. Every- one in Warrington Knew that. (Hear, hear.) He was more proud thatthey had returned a labour candidate in the person of Mr. Stott than irthey had returned him as a Non-trader. He was in favourof the Labour party, and should do all he could for it. • If they brought a man out at the general election he would support him if he was a labour man and a progressive. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He (Councillor Dodds) had been suffering from what was called a "swelled head." (Laughter.) His head was certainly swollen a good deal that night, and it was bigger than it was since he first heard of the result of the election that night.He would tell themthis —that if there had been anything donelthat was improper by the Non-trading party he should go dead against it, and oppose it as much as if it were done by any other party.(Hear. hear.)He WftS for purityland purity only,and if the Liberal party, the Tory party, the Non-trading party, or the Labour party adopted tactics which were wrong. unjust, illegal and immoral, he should denounce them all. (Hear, hear.) He thanked the electors once more for having returned the two men he had named; they were both good men and true men. (Cheers).

div.head: AT THE LIBERAL CLUB. Liberal Leaders and Non-Traders Criticised.
div.p: AT THE LIBERAL CLUB. Liberal Leaders and Non-Traders Criticised.
Mr. Owen Toole's friends assembled in strong force about the Liberal Club later in the evening,and cheered the defeated candidate to the echo.

_ Mr. TOOLE said that, although he had not been suc- cessful he had not been disgraced. (Cheers.) He was sorry their candidate had not been returned, but he had only been in the field four days, and to do the canvas- sing in that time was a tremendous task for one practically unknown. The fight, however, had been a good one, and he was sorry for the brave and gallant band who had so loyally and faithfully workei in his interests. (Applause.) If they considered he was worthy to be their candidate on another occasion he would do his best for them. (Cheers.) Next time they would have a different result. They must not be dis- heartened on his account, but think only of the Liberal cause. He thanked all who had worked and voted for him. (Cheers.) There had been unfair tactics used on the other side. (Hear, hear.) People who had promised to vote for him had been prevailed upon to vote the other way, and he thought it was most unfair. (Hear, hear, and 'Shame.") Signed document a had, however, been left in the proper quarter, and he was prepared to withstand the expense of fighting the thing out if necessary. (Chem s.) Mr. INTER PEACOCK expressed his regret at Mr. Toole's defeat. They had been disappointed and de- ceived and unfair tactics had been used against them. Had it not been too late he would have been very pleased to have wandrawn his own candidature for the ward on Monday next in favour of Mr. Toole. He was determined more than ever that they would give the Non-Trading party such a slating that they would not dare to oppose a Liberal candidate again. (Cheers.) It was monstrous of them to do so. (Cheers.) Mr. JAMES Woons said he was heartily sorry they had not returned Mr. Toole. (Hear, hear.) He had been hoping for another Maginn majority. (Cheers.) He had known Mr. Toole all his life and looked upon him as a perfect gentleman. He hoped that when another vacancy occurred,Mr. Toole would be nominated (Cheers.) He did not think the Liberal councillors acted fairly to candidates. (A Voice : "They don't deserfie the name.") If the cap fitted them, well let them wear it. He was a staunch Liberal, but he did notibeti eve in mimic ipal'matters. He however, considAred it was a disgrace that leaders of the party should neglect to help a young man like Mr. Toole when he contested a ward. (Hear, hear and applause.) He knew for a fact that dirty tricks had been played

by the Non-Traders and hoped to see them crushed out. They were not a purity party. • (Cheers.) Mr. BARRATT said they wanted" truth, honesty, and purity." (Applause.) Councillor PEACOCK also spoke, and regretted the result of the election. Mr. Toole was a progressive Liberal and a business man, and he was surprised the Bewsey electors had failed to elect him. (Applause.) He hoped Mr. Toole would stand again. (Cheers.)

div.head: NEXT MONDAY'S CONTEST IN BEWSEY
div.p: NEXT MONDAY'S CONTEST IN BEWSEY
WARD.

On Monday, another contrist will take place in Bewsev ward. The vacancy has been caused by the death of Councillor Brophy. The candidates are Mr. Peter Peacock (Liberal) and Mr. James Dickenson (Non- trader). Mr. Charles Longshaw was also nominated as a candidate but he withdrew his candidature on "Monday morning. On behalf of Mr. Peacock Ntr. Arthur Browne raised an objection to the nomination paper of Mr. Dickenson on the ground. that one of the subscribers to the paper had no right to subscribe her narne,as she was a married woman liviftg with her husband. The facts were that this lady's name appeared on the register before she was married, but since the register was compiled she had married, and in the eyes of the law she ceased to exist as a woman whose name appeared on the register. Mr. Browne, therefore con- tended that this invalidated the nomination paper. On behalf of Mr. Dickenson, Mr. Wallhead, Mr. Pem- berton and Councillor Gough replied that the appear- ance of the lady's name on the register was sufficient to entitle her to subscribe her name to, the nomination paper.

the Mayor stated that on the advice of the Town. Clerk he thought the objection was fatal to the nomin- ation but he would not accept the responsibility of preventing the election. Therefore the election would be allowed to proceed. _ _

Mr. 13remne asked the Town Clerk if he would accept service for the Mayor if his client chose to go before a High Court and apply a mandamus to stop the elec- tion. The Town Clerk so id he would do so.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES ANO ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES ANO ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
By " Ovalist."

The gool. ship cVarrington struck a rock on Saturday at Bradford when the h. tvieit defeat of the season was sustained. A fourteen points to nil lick- ing looks pretty decisive, and it is, but Warrington were not so weak as the score represents. Everything went against them and it will take a large slice of luck to compensate for the disasters which occurred.

In the first place the weather was atrocious. It had rained about 30 hours before the miteh started and it rained'durino the Whole of the period of play. Naturally the ground, usually firm and fast, was -little better than a quagmire, and everybody who has followed the fortunes of the Warrington, team knows that they are at their worst under such circumstances. This was disadvantage No. 1, and then to make matters worse, two of .the heaviest forwards, Boardman and Cook, were debarred from playing owing to the work- ing clause. In any case Bradford would have been about a stone per man heavier, seeing that their lightest forward was a sweet morsel of some 13 stone 4 lbs. When they tripped on the field, one feared for the outcome of the fray so insignificant did the War- rington men look.

The Bradfordians used their weight for all they were worth and in the first quarter they put in all they knew to get Warrington beaten. The defence was sound- however, until Harris had the dis- gusting ill-luck to break his collar bone for the second time, tn. tackling Dunbavin. The latter scored a try and Harris of course, retired. Hardly had Warring- ton cleared their lines again before Isherwood was seen to be hobbling off with an injured leg, and a second try followed immediately. Warrington played the rest of the game with 6 forwards, and Morrison and Forster on the wings. The homesters also finished with 13 men, but, they had been at full strength during nearly the whole of the game—or at any rate until liTarrington were well beaten,and then a couple of forwards retired. It was really sur- prising how the Warrington men stuck to their work considering their decimated forces, and nothing but additional ill-luck prevented Fish scoring a try under the posts. Bradford did nothing very brilliant, but they won easily enough.

I have a bone to pick with those Bradford forwards They used their weight with: great brutality right through the game—even when Warringtota were a couple of men short. Isherwood was injured .by deliberate kicking during a rush—in fact whenever a man went down the !Bradford heavy-weights plunged over him like mad bulls. It was not football, and loud were the execrations from the Warrington sup- porters when Hallam was kicked in the back while on the ground near the end of the game. The homesters seemedto care about nothing but winning the game, and they will find a few things debited -against them when they visit Wilderspool on March 26th.

Considering the conditioas under which the match was played there was naturally not much scientific football. The Warrington backs never got more than one chance, and that was prior to Harris's injury; when Isherwood and Fish did some smart work on the left. Subsequently it was all kicks and no ha'nence. They deserve praise for dfine defence however. Davies too, was very resourceful and the was: he time and again dribbled the ball from behind his beaten for- wards through the Bradford backs was very clever. Broadley was playing half back, and he let Mahoney and Davies know it when he got the chance. The bulky ex-international carne down heavily, though, on 'several occasions, but it required a Boardman to deal with him effectively. Hallam again did magnifi- cent work' and plenty of it. On the 'other side, Gunn, the new full back, was every bit as good. In him the Bradfordians have made a fine capture.

The Bradford backs did not play a bad game by any means, and Dunbavin's two tries were the result of good combination, while Dachau took a lotof stopping on the other wing. He handed Fish off once in a way that must have surprised "the slippery one." Even in the rear Bradford are a heavy lot, but I thitik Warrington could out-play them under even condi- tions. It is by no means certain that Warrington would have lost but for the injuries to Harris and Isherwood, for the pace Bradford started off with was more than they could keep up. On a wet ground they were undoubtedly the superior team, and they played a game that suited them.

The victory meant a lot to the Bradfordians, for it put them well in the running for the championship, and they are now only a point behind Hull Kingston Rovers and Oldham. The latter met with a rude rebuff at the hands of Broughton, who beat them on their own ground, thus giving the Rovers the lead on matches played. Salford were also defeated at Leeds and they seegt to have fallen away considerably from the form which distinguished them at the commence- ment of the season: Runcorn have won once again, the return to form being coincident with the return of Jolley, the wonderful. His broken ribs have healed with a speed known only among footballers.
The league table up-to-date is as follows : For. _ Against.

The injuries to Isherwood and Harris are serious in view of the important match with Wigan to-day. Harris will ,be some six weeks again, or as he cheer- fully remarked to me on Saturday evening, he " will be ready for the cup-ties." Isherwood's leg is going on nicely and he should be fit for next week's match. In tile emergency the committee will do well to reintroduce Bate at half, and put Mahoney and Hockenhall in the threequarter line. It is not at all a bad side, and ought to be enough to give the Wiganers their quietus at Wilderspool. The fact must not be forgotten that they won here last season, and will make a big effort to do so again.

Warrington's probable team is : Hallam, full back . Fish ,Mahoney,Di ckenson,andHockenhall, th reequ a rters: Davies and It. Bate, half-backs ; Boardman, Morrison,' Edmondson, Swift, Naylor, Jolley, Thomas and Cook, forwards.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.

Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.--An Open Meeting, There was a large congregation in Wycliffe Church on Sunday afternoon when an open meeting of the P.S.A. Society was held, to which the lady friends of members *ere invited. The chair was occupied by Mr. John Taylor, L.D.S. who, stated that he believed the P.S.A. movement had been a wonderful success. Such large numbers could not attend the meetings without being benefited. The great object of those who conducted the meetings was to try and get them to lead better lives. It was difficult at times to live the Christian _

life but if there was any man bound by strict integrity it was the business man who professed to be a follower of Jesus Christ. The speaker referred to the import- ance of prayer to teach them His ways and to lead them aright. Mr. J. E. Balmer, of Eccles, delivered the address and made some homely remarks on the puzzles of life.—Mrs. R. IL Pearson was heard to great advan- tage in the solos "When Thy children fall asleep" and "Glory to Thee my God this night." The service, was also taken part in by the Rev. John Yonge and Mr. William Beswick, jun. A collection was taken on behalf of the P.S.A. funds.
The Compulsory Service Question. SERMON BY THE REV. J, F. MATTHEWS.

I At the Latchford Baptist churCh on Sunday evening ,1 the Rev. J. F. Matthews spoke upon compulsory mili- tary service. The text was" Righteousness exalteth a nation; but sin is a reproach to any people." The preacher said the revelations of the War Office Com- mission, instead of turning the eyes of militnry men to the insane •incompetency at headquarters, with its flunkeyism and red tape, to the old-fashioned methods and immobility of men who did not know their business had set them whining about home defence,deterioration of national physique, and the moral benefits to be de- rived from compulsory military service. In that pulpit during the past six years it had been his habit to view great movements, suggested reforms, and public events, in the light of the high ethic of Christ's teaching, and as he believed, the growth of the military spirit on the part of the nation was to be deplored and checked rather than applauded and nursed. He asked; " (a) What is this compulsory military service? (b) To what is it likely to lead ? and (c) On what grounds is it to be rejected?" Let him say at once, that no one was more devoted to the country's welfare and interests than the Christian patriot. He, quite as much as the soldier, night be trusted, if need arise, to spend his last drop of blood in its defence. The love of home was vety strong in all ages, the love of our liberties and free institutions equally so. They were not going I to be lost without a struggle, severe, and prolonged if I ever they should occur; but was that likely? They ; were told that this country 'was practically depleted of Hits fighting power during the South African War, and that they were left helpless, and at the mercy of their I enemies. What then? Did,any nation dream of attack- ing our sea-girt island home? Were not the commercial interests of foreign peoples so bound up with ours, that to attack us in the very citadel of our strength would spell ruination for any one of them? The idea of compulsion was based upon our supposed insecure position. It was assumed that commercial rivalries created political combinations hostile to this coun try Take from our shores the fighting forces, aud we were open to attack on all sides. That might be so if we were always to have a Colonial Secretary who could not be surpassed for creating irritation among the Con- tinental neighbours, and whose hateful diplomacy was as great a factor in bringing about the South African war as the supposed obstinacy of the Boer President. The best security surely for the satety of this land was the attachment of the people to the freedom they enjoyed, to the real satisfaction and contentment asso- ciated with peace and prosperity. Two features in the situation were ignored: (a) The organic association of colonial life and freedem with the mother country ; and (b) the unrivalled power and easy mobility of the British Navy. What would it lead to ? • The National Service League said that apart from the desired advan- tages of "National security" there were indirect advantages. They were: (a) Discipline of the man- hood; (b) Obedience; (c) Self-respect ; (d) Cleanli- ness; (e) Punctuality. Surely we were not dependent upon compulsory military training for the production and maintenance of the virtues and qualities here referred to. All might be secured (1) by careful and systematic home training ; (2) by placing the boys—. when the time came for them to go to work—with firms where in the very nature of the case habits of obedi- ence, punctuality, &c., were cultivated, and it followed that the training of youths would crystallize into the normal habits of a disciplined manhood. From another point of view, it seemed to him that compulsory mili- tary training would lead to (1) a radical change in our relations to other nations. There was what might be called a natural cleavage between nations, die to differ- ence of language, customs and trade interests. Com- pulsory military training would lead to the belief that every Man not connected with the Empire was a prob- able enemy, and a possible invader of these shores. That he refused to believe The growing and strengthen-- ing relations between oetselves and Italy, Germany- and France, particularly through common interests in science, philosophy, literature and religion, were too valuable to be sacrificed by offensive aggression on the part of any one, or all of these nations together. (2) 'The complete subjugation of civil interests to military power. We would become a military nation, against which they must altogether set their faces. (3) A complete change in their notion of the value of human life and a lowering of the national ideal. What would be the effect upon lads at school, who were familiarized from the beginning with rifles and shooting and military arrangements? The national ideal had been and was still, one of life—preservation, not wholesale murder—an idea necessarily involved in compulsory military training. He did not object to boys being drilled, certainly not to a physical improvement, which any carefully graduated exercises might bring about; but was military drill necessary for that? If they wanted to improve the physique of the boys, that they might be a race of strong men, make a place in every school programme for gymnastics; attach a professional gymnast to every school with a gymnasium properly equipped ; encourage every school boyand girl to learn swimming, and institute boys' life brigades, where they had the best elements of drill without the hateful and baneful art of shooting. The abitrament of sound judgment,a careful weighing of arguments by a judicial tribunal were infinitely better than the arbitrament or, the sword. On what grounds were compulsory service to be rejected? Our complex commercial system would become seriously dislocated; the growth of the military elementwould mean the'curtailment of our civil and religious liberties ; the presence of the military element would inevitably result in unrighteous acts of aggression. Finally, why was this military cry of compulsory service made? It was dne to the loss of the notion that God was a living God, and that He ruled by righteousness and reigned in righteousness. He was looking forward to the time when the world would cease to be a great confederation of armed camps with its loathsome ideal of perpetual and burdensome armaments. He was hopeful that the day had already dawned in which they would see a decrease in our mili- tary expenditure, and our military and naval armaments, when all disputes between nation and nation would be settled by the wisdom of the wise, and not the folly of the fools, when swords would be no longer forged and rifles were safely stored in our museums, as surviving ' ' relics of our state of savagery and barbarism. He was I looking forward to the time when peace, not war, con- solidation of interests, not extension of territory,would mark our European civilization, when the nations should I live in the enjoyment of universal confidence and trust, and when, not the dream, but the reality of the ancient message was the practice of the world's life. "Glory to God in the highest. and on earth, peace, goodwill to. Yard men." •

MUNICIP BYR-ELECTION. TO THE ELECTORS OF BEWSEY WARD. DECEMBER Tra, 1903. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, Through the lamentable and untimely death of out late esteemed representative. Mr. John Brophy, I have been selected by the Liberal Ward Oommittee. to offer you my services to fill the vacancy. I am well-known to you.and am a Progressive Liberal, and a staunch supporter of the Working Classes. Any improvements for the welfare of the Town. and Bewsey Ward in particular would have my special attention if you honour me with your confidence on Monday December 7th. I regret on account of the short notice, my inability to personally visit all the Electors, but I may briefly state I am in favour of healthy Recreation tsrounds. end the one now under consideration which will benefit the Winwick-road part of this Ward will be pressed tor- ward until completed. In my opinion Free admission to the baths for school children should be allowed. Gas should be cheaper instead of the profits being transferred frum one depart- ment to another. The Tramway service is practically melees in this Ward, and, as you pay equal share of the eost, I should advocate a circular route to pass through Kerfoot-street. Folly-line, Lovely-lane into Sankey-street. also reduc- tion to ill fares on Winwiik road route. Being a large ratepayers. I should always watch the spending of public money, taking care to couple economy with efficiency. In all contracts the existing Trades Union conditions must be inserted The long talked of Enquiry should be proceeded with without further delay, and although I om not the official Non-trader, I am in sympathy with the principle. I have no interest in any firm doing business with the Corporation and have no axe to grind. My sole object in appealing to you is to watch the spending of your money, check any extravagance, and expose all irregularities. At all times I should be pleased to receive suggestions or attend to any comolaints. and if elected, endeavour to give entire satisfaction. The Election will take place on Monday, December 7th. I beg, to remain, Yours faithfully, PETER PEACOCK. 66, West-street, Winwick— road.

We should threaten Retaliation. The Protectionis t Government would not be intimidated, and therefore the Retaliatory duties would have to he imposed. Still the Protectionist Government would not give way— though they would by no means take it lying down,and would warmly and unpleasantly reciprocate the injury we were doing them. Thus the duties, imposed for temporary purposes, would have to remain, and would become permanent. But a retaliatory duty (a tax on a foreign import) while in force acts, of course, as a Protective duty to a particular home trade. And why, it would soon be I urged, should this particular trade be protected and not others? Other trades would thereforp claim, and un- answerably be able to claim, Protection would spread over the whole face of our trade and commerce. Yet Mr. Balfour says that his Retaliation is a step in the direction of Free Trade! The fact is that Retaliation, which sounds attractive in theory, and which appears fairly feasible in practice is found on analysis to be impossible of accomplish- ment, on any large scale, without 'involving the taxation of foodstuffs and of raw 'material • and without event- ually leading to Protection all round. ' The advocates of so-ca Iled Retaliation are really Protectionists in disguise, who know quite well that Retaliation is only the first step, and who have either a sneaking hope or a confident expectation that it will finally lead to Protection. The advocates of Preference and of Protection are more honest. They know what , they want, they say openly what they mean. Most of us would be prepared to leave considerable , latitude in the hands of a genuine Free Trade Govern- ment to negotiate commercially with other countries, and even to threaten reprisals. But to put any, additional power in the hands of a Government who declare by their chief that they desire to reverse lite Fiscal policy of the country, would be to place the keys of the house in the hands of the burglar.
